note: Both invocations name God as the one who conquered the five: the Kural's one who quenched the five sense-gates, Tirumular's ஐந்து வென்றனன்.

Both invocations close on the number eight: the Kural's எண்குணத்தான், one of eight qualities, and Tirumular's உணர்ந்தெட்டே. Tradition reads both as the eight divine qualities, though Tirumular's eight may also be the eightfold form.

Both make God the one with no likeness: the Kural's தனக்குவமை இல்லாதான், Tirumular's தன்னைஒப்பாய் ஒன்றும் இல்லாத் தலைமகன். The Kural adds that only reaching his feet ends the mind's anxiety; Tirumular adds that he becomes father to whoever calls him so.

The Kural asks what learning is worth if it does not bow at God's feet; Tirumular turns the test on the worshippers, saying that even those who can recite many hymns lack understanding. Bowing is necessary in one, not enough in the other.
Both rank the householder with or above the ascetic: the Kural's virtuous household life endures more than those who do penance, Tirumular's householders are equal to great ascetics.

The Naladiyar's wise, seeing the pain in pleasure, keep off the household way; Tirumular says those who stay in the household equal great ascetics. The conflict holds if 47's first line is a general claim about householders, not only those who keep the Lord in mind.

Both picture salvation as swimming a sea: the Kural's sea of births, crossed by reaching the Lord's feet, and Tirumular's sea of sin, crossed by thinking of the Lord and reaching the shore beyond pasu and pasam.
13 says the gods cannot measure the Lord; 14 states the result in a refrain, he stands beyond Brahma, beyond Vishnu and beyond everything, yet sees all.
18 has the Lord make Kubera lord of wealth for his penance and say 'take this lordship'; 19 opens on the same இதுபதி and gives another seat granted for true penance.
audit_text_issue: 19's விதுபதி may be a misreading; 18's last two lines are uncertain

note: Both verses praise (போற்றி) the lord of the four directions (நாற்றிசைக்கும் நாதன் / நாற்றிசைக்கும் நடுவாகின்ற நம்பன்) and name him by one deed, கூற்றுதைத்தான், the one who kicked Death. 2 is the poet announcing what he will tell; 2105, in the chapter of counsel, turns the same formula outward: tell his nature and be saved (கூறிநின்று உய்ம்மினே). The near-repeat shows the invocation's praise returning as the means of salvation.

3 sets those who stand at his side (பக்கநின்றார்) and do not know him against the poet who enters within and meditates (புக்குநின்று உன்னி). 1739 says that described in other words he stands beyond them, and that apart from the gods whose work is lofty speech he has entered my mind (என் மனம் புகுந்தானே). The later verse fills out the contrast: nearness and speech fail where entering the mind succeeds.

4 ends with the poet standing free of darkness (இருள் நீங்கி நின்றேனே) through bowing and praising day and night. Kural 352 promises the same removal of darkness (இருள்நீங்கி இன்பம் பயக்கும்) to those of stainless sight who have left confusion. The same phrase is reached by worship in one and by true seeing in the other.

5 says that search as you may there is no god equal to Siva and no one like him (சிவனொடு ஒக்கும் தெய்வம் தேடினும் இல்லை). Kural 7 names God by the same claim, தனக்குவமை இல்லாதான், the one with no likeness. Tirumular makes the Kural's title the outcome of a search and gives it a name.

6 says that without him there are no gods, no rare penance, nothing the three can do, and no way to enter the city (அவனன்றி ஊர்புகுமாறு அறியேனே). 1053 repeats the verse almost word for word with Shakti as subject (அவளன்றி ஊர்புகும் ஆறறியேனே), and the five in place of the three. The near-repeat shows the book giving the Lord's sole sufficiency to his Shakti in the same words.

6 knows no way to enter the city apart from him (அவனன்றி ஊர்புகுமாறு அறியேனே). Kural 8 says that except for those who reach the feet of the sea of virtue, the other seas are hard to swim (தாள்சேர்ந்தார்க் கல்லால் பிறவாழி நீந்தல் அரிது). Both state the goal as reachable only through him, one as entering a city, the other as crossing a sea.

8 says the Lord with hanging matted hair is kinder than a mother (தாயினும் நல்லன்) and near to those who love well. 116 uses the same comparison for what he does: Nandi, dwelling in the body as temple, removes the three malas more tenderly than a mother (தாயினும் மும்மலம் மாற்றி). The invocation's epithet becomes in 116 a description of grace at work on the soul.

9 says Nandi is the Lord whom the poet worships and there is no one whom he himself worships (தன்னால் தொழப்படுவார் இல்லை). Thiruppugazh 156 opens by praising Murugan as the guru who spoke the instructing mantra into both of Siva's ears (சிவனார் மனங்குளிர உபதேச மந்த்ரம் இரு செவிமீதிலும் பகர் குருநாதா). The conflict holds if being a disciple puts Siva below one he reveres; it softens if Murugan is taken as Siva's own form.

11 ends by calling great Nandi the rain-pouring cloud (பெயலும் மழைமுகில் பேர்நந்தி). Kural 11 says the world keeps going by the rain from the sky (வான்நின்று உலகம் வழங்கி வருதலால்), so rain is amrita. The Kural's praise of rain as what sustains the world becomes in Tirumular a name of the Lord.

12 sets the countless gods who are said to have died (எண்ணிலி தேவர் இறந்தார்) against the Lord who stays, and says those of earth and sky do not know he is the Lord. 762 gives the way to that knowledge: look within the things that pass with the mind fixed (கழிகின்ற உள்ளே கருத்துற நோக்கில்) and the thing that does not pass can be seen. The pairing turns 12's complaint about not knowing into a method.

13 says Vishnu, Brahma and the gods cannot conceive the Lord and no one has measured above him (மேலளந்தார் இல்லை), alluding to the search for his top. 88 tells the story outright: Brahma and Vishnu sought foot and crown (அடிமுடி காண்பார்) and failed, and Brahma lied that he saw the crown. 13 uses the legend as a figure of measuring; 88 adds the lie.

14 ranks the Lord step by step beyond Brahma and beyond Vishnu (கடந்துநின்றான் கமலம் மலராதி, கடந்துநின்றான் ... மாயன்). 110 says the ignorant do not know the one great light stood as three and as five, and babble, dividing it into Isan, tall Mal and Brahma (ஈசன் நெடுமால் அயனென்று பேதித்து). If 14 is read as ranking three separate beings, 110 calls that division ignorance; if 14 means the one light exceeds its own forms, they agree.

15 places the Lord as the one standing within the body (உடலுள் நின்ற வேதி) as well as spreading through all. 3028 says that living in the body and seeking the light within (உள்ளொளி நாடி), one can see the god who dwells inside the body (உடலிடை வைகின்ற உள்ளுறு தேவன்) as plainly as the sea's waves. The invocation's claim at the book's opening returns near its end as something one can see.

17 uses musk (கத்தூரி), whose scent prevails over what is boiled with it, as the figure for kinship with the Lord that nothing equals. 1459 says the fragrance of Siva (சிவமணம்) has blossomed within the soul as scent dwells in a flower, and ends on the central post joined with musk (நாவி அணைந்த நடுதறி). Both make the Lord a scent that cannot be overpowered; 17's simile is uncertain, so the pairing rests on the shared figure.

21 calls the Lord the One who ends the flawed birth (ஊனப் பிறவி ஒழிக்கும் ஒருவன்) of Vishnu, Brahma and the gods, placing them inside the round of births. 107 says Brahma and Vishnu are not strangers to us but kin of Nandi, and you will gain blessing through those gods (வயனம் பெறுவீர் அவ்வானவராலே). 107 limits the downgrading in 21: born gods still carry the Lord's blessing.

22 says the Lord who rises in the mind knows what one thinks (நினைத்தது அறிவன), while people do not think of him and complain that the Lord has no love for them (எனக்கு இறை அன்பிலன்). 280 says the Lord knows what we have spurned and what we have gained (இகழ்ந்ததும் பெற்றதும் ஈசன் அறியும்) and returns love with delight to those who love. 280 answers 22's complaint: his love is given back to love.

23 says do not say he is not (இல்லென வேண்டா): the Lord gives grace night and day. 2558 says the world knows that those who say there is no higher state (பரகதி ... இல்லையென்போர்) go the way of hell. 23 forbids the denial and 2558 gives its consequence.

24 says the wealth is always Siva's feet (என்றும் சிவனடிக்கே செல்வம்) and praises those who turn back the deluded mind. 168 says that before favour, king, elephants and wealth pass to others, joining the one who is wealth (செல்வனைச் சேரின்) ends confusion and is the great penance. 168 gives the reason 24 leaves out: ordinary wealth leaves, and the Lord is the wealth that stays.

25 strings names ending in -இலி: பிறப்பிலி, இறப்பிலி, துறப்பிலி, மறப்பிலி (without birth, death, leaving, forgetting). 2941 strings the same form: உருவிலி, ஊனிலி, திருவிலி, தீதிலி, பொருவிலி, மருவிலி (without form, flesh, wealth, evil, equal, clinging). Both define the Lord by what he lacks; 25 ends in a call to worship and 2941 in his entering the mind.

26 says worship the one who follows you (தொடர்ந்துநின்றானை), who spreads through all the earth (படர்ந்துநின்றான்) and stands beyond (கடந்துநின்றாம்). 2643 uses the same three verbs: he followed me (தொடர்ந்துநின்றான்) when he tested me, spread (படர்ந்துநின்று) and, standing beyond (கடந்துநின்று), shows the way. The near-repeat confirms 26's கடந்துநின்றாம் should read as the Lord standing beyond.

28 makes the Lord the companion on the way (வழித்துணை) for those who bow. Kural 36 gives that role to virtue: do it now, for when you perish it is a companion that does not perish (பொன்றுங்கால் பொன்றாத் துணை). The same office of the one companion for the journey is filled by the Lord in one and by dharma in the other.

29 says the Lord has settled as the linchpin (ஆணியன் ஆகி) in the minds of devotees whose nature does not bend. Kural 667 says not to scorn people for their looks, since a great rolling chariot has its linchpin (உருள்பெருந்தேர்க்கு அச்சாணி). The small pin that holds the great moving thing is a person of worth in the Kural and the Lord in the devotee's mind in Tirumular.

29 makes the Lord the linchpin (ஆணி) in the minds of steadfast devotees. 2080 calls him the linchpin of the world (உலகாணி) and of the land in the five, and says the chief work toward him is knowing oneself. The same figure is used for the mind in 29 and for the world in 2080.

30 says the poet stands and calls his Nandi as a cow stands and calls (ஆன்நின்று அழைக்குமது போல்), wanting knowledge. 2446 has Nandi come like a mother rising at the thought of her calf (கன்று நினைந்தெழு தாயென வந்தபின்). The two complete one image: the devotee lows like the cow, and the Lord answers as the cow to its calf.

31 ends with the poet standing in the eye and loving him (கண்ணகத்தே நின்று காதலித்தேனே). 1505 says that for those who hold him as their eye (கண்ணவன் என்று கருதுமவர்கட்கு) the Lord stands held by great love (பேரன்பு பற்றி நின்றான்). Both join the eye with love for the Lord; 1505 turns it round, so that love holds him.

32 calls the Lord the one who fills the ten directions (திசை பத்தையும் மேவு பிரான்) and says no one knows his nature. 1451 says there is one supreme God in the ten directions and no direction where he is not (எத்திக்கு இலர் இல்லை), and turns this into refuge: take the shade of his feet and the sea of deeds will not reach you. 1451 adds what to do with the pervasion 32 praises.

35 says praise the Lord who is the way when nothing else avails (ஆற்றுகிலா வழியாகும் இறைவன்), and he will change you (மாற்றுவன்). Kural 7 says that except for those who reach the incomparable one's feet, it is hard to change the mind's distress (மனக்கவலை மாற்றல் அரிது). The Kural says the change is hard without him; Tirumular promises that he makes it.

36 says praise him in whatever way (எப்பரிசாயினும்) and you can win the Lord's grace in that same measure (அப்பரிசு ஈசன் அருள்பெறலாமே). 130 says however far one's knowing reaches (எவ்வாறு காண்பான் அறிவு தனக்கெல்லை), so far Hara gives grace (அவ்வாறு அருட்செய்வன்). Both build grace as an answer matched to the seeker, by the same எ-/அ- correlation, measured by praise in one and by knowing in the other.

37 says the Lord delights within the body and stands in the flesh (ஊனில் நின்று), and so it lives. 725 draws the consequence: once I held the body to be shameful, but seeing that the Highest has made it his temple (உடம்புளே உத்தமன் கோயில்கொண்டான்), I cherish it. 37's claim that the Lord lives in the flesh becomes in 725 a reason to care for the body.

38 repeats பிதற்றொழியேன், I will not stop babbling of great Nandi (எங்கள் பேர்நந்தி தன்னை). 94 says the same in the poet's own story: always I babble of great Nandi (பிதற்றுகின்றேன் என்றும் பேர்நந்தி தன்னை) and hold him in my heart night and day. The near-repeat makes the babbling a lasting habit, not one verse's flourish.

38 makes babbling of Nandi (பிதற்றொழியேன்) the devotee's vow. 2613 says there is no use sitting and babbling (பேசி இருந்து பிதற்றிப் பயனில்லை) about breath and the needle; cut desire and attachment (ஆசையும் அன்பும் அறுமின்) and the Lord's place is easy. The tension holds if both babblings are taken as speech about the Lord; 2613's babble is yogic talk, so the book praises one kind and dismisses the other.

39 places the light within the minds of those able to praise (வாழ்த்தவல்லார் மனத்துள்ளுறு சோதி), and says grace is won by praising and bowing. 1123 places the inner light (உள்ளொளி) of Shakti in the hearts of those who have driven out their deeds (வினைகடிந்தார் உள்ளத்து). 1123 sets a further condition on whose heart holds the light.

40 says that for those who can praise without hidden guile (மறைஞ்சடம் செய்யாது வாழ்த்தவல்லார்க்கு) the Lord enters and stays. 511 says none of the deceitful (கள்ளத்தினார்), however they mingle, know the One felt within the heart. One promises entry to the guileless; the other shuts out the guileful.

41 says the Lord dwells at ease in a heart made like a tilled field (புனஞ்செய்த நெஞ்சு) by those who praise. 1834 condemns those who carry loads of flowers outward but will not enter the sea of the heart (உள்ளக் கடற்புக்கு) and leave the sea of deceit; they sink. The pairing places worship's work inside the heart, with a farming image in one and a sea image in the other.

42 says that even if those who praise Hara come wrapped in maya (மாயகம் சூழ்ந்து வரவல்லராகிலும்), the king becomes one with them. 2421 says the Lord kindly feeds the soul through the maya he set working (பண்ணிய மாயையில் ஊட்டல் பரிந்தனன்), and grace is the means to his feet. 2421 explains why maya is no bar in 42: it is his own instrument. 42 is obscure in its first half, so the pairing rests on line 3.

43 says the Lord fills those who, speaking of Hara's feet, cry and weep (அரற்றி அழுது) and seek the Supreme's feet daily. 1552 says that if those who weep (இருந்தழுவாரும்) take up rare austerity and think of the Lord, he keeps them from suffering and there is no more birth. 1552 names the end that 43's weeping leads to.

43 promises the Lord's fullness to those who cry out and weep (அரற்றி அழுது) over Hara's feet. Thiruppugazh 1028 sends to Death's town those who never melt saying 'life of the Lord who shares his body with the woman' (மாதுபாகர் வாழ்வே யெனா நெக்குருகார்). The same melting devotion is rewarded in one and its absence punished in the other.
audit_text_issue: Tirumanthiram 43's உரன் அடி / நிரன் அடி are obscure.

note: 33 says even those able to recite many praises and hymns (துதிபல தோத்திரம் சொல்லவல்லாரும்) lack understanding and wither. 44 says gods, asuras and humans all say போற்றி, but the poet has set it to shine within his love (போற்றி என் அன்புள் பொலியவைத்தேனே). 44 names what 33's hymn-singers lack: the word of praise is the same, and love is the difference.

45 says this world runs only by ordinance (விதிவழி அல்லது இவ்வேலை உலகம்), yet by the way of praise the Lord of light becomes the sun showing the way to him. Kural 380 asks what is stronger than fate (ஊழிற் பெருவலி யாவுள), which gets there first whatever one devises. 45 grants fate's rule over the world and adds praise as a way it does not close.

46 ends with the Lord whose form is the intellect entering our mind (புந்தி வண்ணன் எம் மனம் புகுந்தான்). Kural 3 names God மலர்மிசை ஏகினான், the one who went upon the flower, which the commentators, as Pope's rendering shows, read as the flower of the mind. On that reading both place the Lord walking into the devotee's heart.

48 ends with the poet staying with the Lord as a lamp that does not dawn away (விடியா விளக்கென்று மேவிநின்றேனே). 1687 calls the inner seeing behind the strong inner eyelid the lamp that guards against the night not ending (விடியாமை காக்கும் விளக்கு). Both use விடி- with விளக்கு, one for a lamp that needs no dawn and one for a lamp that brings it.

48 holds to the Lord as a lamp that never dawns away (விடியா விளக்கு). Naladiyar 51 says austerity drives off sin as a lamp drives off darkness, but when the oil runs out darkness rushes back (விளக்குநெய் தேய்விடத்துச் சென்றிருள் பாய்ந்தாங்கு). The Naladiyar's lamp of merit fails as merit is spent; Tirumular's lamp is the one that does not.

49 promises that those who think of the Lord of pasu and pasam will cross the sea of sin and pass beyond pasu and pasam (கரைபசு பாசம் கடந்து). 115 states the doctrine behind it: pasu and pasam are beginningless like pati and cannot reach him, but when pati draws near they do not remain (பதியணுகிற் பசு பாசம் நில்லாவே). 115 explains why thinking of the Lord in 49 leads beyond the bonds.

50 lists what the poet will do: sing, scatter flowers, bow, dance (பாடுவன் ... ஆடுவன்), and says this is what he knows today. 96 says he does not know how to sing in the way of those who can sing, nor dance in the way of those who can dance (பாடவல்லார் நெறி பாட அறிகிலேன், ஆடவல்லார் நெறி ஆட அறிகிலேன்). 96 limits 50: the poet sings and dances without the skilled ways.

Tirumular finds all dharma within the Veda; the Kural makes the king's just sceptre the ஆதி of both the Brahmins' books and dharma. If ஆதி is read as support they agree that the Veda needs a guardian; if read as origin, the Kural places dharma's source in rule, not in scripture.

Both separate holding the Veda from living by it. The Kural says the Veda can be relearned but lost conduct ruins a Brahmin; Tirumular complains that reciters keep the six-limbed Veda but practise none of its qualities.

51 says the wise gave up disputation and argument (தர்க்க வாதத்தை விட்டு), recited the Veda and gained release. Thiruppugazh 1028 sends to Death's town those who learn books to quarrel and win arguments (காதி மோதி வாதாடு நூல்கற்றிடுவோர்). Release for those who leave argument in one, death for those who live by it in the other.

52 opens 'the one who spoke the Veda is not a வேதியன்' (வேதம் உரைத்தானும் வேதியன் ஆகிலன்); read as a general claim, uttering the Veda does not make one a Vedic man. Kural 30 says those called அந்தணர் are the virtuous, for their cool kindness to every life. On that second reading both deny that the priestly name comes from recitation; on the main reading, that the Lord spoke the Veda, the link does not hold.

54 says Vedanta teaches as one the single path of thinking of the Lord, the guru's path that is Siva's path (குருநெறியாம் சிவமாம் நெறி). 1435 distinguishes those who have seen Vedanta, holding Brahman alone real and the world false (பிரமமித்தியாதரர்), from Saivas, whose Siddhanta is not other than Vedanta. 1435 limits 54's claim: not every Vedantin reads Vedanta as Siva's path.

54 calls the holy path the great path beyond the sentient and the insentient (சித்தசித்தன்றி), joined through the guru's path. 2058 says the true guru shows the real and unreal and sets the sentient and insentient in Siva the Supreme (சித்தும் அசித்தும் சிவபரத்தே சேர்த்து). 2058 shows the guru doing what 54 names.

55 says no one practises the Veda's qualities as part of themselves; they make it yield gain (பேறங்கமாகப் பெருக்குகின்றாரே). 233 says Brahmins are truly such only when their purity comes from Vedanta's truth, and what lacks it is mere noise (கோலாகலம்). Both judge the Veda by whether it is lived, not by its use or recitation.

56 pictures men who keep no vows (விரதமில்லாதவர்), perform sacrifices and desire (வேட்டு விருப்பார்), and go where wealth is heaped to quarrel. 229 says Brahmins eager for Vedanta heard it and still did not end their craving (வேட்கை ஒழிந்திலர்). Both find Vedic learning and rite in men whose desire is unchanged.
Both end in நீர்மேல் எழுத்து, writing on water. 60 leaves open what is futile; 64 states the condition: Agamas without the knowledge the Lord declared.

The Kural asks what learning is worth if one does not bow at the feet of the one of pure knowledge; Tirumular says crores of Agamas are writing on water without the knowledge the Lord declared. Both measure scripture by what it leads to.

The Naladiyar says worldly books without the books of wisdom are only clamour that never removes confusion; Tirumular says even the Agamas, if their knowledge is missed, are writing on water. Both deny that bulk of learning is the point.

Both face writing beyond counting. The Naladiyar's answer is to choose what is fitting, like the bird that drinks the milk and leaves the water; Tirumular's is that the countless Agamas are hard even for the gods and their count is writing on water.
65 says the Lord spoke Sanskrit and Tamil together; 66 says what both teach, bondage, release and death, and that either leads to knowing him.
59 widens the languages of the Lord's dharma to eighteen; 66 names two, Tamil and Sanskrit. Both refuse to tie revelation to one tongue.

58 gives the Siva Agamas a vast count (இருபத்தெண் கோடிநூறாயிரம்) and says the poet praises their meaning. 64 repeats 58's first line word for word and then turns it: if the knowledge the Lord declared (அண்ணல் அறைந்த அறிவு) is not known, countless crores are writing on water. The pair shows the book setting up the Agamas' bulk and then making its worth conditional on understanding.

59 says the learned are those who know the intent (கருத்தறிவார்) of what the seers of the eighteen languages say, whatever the language. Kural 423 says wisdom is seeing the true thing (மெய்ப்பொருள் காண்பது) in whatever is heard, from whoever's mouth (யார்யார்வாய்க் கேட்பினும்). Both place learning in grasping meaning regardless of the source's tongue or speaker.

61 says the Supreme himself spoke the Siva dharma and Nandi stood as the Agama (ஆகமம் ஓங்கிநின்றானே). 2397 says the Veda and the Agama are the true Lord's scripture (மெய்யாம் இறைவன்நூல்) and both are his word (நாதன் உரையவை). The late verse states as doctrine what the preface tells as a scene of origin: scripture is the Lord's own speech.

62 traces the nine Agamas down a chain from Siva through Shakti, Sadasiva and the gods until 'our Nandi received' them (நந்திபெற்றானே). 67 takes the chain on from Nandi: the masters who received Nandi's grace (நந்தி அருள்பெற்ற நாதர்) are eight, Tirumular among them. Read together, the two chapters give one unbroken line of transmission from Siva to the poet.
Both open 'by Nandi's grace' and both say Tirumular sought Mulan. 68 credits Nandi with his name and his stay in the land; 92 adds what grace did after: he became Sadasiva and entered true wisdom.

72 has the Lord tell the four to keep the observances (நியமங்கள் செய்யுமின்) in all eight directions even if the flood rises. 557, in the chapter on niyama, lists what those observances are: austerity, japa, contentment, faith, giving, Siva's vow, hearing Siddhanta, sacrifice, Siva puja and clear mind. The preface's command gets its content in the yoga tantra.

The Kural says tapas should be striven for here, since it gains what one wishes; Tirumular asks why be born again when people do not strive at tapas beforehand. Both use முயல் and place the effort now.

The Kural's learned love learning more when they see the world delighting in what delights them; Tirumular wishes the bliss he gained on the whole world. Both make a private good complete only when it is shared.
70 has the four masters told 'may you gain all that I gained'; 85 widens the same wish from four disciples to the whole world.

74 says that after seeing the matchless dance in the flawless hall (மன்றில் தனிக்கூத்துக் கண்டபின்) the poet stayed seven crore ages. 132 names what those who worship that dance gain: the great attainment that does not part from that hall (அம்மன்றில் பிரியாப் பெரும்பேறு) and the fruit of not being born. The general promise of 132 is what 74 claims for the poet himself.

75 says the poet served the lady of rare austerity who is Bhuvanapati (புவனாபதியாம் அருந்தவச் செல்வி) and came with her in devotion. 1071, in the chapters on Shakti, praises the red feet of Bhuvanapati (புவனாபதியார்) who turns the deluded mind to the true thing. The title ties the poet's personal history to the Goddess the later tantra teaches.

76 says the poet stayed keeping a measured diet (மிதாசனி யாதிருந்தேன்) until he came to know. 556 counts little food (சுருக்கம்) among the ten rules of niyama. The sense of 76 is uncertain, but read this way the poet's account of himself follows the discipline the book later prescribes.

77 tells Malangan the reason he came: to tell the Veda of the holy dance (திருக்கூத்தின் சீலாங்க வேதத்தைச் செப்ப). 108 gives the commission behind it: the Lord says 'give our feet to the world' (ஞாலத்து நம்மடி நல்கிடு). The pairing shows the book as both the dance's Veda and the giving of the Lord's feet.

78 says the fine-jewelled Goddess cut off his birth and took him as her own (பிறப்பறுத்து ஆண்டவள்). 641 says the Lord, giving great grace, cut off his birth (பிறப்பறுத்தானே) after he saw the pure space. The same verb is given to the Goddess in the preface and to the Lord in the siddhi chapter, so the book does not keep release to one agent.

79 says the poet stayed in the shade of Siva's bodhi tree (சிவபோதியின் நீழலில்) reciting Siva's names; 82 says he stayed beneath the good bodhi tree (நற்போதியின் கீழே) worshipping. Both take the word for the Buddha's tree for the sage's seat, a distinctive borrowing that the two verses share and no other verse of the book uses.

80 says 'I stayed in this body (இக்காயத்தே) for countless crores' as part of his attainment. 725 gives the reason the body is worth keeping: once held a thing of shame, it was found to hold the true substance, the Highest having made it his temple (உடம்புளே உத்தமன் கோயில்கொண்டான்). 725 supplies the doctrine behind 80's claim.

80 offers staying in this body (இருந்தேன் இக்காயத்தே) for countless crores as attainment. Naladiyar 27 praises those who see the body as a bubble in pelting rain that forms and bursts (மொக்குளின் ... கெடும் இதோர் யாக்கை) and resolve to end their wandering. On the literal reading of 80's long bodily stay, the two set opposite values on the body's duration.

84 says the Father gave him by grace a body fitting the Veda (ஒத்த உடலையும் ... அருளால் அளித்ததே). 724 argues why such a body matters: if the body perishes, life perishes and true knowledge cannot be reached, so 'I nurtured the body and nurtured life' (உடம்பை வளர்த்தேன் உயிர்வளர்த்தேனே). The gift in 84 becomes a practice in 724.

86 says the gods, never forgetting Nandi, can recite the garland of mantras in their hearts (மந்திர மாலை ... ஓதலுமாமே). 99 promises that those who recite Mulan's three thousand reach the Lord, but only if they recite knowing the meaning (கருத்தறிந்து ஓதிடின்). 99 adds the condition 86 does not state.

87 says the Lord set fire within bounds (அங்கி மிகாமைவைத்தான்) along with body, worlds and the Tamil sastra. 365, in the chapter on the deluge, uses the same words for the fire he set in the swelling sea so that it would not overflow (அங்கி மிகாமைவைத்தானே). The preface takes the cosmic act of restraint and extends it to the poet's book and its meaning.

89 calls the moving and unmoving world the Supreme's imagining (தற்பரன் கற்பனையாகும் சராசரம்), from which Nandi gave release. 1947 says that when thought is cut off, cause and effect are all imagining (இவை கற்பனை தானே). The shared word கற்பனை shows the book using the same term for the world as the Lord's making and as what dissolves for the freed mind; both verses are uncertain.

90 claims to have explained in full the known, knowledge and the knower (நேயத்தை ஞானத்தை ஞாதுருவத்தினை). 2382 says that in the end the knower subsides in the known (அடங்கிடும் ஞாதுரு) and even the mark of knowledge departs into silence that is Siva's bliss. The triad the preface promises to explain is the triad the late tantra dissolves.

94 says 'always I babble of great Nandi' (பிதற்றுகின்றேன் என்றும் பேர்நந்தி தன்னை), babbling as the devotee's humble speech. 110 says the ignorant babble (பிதற்றுகின்றாரே) as they divide the one light into Isa, Mal and Brahma. The same word marks the poet's praise in one verse and sectarian error in the other.
88 tells how Brahma and Vishnu could not find the foot and crown of the column of fire; 95 turns the same flame into the poet's own confession that he does not know its root.

96 disclaims: 'I do not know how to sing in the way of those who can sing, nor dance' (பாடவல்லார் நெறி பாட அறிகிலேன் ... ஆட). 2093 (repeated at 2559) asks what gain there is for those who cannot sing (பாடகில்லார்) what he did, beside those who can dance (ஆடவல்லார்). The poet's modesty in the preface uses the very lack the later verse treats as fruitless.

97 says the Lord rises within sweet music (இன்னிசை உள்ளே எழுகின்ற ஈசன்) and can be known by contemplation. 31 says the poet loved the one who took to singing sweet music in melody (பண்ணகத்து இன்னிசை பாடலுற்றான்). Both place the Lord in music, once as the one known there, once as the singer loved.

98 says the sages and gods who praise apart do not know this fruit through devotion (பத்திமையால் இப்பயன் அறியாரே), on the reading that ranks tattva knowledge above praise. 284 says the siddhas never discerned the light, but to devotees who bowed in devotion (பத்திமையாலே பணிந்து) he stood before them and gave release. On that reading the two make opposite claims about what devotion alone reaches.
audit_text_issue: 98's last line is ambiguous, as the note says.

note: 69 names Kalangi among Tirumular's seven disciples; 102 makes Kalangar the head of a line through Aghorar and others, carrying the succession one generation further.

101 says Mulan spoke the Agama in nine tantras, three thousand verses (தந்திரம் ஒன்பது சார்வுமூவாயிரம்). 3046 counts the same work as three thousand Tamil verses, three hundred mantras and thirty teachings, and says the three are one (மூன்றும் ஒன்றாமே). The book's account of its own shape is extended from count to unity.
112 names one part of the Lord as the one who stands in the body and breathes; 116 makes the body a temple where Nandi has taken up residence like fire latent in bamboo.

104 says those who do not see the three gods as one divide them and quarrel through the world (பேதித்து உலகம் பிணங்குகின்றார்களே). Thiruppugazh 339 sets aside the quarrelsome sectarians (கலக காரண துற்குண சமயிகள்) who find no single way to end birth among their many texts. Both books treat sectarian division as a failure to see one truth.

104 says the three gods are, on examination, one in continuity, and only those who divide them quarrel. 2397 says of the Veda and the Agama that people call the two ends different but for the great they are not different (பேதமது என்பர் பெரியோர்க்கு அபேதமே). The same 'divided by the many, one to those who see' logic is applied to gods and to scriptures.

105 says the Lord stands beyond the two kinds of deeds (இருவினைக்கு அப்புறம்). Kural 5 calls him the Lord to whom the two deeds of darkness do not cling (இருள்சேர் இருவினையும் சேரா இறைவன்), and so they do not cling to those who praise him. Both define the Lord by his distance from the pair of deeds.

105 says those who call the Lord 'this' or 'that' (ஈசன் அதுஇது என்பார்) have no understanding. 1154 says almost the same words: not knowing him, people call him this or that (அதுஇது என்பர் அவனை அறியார்). A near-repeat; 1154 adds that they miss the Goddess's constancy.
audit_text_issue: Tirumanthiram 105: இருவினைககு has a doubled letter.

note: 106 says that from Siva come the three and the five and then bindu and nada, and all are Sankara's own name. 1776 lists Brahma, Vishnu, Rudra, Mahesa, the five-faced one, bindu and nada, Shakti and Siva as the forms the linga takes (சிவன்வடிவாகி). Both make the gods and the powers of sound forms of the one Siva; 1776 names what 106's numbers leave unexplained.

104 says the three gods are one in continuity and division breeds quarrel. 107 draws the practical consequence: Brahma and Mal are not strangers to us (நமக்கு அன்னியம் இல்லை), they are kin of three-eyed Nandi (நந்தி தமர்), and blessing comes through them. 104's doctrine becomes 107's attitude toward other gods' worship.

108 has the Lord commission the poet: 'give our feet to the world' (ஞாலத்து நம்மடி நல்கிடு). 85 is the poet's answer as wish: may this world gain the bliss I gained (யான்பெற்ற இன்பம் பெறுக இவ்வையகம்). The pairing joins command and response across the preface.

109 says that for gods and men there is no separate god (தனித்தெய்வம் மற்றில்லை) other than Siva's grace. 2104 says 'kin is one and God is one' (ஒன்றே குலமும் ஒருவனே தேவனும்). Both deny any second god; 109 identifies the one with grace.

110 says the ignorant, dividing the one light into Isa, Mal and Brahma, babble (பேதித்தவரைப் பிதற்றுகின்றாரே). 1986 uses the same words, the babble the divided world utters (பேதித்து உலகம் பிதற்றும் பிதற்றெல்லாம்), and says those who know themselves put it to rest with the sun. 1986 gives the remedy for the error 110 names.

104 says those who do not see the three as one divide them and quarrel (பேதித்து உலகம் பிணங்குகின்றார்களே); 110 says the blind divide the one light into the Lord, Mal and Brahma and babble (பேதித்தவரைப் பிதற்றுகின்றாரே). A near-repeat in the same chapter; 110 adds that the light stood as three and as five from the beginning.

111 says the one Lord becomes Vishnu and Brahma and, hidden, works dissolution (கரத்தினுள் நின்று கழிவுசெய்தானே). 2003 says he himself stands as Brahma and Mal and establishes things (தானே அயன்மால் எனநின்று தாபிக்கும்), and is the three lights as one. Both give the three functions to one Lord who takes the other gods' forms.

Tirumular's third line nearly repeats the Kural's: ஒருமையுள் ஆமைபோல் ... ஐந்து அடக்கி. The Kural makes the restraint a protection through seven births (எழுமையும்); Tirumular's version ends instead with those who 'heard both' (இருமையும்) and stand flawless.
audit_text_issue: 133 இருமையுங் கேட்டு may be a corruption of கெட்டு.

note: Both use the bird that drinks milk and leaves water. The Naladiyar makes it the wise learning only what is fitting; Tirumular makes it the parting that turns deeds into seeds that cannot sprout into births.

The Naladiyar makes guarding the craving that enters through the five gates the effort that reaches release; Tirumular says the five come under control of themselves (தானே) once one has met the Lord. Restraint is a cause in one, a result in the other.
The Kural says those who reach the Lord's feet cross the sea of births; Tirumular makes the feet the refuge, the path and the goal itself.
Both call the body the Lord's temple: 116 where Nandi lives like fire in bamboo, 725 where Tirumular, who once thought the body a defect, found the Lord inside it and so tends it.

The Naladiyar calls the body a stinking cart that only the ignorant adorn and praise; Tirumular calls it the temple where the Lord dwells. The conflict holds if கோயில் is read as giving the body worth, not only as locating the Lord in it.
1924 counts the thirty-six tattvas as they unfold from bindu and nada; 126 climbs the same thirty-six as the rungs of a ladder to release.
audit_text_issue: 1924: ஐ ஐந்தும் (25) + ஆறும் (6) + ஈர்இரண்டு (4) gives 35, not ஆறுஆறு (36); a number may have dropped.

note: The Kural counts sloth and sleep among the pleasure-boats of those bound for ruin; Tirumular gives the same words (சோம்பு, தூக்கம்) to the freed resting in Sivam. The Kural's verdict is on worldly duty; Tirumular names a state beyond it.

113 says the Lord came down, took a body suited to the disciple's deeds (வினைக்கீடாய் மெய்க்கொண்டு) and cut away the verdigris. 1527 names the condition and the form: when the two deeds stand balanced (இருவினை நேரொப்பில்) grace comes as the guru (குருவென வந்து) and the three malas end. The pairing turns 113's single scene into the doctrine of when and how the guru comes.

114 says the Lord, once the tarnish was cut, set coral in crystal (பளிங்கிற் பவளம் பதித்தான்): the red Lord shows in the cleared soul. Kural 706 uses the same property of crystal, that it shows what is set beside it (அடுத்தது காட்டும் பளிங்கு), for the face showing the heart. One image serves both a mystic claim and a courtier's rule for reading faces.

115 states the triad: pasu and pasam are beginningless like pati, cannot reach pati, and do not remain when pati draws near (பதியணுகிற் பசு பாசம் நில்லாவே). Thiruppugazh 1218 turns the doctrine into a plea that pati, pasu and pasam be set apart each from each without stain (பதிபசு பாசம் ஆனவை கசடற வேறு வேறுசெய்). The same terms pass from Tirumular's statement to Arunagiri's prayer for the discrimination it implies.

116 calls the body a temple where Nandi has made his home (மெய்யெனும் கோயில் இருந்து குடிகொண்ட கோன்) and is kinder than a mother (தாயினும்). 1728 has the same three words: the body taken as temple (கோயில்கொண்டு), the five dwelling there (குடிகொண்ட), the Master entering as if taken into a mother (தாயில் கொண்டாற்போல்). Both make the indwelling Lord domestic and maternal rather than the body something to despise.

117 says the sunstone does not burn the cotton around it except in the sun's presence (சூரியன் சந்நிதியிற் சுடுமாறுபோல்), so the malas end when the sun appears. 1653 uses the same stone: the sunstone that sees the sun takes the form of fire (கதிர்கண்ட காந்தம் கனலின் வடிவாம்). In 117 the stone shows that grace, not the soul, does the burning; in 1653 it shows the soul taking the form of what it faces.

117 ends: before the sun's appearing the malas are gone (சூரியன் தோற்றமுன் அற்ற மலங்களே). 2245 says the bonds and the three malas are let go by the ray that is Siva (சிவனான கதிராலே), the maddening darkness running off. Both make the removal of impurity the work of a sun that is the Lord, not of the soul's effort.

118 says the Lord made known that the malas are five and removed them by grace (மலங்கள்ஐந் தாமென மாற்றி அருளி). 2059 says those who bow at the feet of the Lord wither the five malas that well up (ஊற்றிடும் ஐம்மலம்). Both count the malas as five, against the more common three of 115-117, and set their removal at the Lord's side.

119 says awareness, caught in the five senses, was lost as if it had perished within awareness (அறிவுஅறி வுள்ளே அழிந்தது போல) until the guru makes the sign known. Thiruppugazh 714 asks for the knowing that knows within knowing (அறிவுள் அறியும் அறிவு) to see the feet no one else could know. The same doubled அறிவு names the loss in 119 and the gift in Arunagiri.

119 ends with the supreme guru making the sign known (குறியறிவிப்பான் குருபரன்). 2580 says those who do not know the sign (குறியறியாதவர்) of putting away both knowing and not-knowing cannot grasp Siva. Read together, 2580 says what the sign is that 119's guru gives.

120 says the guru makes what lodges in the fiery faculties into seeds that have touched fire (எரிசார்ந்த வித்து), so they cannot sprout into the seven births. 1964's riddle has a man who roasts the seed and eats it (வித்துச் சுட்டு உண்பான்), and so knows no harvest. The roasted seed is release in 120 and waste in 1964; the image carries opposite values in the two places.

121 says the Siva-yogis remain with the body as if dead (உடம்பொடு செத்திட்டிருப்பார்). 1907 says those who, still in the world, have died to the three malas (செத்தார் இருந்தார் செகத்தில் திரிமலம்) become Siva and are the siddhas. Both define the goal as a death undergone while living.

122 says Siva-yoga is to enter the yoga of tapas and become one's own light (தவயோகத்துள் புக்குத் தன்னொளி தானாய்). 1638 ends the same way: within tapas the light of the way becomes one's own light (தவத்திடை யாறொளி தன்னொளி யாமே). 1638 adds the means, the sword of understanding and the five turned back, to 122's definition.

125 says the siddhas have seen Sivaloka here and are stainless freed ones (நிமலர் ... முத்தர்). 2526 defines them again: siddhas are those who have seen Siva (சித்தர் சிவத்தைக் கண்டவர்), freed ones rooted at the root of release. The two verses, far apart, give the same definition of a siddha.

126 makes the thirty-six (tattvas) the rungs of a ladder to release (முப்பதும் ஆறும் படிமுத்தி ஏணியாய்). 2020 says Nandi made known the nature of the thirty-six and then stood beyond them (ஆறாறுக்கு அப்புறம் ஆகி நின்றானே). The ladder of 126 needs the guru's teaching of 2020 to be climbed, and its top is beyond the ladder.

126 counts thirty and six as a ladder to release; 154 counts thirty and thirty and thirty-six who live in the walled temple of the body (முப்பதும் முப்பதும் முப்பத்தறுவரும்) and run off when it falls. The same number names the tattvas that lift the soul in 126 and the tenants who desert the dying body in 154.

Kural 339 says death is like sleep and birth like waking from it (உறங்குவது போலும் சாக்காடு). 129 says that sleeping (தூங்கி) the siddhas saw Sivaloka, Siva-yoga and Siva-bhoga within themselves, and 121 calls them dead with the body. Tirumular uses the Kural's sleep-as-death for a sleep from which no waking into birth follows.

129 says sleeping they saw Siva-yoga within and Siva-bhoga within (சிவ யோகமும் ... சிவ போகமும் தம்முள்ளே). 1491 says both yoga and enjoyment come to yogis (யோகமும் போகமும் யோகியர்க்காகுமால்). 1491 sets out as doctrine the pairing of yoga and bhoga that 129 finds in the siddha's sleep.

130 says however far one's knowing reaches, so far the first Hara gives grace (எவ்வாறு காண்பான் அறிவு தனக்கெல்லை அவ்வாறு அருட்செய்வன்). 2005 calls him the One perceived as far as one contemplates him (உன்னும் அளவில் உணரும் ஒருவனை). Both make the Lord's self-giving measured to the seeker's capacity.

133 says those who drew the five within like a tortoise (ஆமைபோல் உள்ஐந்து அடக்கி) remained without flaw. 2158 has the five drawing in within the tortoise (ஆமை அகத்தினில் அஞ்சம் அடங்கிடும்) when the silent and spoken letter meet. In 133 the drawing-in is the seeker's restraint; in 2158 it follows the mantra.

134 says those who feel the guru's word beyond words, when the body falls, merge with the shoreless light like ghee mixed in pure milk (புரைஅற்ற பாலினுள் நெய்கலந்தாற்போல்). 2639 uses ghee in milk (பாலினுள் நெய்யும்) for the Lord present unseen in everything. The same pair names the soul dissolving into the Lord in 134 and the Lord hidden in the world in 2639.

135 asks where the conscient can go except to the Conscient (சித்துக்குச் சித்தன்றி சேர்விடம் வேறுண்டோ) once the five beginning with sound settle back. 1907 says what the dead gain is to join pure consciousness (சித்தினைக் கூடிடில்). Both name the end as the conscient soul joining the Conscient.

136 says the soul subsides into Sivam as salt formed by the sun's heat becomes one again with the water (அப்பினிற் கூடியது ஒன்றாகுமாறுபோல்). 2945 opens with the Father joining like salt in water (அப்பினில் உப்பென அத்தன் அணைந்திட்டு). The two verses use the same image for union without remainder.

136 has salt made from water dissolving back into it, for the soul subsiding into Sivam. 491 runs the image the other way: the subtle body dissolved in the Supreme takes form again as sea-salt crystallizes (திரைக்கடல் உப்புத் திரண்டது போல) and is born. The same salt figures release in 136 and rebirth in 491.

139 places clarity in seeing the guru's form, saying his name, hearing his words and thinking of his form (தெளிவு குருவின் திருமேனி காண்டல்). 2119 gives the reason: worship of Siva alone gave the gods no way to become him, but worshipping the guru who shows the way makes union possible (குருவை வழிபடின் கூடலும் ஆமே).

140 says the five senses come under control of themselves (தானே புலன்ஐந்துந் தன்வசம் ஆயிடும்) once one meets the Lord alone. 1638 asks for effort: draw the sword of understanding and turn the five back so they do not stray (அஞ்சும் போகாமல் மறித்தால்). Read together, the effortless control of 140 follows meeting the Lord, while 1638's labour comes before it.

141 repeats 139's acts point by point with Nandi in place of the guru: meeting his feet, thinking of his red form (சிந்திப்பது நந்தி செய்ய திருமேனி), praising his name. The near-repeat identifies the guru of 139 with Nandi.

The two verses share most of their words: the dancer in the skin bag who worked it and has left, and the indifference of what is then done to the body. Tirumular lists crows, revilers, milk drops and praisers; the Naladiyar dragging, careful burial, casting out and revilers.
Both build the body as a hut with two posts and one ridge beam. 146 says the life can't re-enter once the roof comes apart; 161 adds that it was thatched by a maker, not by ordinary thatchers.
The Kural says the world's 'greatness' is that one who was here yesterday is gone today; Tirumular shows it in a single evening: a meal, a talk with his wife, a small ache, and he is gone.

Both tell a death as a short row of ordinary acts: the Naladiyar's 'he stood, he sat, he lay down, he went', Tirumular's cooking, eating, talking and lying down. The Naladiyar draws the lesson to do good now; Tirumular draws none.
The Kural calls virtue the companion that does not perish when one perishes; Tirumular says that when the body falls only vows and knowledge go on the road with the dead, not wife or children.

Both take a king to make the point: the Naladiyar's kings under moon-white umbrellas were carried off and called dead, Tirumular's lord of the land rides a bier with the town behind and drums in front.
Both make the body a clay pot. 143 has it melt back to clay in the rain; 158 says even a broken pot is kept as shards, but a broken body is not kept a moment.
145 ends the funeral with the bath that ends remembering; 157 retells it with the kin turning back at the town's edge and calls those who bathe and leave 'people without justice'.

143 compares dying people to the unfired vessel that turns back to clay when rain falls (விண்ணின்று நீர்விழின் மீண்டுமண் ணானார்ப்போல்). Kural 660 compares wealth got by deceit to water poured into a pot of wet clay (பசுமண் கலத்துள்நீர்). The unfired pot that water destroys stands for the body in 143 and for ill-gotten wealth in the Kural.

143 opens: from one clay, see, two kinds of vessel (மண்ணொன்று கண்டீர் இருவகைப் பாத்திரம்), and one of them returns to clay. 440 opens almost the same way, one clay becomes many good vessels (மண்ணொன்று தான்பல நற்கலமாயிடும்), to show the one Lord in all wombs. The same opening leads to the body's death in 143 and to the Lord's unity in 440.

144 says nothing goes along the road with the dead but the vows they kept and the knowledge they gained (கொண்ட விரதமும் ஞானமும் அல்லது). Naladiyar 120 says nothing goes with a person but the deeds they did (தாஞ்செய் வினையல்லால்), good or bad. Both strip away kin and body; Tirumular names only the good companions, the Naladiyar the deeds of either kind.

146 counts the body as a hut, two posts, one ridge beam and thirty-two rafters, so that its collapse is final. 594 counts it as a house with seven windows, two great doors, a cave and a bedchamber (எழுசாலேகம் இரண்டு பெருவாய்தல்) where the held breath can make one live long. The same counted house is shown falling in 146 and kept standing by breath in 594.

147 gives death's cause as the store of deeds running out (செய்வினை மூட்டிற்ற). Naladiyar 3 says even kings under the umbrella fall when their deeds are exhausted (வினைஉலப்ப வேறாகி வீழ்வர்). Both make the end come when the karma that held the life is spent.
audit_text_issue: Tirumanthiram 147: சீக்கை and அலகு are unclear.

note: 149 shows the man who built a mansion in the square, rode a palanquin and gave away three crores, and did not turn back when called to go (சென்றத்தா என்னத் திரிந்திலன்). Thiruppugazh 1187 has the walled mansion and gold in the house (மாடமதிட் சுற்று ... கனக்க) until the body is tied to the bier and given to the fire. Both set public splendour directly against the bier.
audit_text_issue: Thiruppugazh 1187: the line on the hunter girl ends corruptly.

note: 156 says people, even seeing the dead man set down and left, think the wealth they seek will not leave them (அச்சகலாதென நாடும் அரும்பொருள்). Naladiyar 182 says fools think their household supports are secure and go heedless (பொச்சாந்து ஒழுகுவர் பேதையார்), though those supports only seem to stand. Both locate the folly in trusting what one has just seen fail.

158 has the potter shaping pots from the tank's clay; broken pots are kept as shards, but a broken body is not kept a moment (உடலுடைந்தால் இறைப்போதும் வையாரே). 443 has the potter shaping whatever is in his mind (குசவன் மனத்துற்ற தெல்லாம் வனைவன்), as Nandi shapes the world. The potter shows the Lord's making in 443 and the worthlessness of the made body in 158.

159 counts the body in riddling numbers, five tufts, six braids, thirty joints, eighteen supports, before it lies burnt. 2888 counts its tenants the same way, ten tigers, fifteen elephants, five skilled ones, sixteen entertainers (பத்துப் பரும்புலி யானை பதினைந்து). Both encode the tattvas of the body as a numbered riddle; 159 ends in the fire, 2888 in the assembly that sits within.

162 says the hall lies there but its adornments are gone and the dancing rhythm has ceased (ஆடும் இலயமும் அற்றது). 189 has a drum and two cymbals and a king within; when the king goes out the drum becomes clay (மத்தளி மண்ணாய்). Both make the living body a place of music that falls silent when the life leaves.

164 says the flame was taken while the lamp bowl remained (இடிஞ்சில் இருக்க விளக்கெரி கொண்டான்), and fools who do not know it is over cry out. 749 repeats the words (முடிந்தது அறியார் ... இடிஞ்சில் இருக்க விளக்கெரி கொண்டு) but turns them to yoga: those who can catch the flame may reach the goal while living. The near-repeat serves death in 164 and the yogi's practice in 749.

165 says those who do not worship the form of the one who made body and life lie in the seventh hell (ஏழா நரகிற் கிடப்பர்). 264 asks those who neither praise the Supreme nor give to beggars whether they will stand in hell (நரகத்தில் நிற்றிரோ). Both name failure to worship as the road to hell; 264 adds failure to give.

165 sets those who do not worship in the seventh hell, crying out as their entrails burn. Thiruppugazh 393 asks for Murugan's two feet so as not to enter the fire-mouthed hell (எரிவாய் நரகிற் புகுதாதபடிக்கு இருபாதம் எனக்கருள்வாயே). Tirumular's warning becomes Arunagiri's prayer.

166 says the time passed between with umbrella, horse and victorious sword (குடையும் குதிரையும் கொற்றவாளும்), and at death the life reaches its place, left or right. Naladiyar 3 has kings riding on elephants under the umbrella (குடைநிழற்கீழ்) who fall when their deeds run out. Both use the royal regalia to show that rank does not decide the end.

167 calls the body a nest (இக்கூட்டையே) the dancer has left, so what is done to it no longer matters. Kural 338 likens body and life to a bird flying off and leaving its nest alone (குடம்பை தனித்து ஒழியப் புள்பறந்தற்றே). Tirumular takes the Kural's empty nest and asks why anyone should care for it.

167 dismisses the nest the dancer has left (புறப்பட்டுப் போன இக்கூட்டையே). 2852 adds that if the nest perishes there is one who will make another (கூடு கெடின் மற்றோர் கூடுசெய் வான்உளன்), and that this is no loss to those who know Nandi. 2852 gives the reason for 167's indifference.
Both use the honey bee whose stored honey others take. The Naladiyar spells out the lesson, that those who hoard without giving lose it all; Tirumular gives only the image.

Both tell the rich to give their wealth away in view of Death, but the Naladiyar says no one has ever leapt past Death and escaped, while Tirumular says one who sheds his wealth may leap past him. The conflict holds if Tirumular's leap means escaping death; if it means dying free of fear or bondage, the two agree.
audit_text_issue: Naladiyar 6 has an encoding glitch: பிழைத்தெரிணஇ

note: Both use the phrase of leaping past Death (கூற்றம் குதித்தல்) as something attainable: the Kural through the power of austerity, Tirumular through letting go of wealth.
The two verses end with the same line (காட்டிக் கொடுத்தவர் கைவிட்ட வாறே): the bees' hoard taken by the strong, and the body left by the kin who raised it.
Both make wealth vanish without trace through a sudden image, the Naladiyar's lightning in a night cloud and Tirumular's capsizing boat; Tirumular adds a treasure in the body that does not sink.

168 urges joining the Lord who is true wealth while life lasts, before favour, kingdom and wealth go to others (பிறர்கொள்ளப் போவதன் முன்னம்). Kural 333 says wealth does not stay, so when you have it do at once what lasts (அற்குப ஆங்கே செயல்). Both turn the impermanence of wealth into a call for immediate action; Tirumular names the lasting thing as the Lord.

169 likens wealth to the moving moon that wanes greatly (இயக்குறு திங்கள் இரும்பிழப்பு ஒக்கும்). Naladiyar 125 likens the bond with the small to the full moon that wanes day by day (வைகலும் தேயுமே). The waning moon marks what is lost by its own nature, wealth in one and friendship in the other.

170 calls fools those who say 'this wealth is mine' (என்னது மாடென்று இருப்பர்கள் ஏழைகள்) though even their shadow does not help them. Kural 346 says one who cuts off the pride of 'I' and 'mine' (யான் எனது என்னும் செருக்கு) enters a world above the gods. 170 shows the 'mine' in action that the Kural tells one to cut.

171 has the bees gather honey and store it, only for the strong to drive them off and take it (அதுவலியார் கொள). Kural 1009 says wealth amassed without love, comfort or virtue is taken by others (ஒண்பொருள் கொள்வார் பிறர்). The bee image of 171 is the Kural's maxim made a scene.

172 says give away your wealth and when Death comes you may even leap past him (கூற்றன் வருங்கால் குதிக்கலும் ஆமே). Naladiyar 5 says those who gave first will escape the waste land through which Death drags his captives (முன்னே கொடுத்தார் உயப்போவர்). Both promise escape from Death through giving, while Naladiyar 6, already linked, denies that anyone leapt Death.

172 opens: be clear and settled, once clear do not be troubled (தேற்றத் தெளிமின் தெளிந்தீர் கலங்கன்மின்). 1533 has the same call: be clear, become settled, then enter without wavering (தேறுமின் தேறித் தெளிமின் தெளிந்தபின் மாறுதல் இன்றி). The formula applies to wealth in 172 and to the six sects in 1533.

174 says a helper who answers when called may come to those who share out the bright wealth that comes to them (விரிவுசெய் வார்கட்குக் கூவும் துணையொன்று கூடலுமாமே). Kural 525 says one who can give and speak sweetly is surrounded by kin layer on layer (கொடுத்தலும் இன்சொலும் ... சுற்றத்தால் சுற்றப்படும்). Both make giving the way to gain support.

175 ends 'this is how those who showed it gave it up' (காட்டிக் கொடுத்தவர் கைவிட்ட வாறே), the line 171 also ends with. 2933, in the riddle chapter, ends with the same line after the fallen mango that calling the jackal cannot save. The near-repeat line closes three verses on things let go.

175 says there is one post to tie to and nine ways out (பூட்டுந் தறியொன்று போம்வழி ஒன்பது). 2025 has one herdsman with a staff and nine ways by which the senses come and go (போம்வழி ஒன்பது). The nine openings of the body are exits for the life in 175 and roads for the senses in 2025.

176 opens with the life leaving the body (உடம்போடு உயிரிடை விட்டோடும் போது), almost the Kural's words for the bond of body and life (உடம்பொடு உயிரிடை நட்பு) in 338. The Kural ends on the bird gone; 176 adds that thinking of the Lord keeps Death's messengers from burning the life.
Both read the sun's daily course as a measure of passing life: the Naladiyar urges help to others before one's days run out, Tirumular faults those who see the sun set and do not understand.
In the Naladiyar Death uses the sun as a measure to eat one's days; in Tirumular the sun and moon measure out the world from within. Both make the heavenly lights the counters of a life.

The Naladiyar says not to put off good deeds because one is young; Tirumular says to hold to Nandi while life lasts, since youth and strength wear away. The urgency is the same, the act urged differs.
The Naladiyar warns men not to desire a woman who will one day stoop over a staff; Tirumular turns the lesson on the man, who was cane to women and is now bitter fruit.

178 says that through the long years none have known the flame of the raised-wick lamp (தூண்டு விளக்கின் சுடர் அறியாரே). 602 tells how to tend that lamp: light the lamp of the mind, press down the lamp of anger, raise every wick alike (திரியொக்கத் தூண்ட), and the mind's lamp becomes a lamp that does not die. The trimmed wick that 178 says goes unseen is in 602 the practice of meditation.

179 says that once youth has worn away and the strength for hard deeds is gone it is late, so hold to Nandi while life is still in you (உயிருள்ள போதே). Kural 335 sets the same deadline in the body, before the hiccup rises and stops the tongue (நாச்செற்று விக்குள்மேல் வாராமுன்), for doing good. The two set one urgency, worship in Tirumular and good deeds in the Kural, against the same failing of the body.

181 names the stages child, youth and old man (பாலன் இளையன் விருத்தன்) and says people see them pass yet do not understand, while the poet lies at the Lord's feet. Thiruppugazh 1068 walks the same course from one mother's womb through youth to wheezing old age (இளையா விருத்த பரிதாபமுற்று) and asks, before death, for a life of saying 'Muruga' with love. The bare list of stages in 181 becomes in Arunagiri a prayer timed against them.

182 says that for those who rise each morning evening falls and the life span passes (மாலை படுவதும் வாணாள் கழிவதும்). Kural 334 says the thing that shows itself as a day is a blade sawing through life (நாளென ஒன்றுபோற் காட்டி உயிர் ஈரும் வாளது). Both make the ordinary day the measure of life lost; 182 adds that the Lord gives joy to those who think of him fittingly.

183's riddle has five thick needles in one bag, and when frost falls on them the needle bag itself flies off (பருவூசிப் பையும் பறக்கின்ற வாறே). Kural 338 makes the bond of body and life a bird flying off and leaving its nest alone (குடம்பை தனித்தொழியப் புள்பறந் தற்றே). Both picture death as a flight from a container; in the Kural the life flies and the nest stays, in 183 the bag of the body goes with it.

185 says the base do not reflect, so harsh Death puts them in the womb-pit (காலன் கருக்குழி வைத்தபின்) and they fall into it again. Thiruppugazh 301 asks not to fall face down into every womb-pit (கருக்குழி தோறுங் கவிழாதே) but to be given the art of singing the feet's praise. Tirumular's statement of the fall becomes Arunagiri's prayer against it, in the same word.

186 repeats 'in the days you have' (எய்திய நாளில்) and urges praising the Lord in song so that youth does not pass in vain. Kural 38 says that if one does good so that no day falls away (வீழ்நாள் படாஅமை) it is a stone that blocks the road of one's days. Both count the days one by one; the Kural fills them with good deeds, 186 with sung praise.
The Kural says hunger never touches one used to sharing his food; Tirumular asks for a ladleful given before each good meal, the same habit in its smallest form.

Both make shared food the right use of plenty: the Naladiyar tells one who gains wealth to eat with many from that day, since wealth turns like a cart wheel; Tirumular asks for a ladleful before one eats.
In 167 the dancer leaves the skin bag, in 189 the king leaves the drum and it turns to clay. Both make the life a performer or ruler inside an instrument that is nothing once he goes.
151 has the five who ate rice with ghee depart at death; 188 makes the five guardians of a field who abandon it when their master's summons comes.
Both say people do not understand that the sun measures out their lives, using the same verb (அளக்கின்றது) and the same complaint (அறிகிலார்).
audit_text_issue: 191 line 4 (பொன்றுணர்வாரிற் புணர்க்கின்ற மாயமே) is hard to construe

note: Both take grey hair as the sign to heed: the Naladiyar's wise renounced in childhood knowing it would come, Tirumular faults those who see black hair turn white and still do not grasp it.

187 says that all that grows on the branch with red shoots and cool flowers (செந்தளிர்த் தண்மலர்க் கொம்பில்) comes to die, yet people do not praise the Lord's feet. Naladiyar 17 says youth falls as fruit drops from every tree in the dewy grove (கனியுதிர்ந்து வீழ்ந்தற்று இளமை), so do not desire her spear eyes. One image of the tree shedding what grew on it serves two lessons: worship in Tirumular, turning from desire in the Naladiyar.

193 says there is one measure of rice for the pot and fire for the hearth, give out the rice before it burns too close (அடுத்தெரியாமல் கொடுமின் அரிசி), for the days let go are gone. Thiruppugazh 858 tells the life of a miser who would not let a husk fall (அணுவளவு தவிடு), drove off the ascetic asking for food, and ended on the pyre. 858 is the life that ignored 193's command, told to its end in the fire.

194 begins with the bee that delights here and goes to clusters of flowers to drink scented honey (இன்புறு வண்டு ... உண்பது வாச மது) as a figure for the state of the life. 2097 opens with the same bee delighting among honeyed flowers (இன்புற வண்டு) and says no one knows the honey that enters the mouth unsought. In both the bee's honey-seeking points to an inner sweetness that ordinary seeking does not hold.

195 says: considering how the earth must pass, do good (அறஞ்செய்மின்) and praise the Pure One. Kural 36 says do good without putting it off, for when you perish it is a companion that does not perish (பொன்றுங்கால் பொன்றாத் துணை). Both ground the call to virtue in the certainty of passing.
Both rank not killing above ritual offering: the Kural above a thousand oblations of ghee, Tirumular as the brightest of the flowers of worship.

Both say killing is paid for after this life, but differently: the Kural through rebirth in a wretched, diseased body, Tirumular through hell; and Tirumular extends the guilt to those who only urged the killing.
Both send the flesh-eater to hell; the Kural says hell's mouth will not open to let him out, Tirumular describes his being flung into fire-mouthed hell.
Both make eating creatures a deed that returns on the eater; the Naladiyar's crab-eater gets a wasting disease in a later life, Tirumular's flesh-eater hell.

200 lists killing, theft, lust and lying (கொலையே களவுகள் காமம் பொய்கூறல்) as mountain-sized sins whose giving up leads to Siva's feet and the bliss of knowledge. 554, in the chapter on yama, defines the one who stands in it as not killing, not lying, not stealing (கொல்லான் பொய் கூறான் களவிலான்) and without drink or lust. The same list, here a set of sins, there becomes the first limb of yoga.

200 says those who give up killing, theft, lust and lying reach Siva's feet. Thiruppugazh 124 shows the other side: men who think the body lasting, steal, lie and kill (களவுபொய் கொலைகள் ஆடி) fall into Death's hell and are born again in the sea of two deeds. The same three sins decide the road in both, upward in Tirumular, downward in Arunagiri.
Both argue from the wife already at home: the Naladiyar asks why a man with a loving wife looks at another's, Tirumular calls it leaving ripe jackfruit for a wild date.
Both end the adulterer with a lost leg: in the Naladiyar the leg is cut off as the king's punishment if he is caught, in Tirumular he breaks it falling from the sour mango he climbed.

203 says even the man who has grasped the meaning, those who command knowledge and those holding the light in the dark are infatuated with bewildering women (மருள்கொண்ட மாதர் மயலுறுவார்கள்). Thiruppugazh 641 describes women who bring under their bodies' power even those on the paths of chariyai, kiriyai and yoga (சரியைக்ரியை யோகத்தின் வழிவருக்கு). Both say the spiritual path itself gives no protection against this pull.
Both say a woman's attractive surface hides what should repel: the Naladiyar the body's foulness under the skin, Tirumular poison under fair leaves and fruit.
Both shrink the adulterer's pleasure: small against great fear in the Naladiyar, a dream and a whirlpool in Tirumular.
Both describe a woman who promises closeness and then turns away; the Naladiyar's said she would never part, Tirumular's bids the man stay near and leaves talking to others.

Both use sugarcane to show sweetness changing over time: the Naladiyar's cane eaten from the tip grows sweeter like the friendship of the learned, Tirumular's cane juice in the hand turns to neem in the body.
audit_text_issue: naladiyar:138 line 3 'துரி஢ன்தின்' contains a stray character.

note: 205 says the pleasure of the man who enters another's home seeps up like a dream and cannot be had as things are had awake (கனவது போலக் ... நனவது போலவும் நாடவொண்ணாதே). In Kural 1215 the woman sets waking and dream side by side and finds each sweet when seen (நனவினால் கண்டதூஉம் ... கனவுந்தான்). The same dream and waking pair, which the Kural uses to make the dream equal to waking, 205 uses to show the stolen pleasure is no more than a dream.

208 likens weak-willed conduct to wading to the middle of a moss-covered pond to sound its depth (குளமூடு பாசியில் ஆழ நடுவர்). 1506 says the mind of those who only recite and gather flowers is a stone dropped in a mossy pond (பாசிக் குளத்தில்வீழ் கல்). Tirumular uses the moss-covered pond twice for a mind that sinks out of sight, once in lust and once in empty ritual.
Both say kin and dependants fall away from the poor: the Naladiyar's crows leave the carcass and no one asks 'are you well?', Tirumular's dependants turn unloving.
Both describe the poor man estranged from those closest to him; the Kural goes as far as his own mother.
Both say what can never be filled is ended not by filling it but by removing its cause: craving in the Kural, impurity in Tirumular. This depends on reading the pit as desire and not only the belly.
Both treat ties as obstacles to ending births: the Kural asks why one bent on that would keep other ties when even the body is excess, Tirumular calls clinging kin worse than deeds.
Both name the five senses as what must be overcome; the Kural says their domain must be crushed, Tirumular describes the suffering they cause until one turns to the Lord.

211 is a near-repeat of 210: people seek gold to fill the pit, and the pit fills only as impurity goes (அக்குழி தூரும் அழுக்கற்ற வாறே). 210 ends with the same line on the pit filled when impurity is gone, but its remedy is to praise the Lord; 211's is to know the understanding that fills it (அக்குழி தூர்க்கும் அறிவை அறிந்தபின்). Read together, the pair offers worship and knowledge as two routes to one cure.
Tirumular praises the oblation as sustaining sky, earth and gods; the Kural ranks not killing above a thousand oblations. Read together, the rite keeps its worth but not the first place.
If புறங்கொடுத்து உண்ணுவர means eating after giving, both describe the worthy as feeding others first and eating after.

220 says those who know great wealth to be ruin (பெருஞ்செல்வம் கேடென்று) keep to the oblation as the rare wealth (அருஞ்செல்வத்து ஆகுதி). Kural 241 ranks the wealth of grace as the wealth among wealths (அருட்செல்வம் செல்வத்துள் செல்வம்), since goods are found even among the base. Both keep the word செல்வம் and move it from goods to something else: the fire rite in Tirumular, kindness in the Kural.

221 calls the Lord the bright flame who dwells in the heart and is also the cool flame that heads the fire offering (தண்சுடர் ஓமத் தலைவன்). 1565 names him the one whose sign in the Brahmins' Veda is fire (வேதியர் வேதத்து அனற்குறியாளன்) and whose sign is thought. Both read the Vedic fire as a sign of the Lord who also stands within.
Both define the Brahmin's state by regard for every living being: the Kural's அந்தணர் are clothed in kindness to all lives, Tirumular's Brahman includes knowing all lives as one's equal.
Both define the goal by the end of craving: the Kural says the freed are those freed of craving, Tirumular that Vedanta is the place where craving ends.
Both deny that marks of the body make the holy man: the Kural says neither shaving nor long hair is needed, Tirumular that the thread is cotton and the tuft hair.
Both make the Brahmin depend on conduct, not birth: the Kural says his birth is ruined when conduct declines, Tirumular denies the name to those without truth and knowledge.
Tirumular's அந்தண்மை பூண்ட echoes the Kural's செந்தண்மை பூண்டு: both define the அந்தணர் by a coolness of heart they wear. Tirumular adds that the land where they live prospers.
If the two attachments are 'I' and 'mine', both say cutting them raises one above the gods: the Kural to a world higher than theirs, Tirumular to an offering they receive.
224 defines Brahmins by the daily rites; 232 makes the highest state one reached once the rites are set aside, so the rites are a stage, not the goal.

225 says true Brahmins enter the Pranava and see the Lord who is the end of sound, Veda and knowing (நாதாந்த வேதாந்த போதாந்த நாதனை). 2386, in the chapter on the six ends, sets these ends out together: Vedanta and Siddhanta a single seal, bodhanta, yoganta and nadanta becoming bliss in the silence (மோனத்து மூழ்கவே). The terms named in passing in the Brahmins' chapter are given their full scheme later in the book.

227 says faultless Brahmins grasp the Pranava, join the word by the guru's way (குருநெறியால்) and keep to the rites of the four Vedas (நால்வேதத் திருநெறியான கிரியை இருந்து). 232 takes the same guru's way (குருநெறியாலே) further: turiya samadhi comes when rites and rules are let go (கரும நியமாதி கைவிட்டு). Read together, the rites 227 requires are a stage that 232 says is left behind.

235 says that for those in whom Vedanta knowledge shines, the course toward the awareness at the end of sound reaches the Supreme and gains release at the end of sound (நாதாந்த முத்தி). 2821 says the good path of knowledge is the good path of nadanta and its release is the Veda of nadanta (ஞானத்தின் நன்மோக நாதாந்த வேதமே). Both place release at nadanta and bind it to knowledge.
Both say Death does not approach the good: the Kural that it does not advance on one who keeps from killing, Tirumular that it spares the good while the unlearned king kills.
Both tie the land's prosperity to the king's conduct: the Kural rain and harvest to just rule, Tirumular the land's decline to a king who neglects austerity.
Both condemn holy garb worn without the life it stands for; Tirumular adds that the king should force such men to live by it.
230 says the thread and tuft are only cotton and hair; 241 says they should be cut off from the ignorant who wear them, a ruler's remedy for what 230 diagnoses.
Both say the king who fails to guard harms cows and the virtuous; the Kural gives the cost to the land (less milk, forgotten books), Tirumular the cost to the king (hell).
Both make punishing wrongdoers a king's proper work, not a stain on him; Tirumular sets it beside punishment in the next world.

The Tirumanthiram says that if the king does not look daily to the right way, 'நாள்தோறும் நாடு கெடும்', the land declines day by day; Kural 553 says the king who does not examine and do justice daily, 'நாடொறு நாடு கெடும்'. The two share the same closing phrase almost word for word; Tirumular makes the daily duty a matter of தவநெறி, the way of austerity, where the Kural makes it முறை, justice.

The Tirumanthiram has the king test, through the wise, those who wear matted hair, tuft and thread (சடை சிகை நூல்) while lacking knowledge, and bring them to knowledge; Kural 280 says shaving or long hair is not needed at all if one gives up what the world condemns. Both make the marks worthless without the inner substance, but the Kural drops the marks while Tirumular keeps them and has the king correct those who wear them.

The Tirumanthiram says that one who wants release and wealth (முத்தியும் செல்வமும்) must keep to the path of dharma without lapse; Kural 31 says virtue yields distinction and wealth (சிறப்பு ஈனும் செல்வமும் ஈனும்) and asks what gain is greater. Both make virtue the single source of both worldly and higher goods; Tirumular names the higher good as முத்தி.

On the tentative reading, the Tirumanthiram says one who comes to seize the world, for others or himself, has the evil nature of a pouncing tiger (பாய்ந்த புலியன்ன); Kural 552 says a king's demand is like a robber with a spear saying 'hand it over'. Both picture the grasping ruler as a predator, the Kural as a highway robber, Tirumular as a tiger.

Both verses set the yogi's nectar against toddy: here those who do not bind the breath (கால்கொண்டு கட்டி) and drink from the moon (சோமன்) drink liquor and are to be punished by the king; in 335 yogis who bind the breath (கால்கட்டி) taste the nectar of the bright moon while the deluded drink liquor and lose their sense. 335 is a near-repeat in the chapter against drink; 246 adds that suppressing drink is the king's duty.
Both call rain nectar (அமிழ்தம், அமுது): the Kural because the world is sustained by it, Tirumular because it makes the trees flow with nectar.

The Tirumanthiram compares the Lord's river springing within the heart (உள்ளத் தகத்துநின் றூறும்) to a waterfall coming down from the mountain (வரையிடை நின்றிழி ... அருவி); Thiruppugazh 162 asks to climb the mountain of Namasivaya (நமசிவாய வரையேறி) so that the waterfall of bliss (ஆநந்த அருவி) pours. Both place a mountain waterfall inside the devotee, supporting the yogic reading of 249's mountain as the head.
Both use the crow that calls its flock before eating: the Kural for the wealth that comes to those who keep kin close, Tirumular as a lesson in giving.
Both say to share food with all before eating, friend or not; the Naladiyar warns that the door of the other world is shut on those who shut their door and eat.

Both set the bar for giving so low no one can refuse it: the Naladiyar asks for even a fragment of a rice grain daily before eating, Tirumular a handful before eating, with a leaf for God and a kind word added.
Both make feeding those who have nothing the very form of virtue; the Kural calls it where the wealthy store their wealth, Tirumular says the learned call such food virtue itself.
Both press good deeds by picturing the deathbed: the Kural's hiccup that stops the tongue, Tirumular's fever and eyes that no longer open.
Both reject youth as a reason to put off virtue: the Naladiyar's storm drops unripe fruit, Tirumular's Death does not ask whether one is young.
Both picture a great sea to be crossed. In the Kural it is the sea of births, swum by reaching the Lord's feet; Tirumular makes it the sea of deeds, crossed in the boat of austerity and virtue.

Here the Supreme becomes kin (தமர்) to those who know themselves and uphold virtue; in 2865 the one with the forehead eye is the kin (சுற்று) of those who have no kin and stands around those who have no one around them. 2865 extends 251's image: the Lord is kin especially to those who have given up their own.

The Tirumanthiram compares the merit of feeding the destitute to a well or tank (கூவல் குளம்) that people come to and drink from; Kural 215 says the wealth of the wise man who serves the world is like a full village drinking tank (ஊருணி). Both use the public water tank as the figure of wealth that belongs to everyone who needs it.

The Tirumanthiram says to do austerity in its right way before Death comes, Death that takes no account of whether one is young (இளையர் என்று ஓராது); Kural 36 says do virtue without saying 'later' (அன்றறிவாம் என்னாது), since it is the companion that does not perish when one perishes. Both answer the excuse of delay with the coming of death; Tirumular names youth as the false comfort.

Here, for one who has renounced there is no kin from then on (துறந்தான் வழிமுதல் சுற்றமும் இல்லை); in 2865 the Supreme is the kin (சுற்று) whom those without kin (சுற்றற்றவர்) hold to. 2865 limits the loss 256 states: renunciation ends human kinship but gains the Lord as kin.

Here, to one who has forgotten him the Lord has not come (மறந்தான் வழிமுதல் வந்திலன் ஈசன்); in 1614, to those who never forget (மறப்பிலராய்) and daily speak of him, the Lord shows the abode of dharma. The two verses state the same rule from opposite ends, and both join remembrance of the Lord to அறம்.

Here the many who live taking the flesh as their god (ஊன் தெய்வமாக) meet Yama, who says 'I am god'; in 725 Tirumular, who once held the body a thing of shame, cherishes it (உடம்பினை யானிருந்து ஓம்புகின்றேனே) because the Highest has made it his temple. The conflict holds on the reading that 257 condemns serving the body as such; 725 answers that tending the body is right once it is seen as the Lord's shrine, not as the god itself.

The Tirumanthiram calls the Lord 'the support that stands as support' (பற்றது வாய்நின்ற பற்று) and ties his teaching to the path of virtue and giving; Kural 350 says to cling to the clinging of the one without clinging (பற்றுக பற்றற்றான் பற்றினை). Both play on பற்று to make the Lord the one attachment worth holding.
audit_text_issue: Tirumanthiram 259 line 3 (உற்று உங்களால் ஒன்றும் ஈந்தது வேதுணை) looks corrupt.

note: Both compare unshared wealth to the fruit of the poisonous etti. In the Kural it ripens in the middle of town where no one can use it; in Tirumular it ripens and falls, and the usurer buries his store in the ground.
Both fault the person who watches beauty, youth and bodies pass and still does no good thing.
The Kural says the fiery disease of hunger will not touch one who shares his food; Tirumular extends the promise to cough, fever and tumour, taking literally what the Kural keeps to hunger.
Both read present fortune as the fruit of past virtue: the Kural points to the palanquin's bearer and rider, Tirumular to joy and sorrow settled by former deeds.
Both refuse gain got by leaving fairness: the Kural says to give it up the same day, Tirumular that the Lord will not let pleasure sought that way stand.

The Tirumanthiram says those who do not know virtue (அறம்அறியார்) do not know how to think of the Lord's feet (அண்ணல் பாதம் நினையுந் திறம்); Kural 8 calls the Lord a sea of virtue (அறவாழி) and says only those who reach his feet cross the other seas. The Kural joins virtue and the feet in the Lord; Tirumular makes knowing virtue the condition of approaching those feet.

On the tentative reading, the Tirumanthiram says those who stray from the path go back into the womb (கருப்பு ஆரும்) while those who keep it drive off the stain of deeds (வினை மாசு); Kural 38 says doing good every day is a stone that blocks the road of births (வழியடைக்கும் கல்). Both make steady right conduct what closes rebirth, and both use the figure of the road (வழி).

Here those swollen with pride (மலிந்தவர்) die without support, fallen into anger (சினம்), while the ripened see the Lord's feet; 1686 lists burning anger (கன்றல்) and boasting of greatness (பெருமை கூறல்) as not the nature of one near the Lord. Both put pride and anger on the far side from the Lord.

Both correct what 'the ignorant' (அறியார், அறிவிலார்) say about love: the Kural that love serves not only virtue but also against wrong, Tirumular that love is not a second thing beside Siva. Each widens love past a limit set on it.
