Both join bones, burning and love. In the Kural virtue scorches the loveless as the sun a boneless worm; in Tirumular a man burns his own bones and flesh, and without love it still does not reach God.
270 says love is Siva; 279 spells out what follows: he dwells within love and is close support only to those who dwell in it.

The Tirumanthiram says those with longing (ஆர்வம் உடையவர்) see Hara and those with tenderness (ஈரம்) see his feet; Kural 74 says love begets longing (அன்பு ஈனும் ஆர்வம் உடைமை), which begets friendship. The Kural's chain from love to longing to friendship among people is carried by Tirumular to longing that ends in seeing the Lord.

Here Tirumular tells the hearer to melt in love (அன்புருக்கி) and praise the Lord, and says that when he melted, Nandi's love stood foremost for him; in 1456 he melts in love (அன்பின் உருகுவ) and serves daily, and the Lord shines as a light within his bones. Both make melting love the act the Lord answers, there with his love, here with his light.

The Tirumanthiram urges melting love (அன்புருக்கி) as the way to praise and seek the Lord; Thiruppugazh 1028 says those who never melt (நெக்குருகார்) calling on the Lord who shares his body with the woman go to the town of Death. The two state the same demand from both sides: the melting heart reaches the Lord, the unmelting one reaches Death.

In 28 the Lord is a companion on the way (வழித்துணை) only to those who stand bowing (வணங்கி நின்றார்க்கே); in 275 even one who praises him once (ஒரு காலம்) as the self-born finds him a companion on the way (வழித்துணையாய் நிற்கும்). 275 lowers the bar that 28's emphatic ஏ sets: a single praise suffices.

Here one who sets the golden-bright Lord in the mind, praises him and seeks his grace with longing (அருத்தி) is granted increase (விருத்தி) by the king of the gods; in 1500, each time one worships with strewn flowers, the Lord of the gods comes forth and appears (தொழுந்தோறும் சென்று வெளிப்படும்). Both promise a return for each act of worship, one as increase, one as appearance.

On one reading the Tirumanthiram speaks of the Lord who made daily sleep and birth (நித்தலும் துஞ்சும் பிறப்பு); Kural 339 says death is like sleep and birth like waking. The Kural's figure of sleep as a small death helps read 278's compressed phrase as the order of sleep and birth that men know yet ignore.
270 says those who know love is Siva rest as that love; 287 warns that people who claim to know him through love, while blind to their own births and deaths, do not.
Both set love above attainment: 272 says self-burning austerity does not reach him without love, 284 that the siddhas never discern him while devotees receive release.

Here the Lord knows (ஈசன் அறியும்) what we have spurned and gained and returns love with grace; in 109 it is Siva's grace that knows those who dwell in flesh (ஊனமர்ந்தோரை உணர்வது). Both turn the usual question round: not whether we know the Lord, but that he, through grace, knows us.

On the reading that a birth lived mingling in love with the Lord is where births end (இப்பிறவி முடிவது), 281 agrees with 2973, where the heart joining the Lord's feet cuts birth away entirely (முழுதும் பிறப்பறும்). Both make union of the heart with the Lord, not works, the end of rebirth.

The Tirumanthiram asks the hearer to be free of the tangle of the five sorrowful snares (துன்புறு கண்ணி ஐந்து) and seek the mind friendly to the Lord; Kural 343 says the domain of the five (ஐந்தன் புலம்) must be crushed and all desires let go. Both name the five senses as what binds; Tirumular sets the freed mind on the Lord.

283 takes the union of man and woman (புணர்ச்சி) as the figure for the joy of subsiding into the Lord; 1960 says that in bodily union, by the yoga that keeps the bindu, the pleasure becomes Siva's pleasure (சிவபோகம்). Both bring sexual union and Siva's joy together, 283 as a comparison, 1960 as a practice.

Here Tirumular repeats 'கண்டேன்' (I saw) of the Lord's feet and finds the anklet within his love; in 1816, dancing, singing and weeping, he found (கண்டேன்) Siva's great nature and the Lord stood within him (ஊடுநின்றான்). Both are first-person reports of seeing the Lord, and both place the vision inside the seer.

Here the Lord knows those who keep themselves within the bond (பாசத்துள் வைத்து) and show him care, and comes to stand among them; in 1128 the Father can enter only into love set in blissful union, and Shakti is present within the bond where people suffer (துயருறும் பாசத்துள்). Both place the Lord's coming inside பாசம், which supports reading 288's bond as the soul's fetters rather than only the bond of love.

Here mingling with the Lord who stands as one's life is the true sacred bath (மஞ்சனம்); in 1823 the heart is the great temple and the soul the Sivalinga. Both turn temple ritual inward; 1823 sets out the whole inner temple of which 289's ablution is one rite.
Both give the learned eyes. The Kural says the unlearned have two sores for eyes; Tirumular places an eye in the thought of the learned.
Both make learning something that goes with a person: the Kural through seven births, Tirumular as a companion, without saying how far.
Both turn attachment toward the Lord: the Kural says cling to the one free of clinging in order to let go, Tirumular says if you would cling, cling to the Supreme.
252 asks of everyone a leaf for God; 292 makes such worship of his feet the content of learning itself.

The Tirumanthiram tells the hearer to learn to serve the feet of the Steady One (நிலையுடையான் கழல் கற்கின்ற செய்மின்) while still alive; Kural 2 asks what learning has achieved if the learned do not bow at the feet of the one of pure knowledge (நற்றாள் தொழாஅர்). Both make worship of the feet the purpose of learning; Tirumular makes them a single act.

On the tentative reading, the Tirumanthiram says the learned pass away (கல்வியுடையார் கழிந்தோடிப் போகின்றார்) but praising the Lord night and morning makes the body lasting; Naladiyar 135 says learning has no shore and learners have few days, so they should learn only what is fitting. Both start from the shortness of the learner's life; the Naladiyar's answer is choosing what to learn, Tirumular's is worship.

On the reading of 295 as a verse against partisan learning, those who cling to one side (பாலொன்று பற்றி) lose the fruit of good nature and are bewildered by one delusion; in 1558 those who say of the six sects 'this is good, this is bad' are like a dog that barks at a hill. Both treat partisan clinging to one school as delusion.
audit_text_issue: 295 is compressed; பால் may be milk or side.

note: The Tirumanthiram says that to those who search (ஆய்ந்துகொள்வார்க்கு) Hara appears, and that learning becomes a thread ladder (நூலேணி) for the ready mind; Kural 2 says learning is fruitless if it does not end at the Lord's feet. Tirumular gives the positive side of the Kural's warning: learning rightly used is the ladder up to him.

Here the Lord, medicine and companion on the way (வழித்துணை), is companion through all the seven worlds while the unlearned mind is set aside; in 28 he is a companion on the way (வழித்துணை) to those who stand bowing. Both use the same epithet, and both make the companionship depend on the state of the one who seeks it.

Here the Lord who owns the sea and the mountains and has the five elements as his body dwells in the hearts of those who have room for him (இடமுடையார் நெஞ்சத்து); in 1823 the heart is the great temple (உள்ளம் பெருங்கோயில்). 1823 develops 299's dwelling into a whole temple with the body as shrine.
Both raise listeners to the gods: the Kural's listeners, though on earth, equal the gods fed by oblation; Tirumular's hearers of Siva's word become gods.
Both picture the moral life as walking on slippery ground. The Kural gives the words of the virtuous as a staff there; Tirumular asks the mind not to slip from listening and conduct.
Both call listening a துணை, a support. The Kural makes it a staff in faltering; Tirumular places it between the body and the mind on Siva's feet in a ladder of supports.
An image without life: the Kural likens the unlearned man's good looks to a clay doll; Tirumular makes the Lord a stone cow, giving no milk, to those who neither recite nor realise him.

300 lists many hearings, of virtue, of the andhanar's words, of the gods' mantras, and ends that hearing the Lord's ways (ஈசன் திறங்கேட்டும்) gains the Siva-state (பெற்ற சிவகதி). Kural 411 ranks the wealth of the ear first among all wealth (செவிச்செல்வம் ... செல்வத்துள் எல்லாம் தலை). Tirumular keeps the Kural's ranking of listening and names the hearing that ranks first and what it yields.

301 sets an order: once you know him, recite, listen and realise (ஓதுமின் கேள்மின் உணர்மின்), and those who recited and realised stood exalted. Kural 391 has learning followed by standing in keeping with it (கற்றபின் நிற்க அதற்குத் தக). Both make learning a first step that must be completed by something else; for the Kural it is conduct, for Tirumular realisation (உணர்தல்).

301 promises that those who recite and realise (ஓதி உணர்ந்தவர்) stand exalted. 319 mocks those who say 'we can recite and know him' (ஓதி உணரவல்லோம் என்பர்) yet do not know the inner light that moves them. The same pair of verbs is praised in one verse and doubted in the other: the claim to recite and realise is not the realisation.

303 says the holy people who keep saying of him 'this is the Lord' will later become gods too (பின்னைத் தேவரும் ஆவர்). Kural 50 says the one who lives the household life as it should be lived is placed among the gods in heaven (வானுறையும் தெய்வத்துள் வைக்கப் படும்). The same promise, an earthly person counted among the gods, is attached in the Kural to right household living and in Tirumular to speaking of the Lord.

304 ends with the Lord abiding like the scent in a fragrant flower (வாச மலர்க்கந்தம் மன்னிநின்றானே) among those who speak of him in delight. 1459 has the same simile turned inward: as scent dwells in a flower, Siva's fragrance has blossomed within the soul (பூவினிற் கந்தம் ... சீவனுக்குள்ளே சிவமணம் பூத்தது). Both use the scent to name a presence that is felt and not seen; 1459 places it in the soul itself.

306 mocks those who think the experience of the Real comes by mere closeness (செறிவால் அனுபோகம்), like children belching over rice made of sand (மணற்சோற்றில் தேக்கிடுமாபோல்). Naladiyar 321 says the fool scorns the teaching of virtue as the ladle cannot taste the milk-rice it stirs (பாற்கூழை முழை சுவையுணராது). Both use food that is handled but not tasted for people near the truth who do not receive it; the pairing depends on reading செறிவு as closeness.

308 says that to those who stand apart without reciting and knowing the First, he is a cow of stone (கற்பசு), one that looks like a cow and gives no milk. 2937 says that writing the Cause on a palm leaf without the guru joining one to it is like the teat hanging on a goat's neck (ஆட்டின் கழுத்தில் அதர்). Both reach for a milkless likeness of the source of milk to describe a relation to the Lord that has the form and none of the yield.

309 says that whatever one holds in mind or speaks, the First comes near only to those who know him with longing (நச்சு உணர்ந்தார்க்கே நணுகலுமாமே). 278 faults people who call him 'our father, our Lord' but keep him within their wants and do not seek him with longing (நச்சியே அண்ணலை நாடுகிலாரே). The same word நச்சு marks in both what naming and speaking him lack.

Both deny learning its fruit without the Lord: the Kural asks what learning gains if one does not worship the feet of the one of pure knowledge, Tirumular calls the learned without Siva-knowledge wretches and fools.

The Kural makes learning the eyes and gives the unlearned two sores; 310, if read as it seems, gives sight to the unlearned who have the grace-eye and denies the learned their joy. The contrast depends on reading கல்லாதவர் as the book-unlearned.
The Kural finds the unlearned very good if they keep silent before the learned; Tirumular will not even look at or listen to unlearned fools, though he too grants that the merely unlearned are good.
315 mocks those who reckoned and wrote till they wore out; 316 keeps reckoning (கணக்கு) but makes the true one the only way to see. Reckoning is not rejected, only the wrong kind.

310 says the unlearned (கல்லாதவர்), if they have the vision that knows the meaning, hold to the truth, and even the learned cannot see their joy (கற்றோரும் கல்லாதார் இன்பம் காணுகிலாரே). Kural 410 says others stand to those learned in the shining books as beasts to men (விலங்கொடு மக்கள் அனையர்). If 310's கல்லாதவர் are the literally unschooled, Tirumular grants them what the Kural denies; on a reading that limits 310 to the unschooled who have the inner vision, it is a condition rather than a conflict.

312 addresses those who feel the perishing hut of the body is lasting (நில்லாக் குரம்பை நிலையென்று உணர்வீர்காள்). Kural 340 asks whether the soul, lodging in a corner of the body (உடம்பினுள் துச்சில் இருந்த உயிர்), has no home of its own. Both make the body a temporary shelter, a hut or a borrowed corner, and the mistake is to take it for a dwelling.

312 says that though he is Lord of all lives, he cannot be seen in the hearts of the unlearned (கல்லாதார் நெஞ்சத்துக் காணஒண்ணாதே). Thiruppugazh 904 praises Murugan as the one whose mind does not stay with the minds of the unlearned (கல்லார் மனத்துடன் நில்லா மனத்தவ). The same exclusion, the Lord absent from the unlearned heart, passes from Tirumular's teaching to Arunagiri's epithet.

96, the poet's modesty verse, says he does not know how to dance in the way of those able to dance (ஆடவல்லார் நெறி ஆட அறிகிலேன்). 313 has the same speaker call himself unlearned and deluded, yet with the Giver in his mind he can go beyond and dance (கழியநின்று ஆடவல்லேனே). The pairing shows the condition under which the one who could not dance can: not skill but the Giver held in mind.

314 says the able, thinking that life does not stay (நில்லாது சீவன் நிலையன்று), have entered virtue and tapas, while the unlearned live out the suffering of evil deeds. Kural 335 says good deeds must be done at once, before the hiccup stills the tongue (நாச்செற்று விக்குள்மேல் வாராமுன்). Both draw the same practical conclusion from the shortness of life: turn to good deeds now.

315 says the shining fruit ripened in the sky is already mingled within the eye, while those on earth reckoned, thought and wrote and wore themselves out (எண்ணி எழுதி இளைத்துவிட்டாரே). 2937 asks what use it is to write the Cause on the outside of a palm leaf (ஏட்டின் புறத்தில் எழுதிவைத்து என்பயன்) unless the guru joins one to it. Both set writing against what is reached within, and 2937 names who does the joining.

316 says the vision is won only by those who know the reckoning (கணக்கறிந்தார்க்கு அன்றிக் கைகூடாக் காட்சி). 571 uses the same word for breath control: no one knows the reckoning of holding the breath (காற்றைப் பிடிக்குங் கணக்கறிவாரில்லை), and for those who know it, it kicks Death. The pairing gives 316's undefined கணக்கு one concrete sense in Tirumular's usage: a method, not book learning.

316 says only those who know the reckoning (கணக்கறிந்தார்) see the truth and are the truly learned, without saying who they are. 318 defines them: those who stand in love after learning are the ones who know the reckoning (கற்றன்பில் நிற்போர் கணக்கறிந்தார்களே), while the learned without Siva-knowledge are fools. 318 supplies the content 316 leaves open.

319 says people claim they can recite and know the Lord (ஓதி உணரவல்லோம் என்பர்) yet do not know the course of the light within (உள்நின்ற சோதி நடத்தும் தொடர்வு). 1506 says those who recite, worship and gather flowers (வாசித்தும் பூசித்தும்) have minds like a stone in a mossy pond and do not know the remembrance that dwells in love. Both say recitation can go on with the inner thing missing.

The Kural says the world won't count as ruin the low estate of one who stays fair; Tirumular promises those who stand in the middle knowledge, no hell and godhood. The same virtue, given rewards beyond this world.

321 and 322 are near repeats: both say some who stood in the middle became jnanis (நடுவுநின்றார் சிலர் ஞானிகள் ஆவார்) and became the Lord (நம்பனும் ஆமே / நம்பனு மாவார்). 321 begins with the cloud-coloured one and the Veda-reciter standing in the middle; 322 ends with the poet standing among them.

322 ends 'and I too stood with those who stood in the middle' (நடுவுநின்றாரொடு நானும்நின்றேனே), almost the last line of 320 (நடுவுநின்றார்வழி நானும்நின்றேனே). Both list what standing in the middle yields (knowledge, godhood, freedom from hell) and close on the poet's own stand: a near repeat.

Kural 118 makes fairness the balance that first levels itself and leans to no side (சமன்செய்து சீர்தூக்குங் கோல்போல் ... ஒருபால் கோடாமை). 323 says those who stand in the middle (நடுவாகிநின்றார்) are those who always hold the Lord's two feet and cling to his name. The same word for steadiness is used for leaning to no side in the Kural and for being fixed on one support in Tirumular.

Both find the fault of drinking in self-forgetting: the Kural's drinker pays to buy self-oblivion (மெய்யறியாமை), Tirumular's sectarians lose the power they sought because they forget themselves (தம்மை மறத்தல்).
325 names the nectar of bliss that comes in samadhi; 335 says how, by binding the breath to taste the moon's nectar, and sets it against liquor's loss of understanding.
The Kural simply says do not drink. Tirumular agrees, but keeps the vocabulary of drink: the clear toddy (தேறல்) he commends is Siva's bliss. Abstinence becomes a substitution.

326 says lust and liquor belong to the wretched (காமமும் கள்ளும் கலதிகட்கேயாகும்). Kural 920 says double-hearted women, liquor and dice are the company of those whom fortune has left (திருநீக்கப்பட்டார் தொடர்பு). Both pair desire and drink as the marks of the luckless; Tirumular sets against them the nectar of bliss at the feet.

327 ranks the paths: left-hand worshippers drink and die, the lustful are confused, those of the fire rite know the inner light, and those of the Name draw near that very day (நாமத்தோர் அன்றே நணுகுவர்). 1850 gives the practice: long for the Lord at three times of day and sow his name with 'nama' (நமவென்று நாமத்தை விச்சிமின்), and Nandi becomes your master. 1850 spells out the path of the Name that 327 puts first.

328 says those who drink do not ponder the inner truth, know pasu and pasam, or reach Siva-yoga: they do not know the meaning (கள்ளுண்ணும் மாந்தர் கருத்தறியாரே). Kural 929 says giving reasons to the drunk is like searching with a torch for a man sunk under water (கீழ்நீர்க் குளித்தானைத் தீத்துரீஇ அற்று). Tirumular lists what the drinker cannot know; the Kural says he cannot be taught it.

329 says fools who drink deluding liquor do not discern maya, and to feel clear inside delusion is itself delusion (மயக்கில் தெளியின் மயக்குறும்). Kural 928 tells the drinker to stop saying he has never been drunk (களித்தறியேன் என்பது கைவிடுக), since what is hidden grows. Both distrust the drinker's own sense of being clear; Tirumular extends it from liquor to the delusion of maya. The 329 line is uncertain.

330 says liquor bewilders and destroys truthfulness (கள் வாய்மை அழிக்கும்) and leaves the drinker in the pleasure of women. Naladiyar 157 lists among the marks of the faultless that they do not drink (கள்ளுண்ணார) and never lie even by a slip (வாயில்பொய் கூறார்). Both join abstaining from liquor with keeping one's word true.

331 and 1856 are near repeats: the place where there is neither night nor day (இராப்பகல் அற்ற இடம்), the nectar of bliss drunk without distraction (பராக்கற ஆனந்தத் தேறல்), the joy of the feet where night, day and maya are left. 331 says the drinkers of liquor do not drink it (பருகார்); 1856 says the speaker drinks it (பருகி). The same verse serves the liquor chapter as reproach and the guru chapter as testimony.

333 says Siva's grace and Shakti's grace bring each other, and holding both within gives the eight attainments (எண்சித்தித் தன்மை). 670 says the eight siddhis come into being when Shakti Tripurai grants grace (சத்தி அருள்தரத் தானுளவாகுமே). 670 takes one half of 333's mutual grace and ties the siddhis to it.

334 says the nectar of Siva's bliss removes false tapas and enters true enjoyment (பொய்த்தவம் நீக்கி மெய்ப் போகத்துள் போகியே). 1659 says false tapas leads to hell and that false and true tapas alike are spent in experience (பொய்த்தவம் மெய்த்தவம் போகத்துள் போக்கி), the tapas holding only through true knowledge. The two share the words பொய்த்தவம் and போகம், and both make knowledge or bliss, not austerity itself, what holds.

336 says to open the spring where the inner nectar wells (அமுதம் உறும் ஊறலைத் திறந்து), think on the guru's feet and enter samadhi, so the good flows by the nadis along the breath. Thiruppugazh 94 longs to drive the breath up to the moon in the head where the nectar of bliss wells (இன்ப அமுதூறல்) and to go up through the nadi beyond. The same welling nectar (ஊறல்) reached through the nadis is Tirumular's instruction and Arunagiri's longing.

The same phrase in two domains: in 320 those who stand in the middle (நடுவுநின்றார்) gain knowledge and godhood; in 337 the earth that does not stand level (நடுவுநில்லாது) tilts toward ruin until a sage restores it.
The Kural's fair man is a balance whose beam leans to no side; Tirumular's world, leaning to one side, is set level by Agastya. One image of rightness as balance, moral in one, cosmic in the other.
343 says the myth of the three cities is about the soul's impurities; 345 does the same for the slaying of Death, turning it into breath and fire raised in the body.
A third deed read inwardly: after the cities as impurities (343), the burning of Kama becomes the yogi's restraint of the mind and the linga's way.
Both tell Daksha's punishment by Siva: 340 the head cut and burned and restored, 353 the sacrifice broken by Siva's anger and the gods scattering.

343 says fools take the burning of the three cities literally; the three cities are the work of the three impurities (முப்புரமாவது மும்மல காரியம்). Thiruppugazh 343 speaks of the seeker burning the forest of the three cities to ash and uprooting the sheath of sleep on the way to jivanmukti (முப்புரக் காடு நீறெழச் சாடி ... சீவன் முத்தியில்). Arunagiri applies Tirumular's inward reading to the seeker's own release.
audit_text_issue: Thiruppugazh 343 has a corrupt glyph in the shrine list (புலி஧வ்ளுர்).

note: 344 says at the sacrifice of three fires the gods did not know who Hara was, and the killing arose from within that fire (அத்தீயின் உள்ளெழுந்தன்று கொலையே). 353 tells the same event at Daksha's sacrifice: when the Lord grew angry fire burst through the flame (வெந்தழல் ஊடே புறப்பட) and the gods' worship broke off. One episode appears in two chapters, the deeds of Siva and Daksha's sacrifice, both placing the destruction inside the sacrificial fire.

343 calls fools those who say he burned three cities, meaning the cities are the impurities; 348 still names him the destroyer of the three cities, so the epithet stands and only its literal sense is questioned.

197 makes not killing the finest flower of worship; 351 tells, with approval shown by the reward, of a devotee who cut down his own father to protect his worship. The conflict depends on reading 351 as commending the act rather than only reporting a legend.

348 tells the reader not to tire thinking the Lord is hard to reach (அரியனென்று எண்ணி அயர்வுற வேண்டா): he is not false to those who love him (புரிவுடையாளர்க்குப் பொய்யலன்). 309 says the First comes near only to those who know him with longing (நச்சு உணர்ந்தார்க்கே நணுகலுமாமே). Both make love the one condition of his nearness; 348 says it as reassurance, 309 as restriction.

359 says gods who did tapas and whisper mantras in the ear, laying out the oblation with mantras while looking to their own gain (தாமுற நோக்கும்), make a cruel thing (கொடியது). Kural 276 says none are harder of heart than those who live by deceit, renouncing in appearance and not in heart (வஞ்சித்து வாழ்வாரின் வன்கணார் இல்). Both judge religious form used for self-interest as cruel, not merely false.

362 mentions in passing the two who quarrel over who is king while the Lord stands as light; 372 tells the same quarrel as the search for the head and feet of the column of fire, naming Brahma and Vishnu and their folly.
Both turn on Siva carrying a skull: 366, as tradition reads it, the head he took from Brahma; 371 the bones and skulls of the gods he bears so they won't crumble to dust.
audit_text_issue: 366 is obscure throughout; வலம்பன் in 371 may be corrupt.

note: In 363 the Lord, seeing the world in the flood, says அஞ்சல் so that they do not fall into the mouth of the waves; in 1108 the goddess who gives the means roots out danger within and ends with அஞ்சல் என்றாளே. The same word of protection is spoken at the cosmic deluge in one and inside the yogi's heart in the other, by Siva in one and by Shakti in the other.

364 says the gods bow to him as Lord yet கருத்தறியாரே, do not know his purpose; 521 says கருத்தறிவாரில்லை about the darkened throat, which the undiscerning explain as mere poison. Both verses separate praise or story from knowing his intent, and use the same phrase for it.

366, as tradition reads it, has Siva take the head of the one in the lotus and then take up a way of life heaven does not blame (விண்பழியாத விருத்தி). 1887 says what that life is: he took alms (பிச்சையது ஏற்றான்) in Brahma's skull, to do unfailing dharma and so that Brahma might become supreme, turning the beheading into an act for Brahma's good.
349 says only that Siva gave the discus to Achyuta; 368 and 369 tell how Vishnu could not bear it until he worshipped Siva, who then divided its power.
353 tells of Daksha's sacrifice breaking down at Siva's anger; 370 adds an episode from it, Vishnu turning the discus Siva gave him against Siva's side.

368 says Damodara received the discus and, unable to bear it, worshipped Hara with longing (விருப்புடன் அர்ச்சிக்க). The Thiruppugazh song tells the story behind the gift: Vishnu worshipped with a thousand lotuses a day, offered his eye when one was missing, and was given the ஆழி that cut Jalandhara. Both make Vishnu's discus a gift won by worship of Siva.

369 says Siva divided the discus and gave one share to Mal and one to Shakti (கொடுத்தனன் சத்திக்கு). 1085 shows Parashakti bearing conch and discus (சங்கு சக்கரம்), the weapon usually Vishnu's, which is what 369's sharing would lead one to expect.

Both turn to skulls. The Naladiyar's skulls in the burning ground grin at the living as proof of what the body comes to; Tirumular's are borne by Siva, and his bearing them is what keeps them from becoming dust. One image teaches the body's end, the other the Lord's hold even over what is dead.

The Kural defines folly as the pride that says 'we are bright'; Tirumular shows it at the top of the cosmos, Brahma and Vishnu each saying 'I am the Lord' through folly (பேதைமை), and failing before the fire.
349 records Siva's giving the sword to Brahma and the discus to Vishnu; 379 judges such gifts: the gods who worship the giver of the sword do not reach his feet, as those who give themselves do.
Both open on circling through the aeon (ஊழி வலஞ்செய்): in 349 Brahma and Vishnu circle Siva and receive weapons, in 380 one who circles is answered as Siva outshines the sun of dissolution.

373 sets the two gods' failure against the speaker's claim: நானே அறிந்தேன் அவனாண்மையாலே, I knew him by his might. Arunagiri names the same Siva whom Brahma and Vishnu could not find (அரிதான), the fire filling the sky, and asks whether a day will come when he too (அடியேனும்) will know and praise. Tirumular states the knowing as done and as the Lord's gift; Arunagiri keeps it as a hope.

374 has the Lord pass from flesh, life and fire through the sun and moon until he stands as the whole universe (முழுதண்டமுமாகி). 2836 lists sea, wind, fire and space and says the one who stretches long and wide through earth and sky cannot be marked off. Both make the elements and the cosmos his extent rather than his boundary.

377 says the great being is felt ஊனத்தின் உள்ளே உயிர்போல், within the flesh like its life. 2324 reports what was seen ஊனிடை, within the flesh: the lord of knowledge, the light of a great gem and Shakti. The first states the presence in the body as doctrine, the second as something seen.

378 has the world embrace the supreme light that rose and walk around it (உலகம் வலம்வரும்), traditionally the linga. 2836 says the speaker does not know how to mark off (வரைந்து) the one who spreads through earth and sky so as to walk around him (வலம்செயுமாறு அறியேனே). Circling needs a bounded form; 2836 points out that what is circled is not bounded.

The Kural says the world has the Primal Lord as its first, as letters have 'a'; Tirumular says one alone creates, protects and removes the worlds. The Kural names only primacy; Tirumular spells it out as the three acts.

Both speak of the one who made the world. The Kural, conditionally, curses him if he meant some to live by begging; Tirumular praises him without reserve. Because the Kural's curse is conditional, this is a difference of attitude, not a contradiction.
The same quatrain twice, with ஓராயமே (one host) in place of ஒருவனுமே (one alone): if ஆயம் is the assembled powers, the second recasts the one agent as a company.
audit_text_issue: ஓராயமே may be a corruption of 404's ஒருவனுமே.

note: 386 gives creation to one He and one She with five sons; 404 to one alone. Read with 396 and 401, the She is his Shakti, so the two agree that the agent is one.
386 names the pair who create; 396 says what their creating is: play that bears fruit in every season.
382 has bindu rise from nada and the will; 1923 lists what unfolds from bindu as it rises: kundalini, the gods, the powers and speech.
Both make the bindu of Maya the source of everything: 410 by listing sun, moon, elements, speech and mind, 1930 by calling bindu the cause in all its effects, as clay in a pot.
1927 gives the five acts to the Supreme; 398 says the five lords who carry them out are born of bindu and still bound by anava. The acts are his, the agents are not.
audit_text_issue: Both verses are obscure; 1927 வீயம் may refer to bindu.

note: 381 sets out the order of manifestation in the terms பராபரம், பராபரை, சோதி and நாதம். Arunagiri's song uses the same vocabulary, பூரணி காரணி விந்து and நாத பராபரம், as stages the yogi must know before reaching the feet. The Tirumanthiram's cosmology becomes in the Thiruppugazh a checklist of inner attainment.

383 says what comes to be in Shakti's place stays கல்லொளி போலக் கலந்துள் இருந்திடும், mingled within like light in a gem. 1028 has nearly the same line about Shakti, கல்லொளியாகக் கலந்துள் இருந்திடும். The near-repeat fixes the gem's light as Tirumular's image for a presence inside a thing yet not mixed with it.

384 traces the light becoming a Shakti, then nada and bindu, with Sadasiva as the support of the elements. 1713 says whatever arises in the world arises first as Shakti, in her form and qualities, and is Sadasiva himself (சதாசிவன் தானே). Both put Shakti first and Sadasiva at the point where the world takes form.

389 says the Being creates this world together with (உடனாகி, தன்னொடும்) the one who swallowed the worlds, the head of the gods and the four-faced one. 404 says ஒருவனுமே, one alone, created, protected and destroyed. 389 grants the other gods a share as companions while 404 denies any second agent; read together, they are helpers and not creators.

392 calls the Lord one whose kindness is easy to reach (நயன் எளிதாகிய நம்பன்) and repeats எளிது. The Kural says the land of the king who is காட்சிக்கு எளியன், easy to see, is praised above others. Easy access, a virtue of a good king, is here a mark of the Lord.

393 says the pure one grants going and coming in grace (போக்கும் வரவும் புனிதன் அருள்புரிந்து) and calls the one who stirs the directions தயாபரன். 2256 says bondage and release both come by Hara's grace (அரன் அருளே), as play. Both make the round of birth itself an act of grace, not its opposite.

394 says the spotless one fits life to a body and is help (துணை) even to the body that brings earlier suffering. 725 tells how the speaker once held the body as shame and then, seeing the Highest had made it his temple, cherished it. 394 gives the Lord's side of the care that 725 learns to give the body.

395 says the Lord enters the departing soul (போகின்ற சீவன் புகுந்து) and is there as its body. 2131 describes the body leaving one coat of flesh and putting on another (துகிர் போர்வை ஒன்றுவிட்டு ஆங்குஒன்றிட்டு). 2131 shows the passage from body to body; 395 puts the Lord inside that passage as its maker.

396 says the play (விளையாட்டு) of One He and One She brings forth everything. 1772 says the earth is the play of Shakti and Siva (சத்தி சிவன்தன் விளையாட்டு) and nothing fixed exists apart from them. Both make creation play, not need or labour, and both give it to the pair.

397 says the lord of the worlds, the lord of the discus and the god on the flower enter and know only up to the crown (முடிக்காகி), on the reading that sets limits on them. Arunagiri names Indra, Brahma and Vishnu of the discus as wandering in search (திரிய) of the One, and asks to be given it so that the waves stop. The gods' limit in Tirumular becomes in the Thiruppugazh the measure of what the devotee asks for.

399 ends its account of maya, bindu and nada with பரசிவன் தொல்விளையாட்டு, the ancient play of the supreme Siva. 492 says what that play does: Shakti and Siva by their play make souls, yoke them in the two mayas and lead them to turiya and to being full of Siva. The play that unfolds the tattvas in 399 is aimed at the soul's freeing in 492.
audit_text_issue: 399's count of parts does not add up as read; a word may be lost.

note: 400 has Sadasiva, the great Isa, Hara, Mal and Brahma go out together within Shakti to tend space and earth. 62 runs the same ranked chain, Siva, Shakti, Sadasiva, Mahesa, Rudra, Mal and Brahma, as the line through which the nine Agamas were handed down. The order by which the world unfolds is also the order by which the teaching came down.

401 says she, Tripura, settles as Sadasiva and herself performs the five acts (கருமங்கள் ஐந்து செய்வாளே). 404 gives creating, protecting and destroying to ஒருவனுமே, one alone. The two meet only if Shakti is the One's own power; read as separate agents they conflict.

402 strings names of the goddess, மனோன்மணி, காரணி, ஆரணி, மோகினி, பூரணி. Arunagiri's song ends in the same kind of litany and uses the same names, பூரணி காரணி, before Sarvesvari, Kali, Vani and Abhirami. The pairing shows Tirumular's names for Shakti still in use in the Thiruppugazh.

403 says the Lord agreed to be (இசைந்திருந்தான்) Maheshvara, Hara, Tirumal and Brahma. 111 says the one in the supreme becomes Mayavan and Ayan (மாயவனாய் அயனாகி), taking many natures. Both make the gods the one Lord's forms rather than rivals.

405 says the Lord stands having cut off (அறுத்து) the birth that comes in Maya's bond and in union with flower-haired women. Arunagiri, his mind on women with dark kohl eyes, asks Murugan to cut off this birth (இப்பிறப்பறுத்து) that bears the false pot of the body. What the Tirumanthiram states as the Lord's act, the Thiruppugazh asks for.
audit_text_issue: Tirumanthiram 405 has a variant last line of opposite sense.

note: 406 and 414 are the same verse, word for word, except that 406 has கூடும் பிறவிக் குணஞ்செய்த where 414 has கூடு மரபிற் குணஞ்செய்த. The repeat sets the verse in both the creation and the protection chapters: the one who makes the births is the one who keeps them.

362 has the two (இருவர்) quarrel, each claiming to be king, while the One alone (ஒருவனும்) stands as light. 408 has the one Lord (நாதன் ஒருவனும்) and the good two work together, the two asking 'what is our task' (ஏது பணி) and receiving grace. The same One and two appear first as rivals and then as servants given work.

409 says the Lord, spread as life through all kinds, stands covered by darkness (இருள் மூடி) to men who speak falsely (பொய்ப்பரிசு). 40 says that for those who praise without hidden guile (மறைஞ்சடம் செய்யாது) he enters and stays. The two verses state the same condition from both sides: guile hides him, its absence lets him in.

410 lists sun, moon, the guardians, the elements, speech and mind as coming from the bindu of maya (மாயையின் விந்து). 1928 says that by bindu's power the cosmos spreads and the body's five elements arise in maya as effect (காரிய மாயை), so that bindu is inside and outside. Both derive the outer world and the inner faculties from the same source.
Both use the pot. In 1930 bindu is the clay that stays in the pot, the material cause; in 417 the Lord is the potter who shapes it. Read together they separate maker and material.

411 says the Lord has entered and stands as praise and blame (புகழ்வாய் இகழ்வாகி) among other opposites. 1875 says that, since the Lord took the speaker's soul as his field, blame and praise (பழியும் புகழும்) fall away. If he is both praise and blame, the one he holds is no longer moved by either.

412 repeats தானே: he himself stands as the directions, the gods, body, life, tattvas, ocean and mountain. 3043 says he goes through the whole world with many things and yet is skilled in standing as one that is not many (பலவிலதாய் நிற்கும்). 3043 adds what 412's list leaves out: being all these does not make him many.

The Kural says the world keeps going (உலகம் வழங்கி வருதல்) through rain, so rain is amrita. 413, in the chapter on protection (காத்தல்), has the Lord stand as the ocean, the dark cloud and the sky that pours rain. The Kural's rain that keeps the world becomes one of the Lord's forms of keeping it.

The Kural says it is rain that ruins and rain again that lifts the ruined (கெடுப்பதூஉம் ... எடுப்பதூஉம் எல்லாம் மழை). 415 has the Lord stand at one time as a fierce gale (சண்ட மாருதம்) and at another as cool rain (தண்மழை). Both make one power the source of both harm and care.

416 opens: he stands as love, knowledge and restraint (அன்பும் அறிவும் அடக்கமுமாய் நிற்கும்). 270 says the ignorant hold love and Siva to be two, and that love itself is Siva (அன்பே சிவம்). 416 lists love first among his forms; 270 makes it his identity.

In 417 the Lord is the potter (வனைவான்) who shapes births. In 158 a potter (குயவன்) shapes pots, and when a pot breaks people keep the shards, but when the body breaks they will not keep it a moment. The same potter's craft shows the Lord's making in one verse and the body's worthlessness at death in the other.

418 says Nandi spreads in the body as awareness and holds it so that life is not cast off (தள்ளுயிரா வண்ணம் தாங்கி). 724 says if the body perishes the life perishes, and so the speaker learned to nurture the body. Both value the body as what keeps life; 418 gives the keeping to the Lord, 724 to the yogi's practice.

419's first two lines nearly repeat 650: தாங்கருந் தன்மையுந் தானவை பல்லுயிர் வாங்கிய காலத்து மற்றோர் பிறிதில்லை against தாங்கிய தன்மையுந் தானணுப் பல்லுயிர் வாங்கிய காலத்து மற்றோர் குறையில்லை. 650 uses them for the siddhi of drawing in all lives, 419 for the Lord who takes them back in protection, so the same words describe the yogi's power and the Lord's.

8 says the Lord is far off yet near (சேயினும் ... அணியன்) to those who love well. 420 says that even when approached he is far (அணுகினும் சேயவன்), though he gives a shoot of knowledge to those who draw close. 420 keeps a distance that 8's nearness to lovers might seem to remove.

Both put the world in the pot on the fire (உலை). The Naladiyar's turtle plays in the water not knowing it is being cooked, as men revel while Death waits; Tirumular sees the whole world softened and burnt like rice, a cosmic act he says he has come to know, not a warning to the heedless.
The same four names of dissolution, defined differently: daily dissolution is sleep's stupor in 425 and shedding the two bodies in 426. Only the last, grace, stays fixed across 425 to 428.

421 says plainly that the Lord who made fire burned the asuras, with fire as the arrow in his hand (அங்கியவ் வீசற்குக் கைஅம்பு). 343 calls those who say he burned the three cities fools (என்பர்கள் மூடர்க்கள்) and reads the cities as the work of the three malas. Read beside 343, the burning of the asuras in 421 is the burning of the bonds, not only a battle.

421 makes fire (அங்கி) the Lord's weapon that burns earth, sea and asuras; 2799 reads the fire in the dancer's hand as dissolution itself (அரன் அங்கி தன்னில் அறையிற் சங்காரம்). Both make fire the sign of the destroying act, one as an arrow and one in the dance.

424 says he set fire upon the pit beyond Om (ஓம்என்ற அப்புறக் குண்டத்தின் மேலங்கி). 2804 places Om and fire both within the heart (உள்ளத்துள் ஓம்என்ற ஈசன் ... உள்ளத்துளே அங்கியாய). Read with 2804, the obscure fire-rite of dissolution in 424 may be inward, with Om and fire in the same place.

425 names the held dissolution as the state beyond waking (சாக்கிராதீதம்) and calls kevala, where action ceases, pure dissolution (சுத்தசங்காரந் தொழிலற்ற கேவலம்). 2302 puts kevala and sakala among the conditions to be passed and finds purity in the faultless waking-beyond (தீதறு சாக்கிராதீதத்தில் சுத்தமே). If kevala is the mala-bound state, as in 2302, 425's 'pure' kevala must mean something other than the soul's purity.

426 defines daily dissolution as putting off the two bodies (இரண்டுடல் நீவுதல்); 427 gives that work to its second dissolution, shedding body and life (ஒத்தசங்காரமும் உடலுயிர் நீவுதல்), and makes daily dissolution the removal of the instruments' troubles (கருவிடர் நீக்கல்). The series keeps the last term fixed, grace, while the lower terms shift, which shows that only the dissolution that lifts up is settled.

428 ends its four dissolutions in the Supreme's untouched grace (தோயாப் பரன்அருள்). 2062 explains why destruction can be grace: the five acts (ஐங்கருமம்) are the way he makes the soul pure and wipes away its mala (துடைத்து மலத்தினை). 2062 gives the reason 428's series names grace as the highest dissolution.

143 says the unfired pot returns to clay when rain falls (மீண்டுமண் ணானார்ப்போல்), and so people die; 429 says the crop that rose from waste ground sinks back into it while the old waste does not waste away (பண்டைப்பாழ் பாழாகா), and so do the works of Mal and Ayan. The same logic, the product returning to a source that outlasts it, runs from the body in 143 to the whole created order in 429.

Kural 5 says the two deeds born of darkness do not cling (இருவினையும் சேரா) to those who praise the Lord. 430 says there is one strong Lord who made the deeds that cling (சேரும் வினை) to evildoers perish (மாயவைத்தான்). On the reading of மாயவைத்தான் as 'made to perish', 430 makes the Lord the agent of what Kural 5 states as a result, and extends it to the evildoers themselves.

372 has Brahma and Vishnu, each claiming lordship, searching in vain for Hara's feet; 433 says the three gods together do not know how he placed the body. The gods' ignorance of Siva is the same theme, turned here to concealment.
386 gives the world-maker five sons and calls the creator the holy one; 438 names the gods (Maheshvara, Hara, Tirumal, Ayan) as forms the one Lord becomes and works through.

Both use clay and pot. In 1930 bindu stays in the worlds as clay stays in the pot, the material cause; in 440 one clay making many vessels is the one Lord behind all wombs, who like the eye is not seen.

431 says the heart and the One are together, yet the heart does not know his form (உள்ளம் அவனை உருவறி யாதே). 2101 says people set him above as one god without knowing him as mingled with them (விரவுஅறி யாமலே). Both name the same blindness: he is unknown not because he is far but because he is joined to the one who looks.

Both open with the Lord who made a birth for joy (இன்பப் பிறவி). 432 says he also shut it in the sorrow of the bond (துன்பஞ்செய் பாசத் துயருள் அடைத்தனன்); 281 grants that the toils of a sorrowful birth are many but says a birth mingled with him in love (அன்பிற் கலவிசெய்து) is where births end. 281 adds the condition under which 432's enclosure gives way.

433 calls the body that the Lord made a great machine (இரும்பொறி யாக்கை) whose making even the three gods do not understand. 467 lays out that machine piece by piece, the leaf-machine, the balance-machine, the forge-machine (பொறி in every line). 467 shows the contrivance that 433 says stays hidden.

434 names the First who stands as male, female and neuter forms (ஆண்பெண் அலியுருவாய் நின்ற ஆதி). 477 places that fashioning in the womb, where the forms male, female or neither (ஆண்பெண் அலியெனுங் கற்பனை) are brought about by the Light's power. 477 shows how the Lord's standing as all three forms in 434 is worked out in each birth.

435 says the pure white flame stands where darkness ends and yet becomes a dark chamber (இருளும் அறநின் றிருட்டறை யாமே), the Lord concealed. 1514 sets an old woman in the corner of a dark room (இருட்டறை மூலை) who removes the blind man's blindness and weds him, traditionally grace freeing the soul. Together they make the dark room both the place of concealment and the place where grace begins.

431 says the One stays in the heart while the heart cannot see him. 437 turns this round: the devotee, knowing the kinship within, hides the Lord inside himself (ஒளித்துவைத் தேனுள் ளுறவுணர்ந் தீசனை), and the Lord comes out in grace (வெளிப்பட்டு நின்றருள் செய்திடு). The chapter's concealment begins as the Lord's act and ends as the devotee's.

Near-repeat: 438 is 403 almost word for word (நின்றது தானாய் நிறைந்த மகேசுரன் ... மலர்மிசை மேலயன்), with ஆகி for ஆக. The same verse naming the gods as the one Lord's forms stands in the chapter on creation and again in the chapter on concealment.

439 says that keeping to the rare bank of the Ganga (கங்கை அருங்கரை பேணில்), without reckoning on the shore to come (வருங்கரை ஓரா), washes impurity away. 1498 says what the rare bank is: the shade of his feet (அருங்கரை யாவது அவ்வடி நீழல்), the one shore for souls coming toward it (வருங்கரை). 1498 turns 439's bathing bank into refuge at the Lord's feet.

Near-repeat: 2351 repeats 440 almost exactly, the one clay in many vessels and the eye that sees many things but not itself (கண்ணொன்று தான்பல காணுந் தனைக்காணா). The same verse closes the chapter on concealment and recurs in the chapter on the stainless states.

Kural 9 calls the one to be worshipped எண்குணத்தான், possessor of eight qualities, without naming him; Tirumular gives the eight qualities to the matted-haired Siva who keeps the world and stays near the mind.
404 repeats ஒருவனுமே: one alone made, kept and removed the worlds. 445 to 447 use the same refrain form for creation, and 447 ends, like 404's second line, with his keeping what he made.

Both see the body as a pot. In the Naladiyar it is a woman's body, a pot oozing filth that fools admire for its skin; in Tirumular it is the vessel in which the Lord's form stands like milk in water, so to see within it is bliss.

Both use milk mixed in water. The Naladiyar's swan separates them, as the wise sort what is worth learning; Tirumular's milk stays in the water, the Lord present throughout the body and seen only by steady sight.

431, opening the chapter on concealment, says the heart lives with the Lord and does not know his form; 450, closing the chapter on grace, has the poet see that form standing in the body like milk in water.
Both turn to clay. In 440 one clay making many vessels shows one Lord behind many wombs; in 443 the potter shaping clay as he wishes shows the world becoming whatever Nandi wills.

Near-repeat of the last line: 441 has the brow-eyed Lord tie and untie the body-bag (காயப்பை கட்டி அவிழ்ப்பான் கண்ணுதல் காணுமே), as 473 does (காயப்பை கட்டி அவிழ்த்திடுங் கண்ணுதல் காணுமே). 441 builds the bag from the five elements, 473 from the senses and inner faculties.

441 calls the bag that binds the five elements the seat of life (உயிர்நிலை என்னுமிக் காயப்பை). Kural 80 says the seat of life goes by way of love (அன்பின் வழியது உயிர்நிலை), and without it a body is bone wrapped in skin. The Kural adds a condition 441 does not state: the elemental bag alone is not yet what it calls உயிர்நிலை.

Naladiyar 6 says no one here has leapt clear of Death and escaped (கூற்றம் குதித்துய்ந்தார் ஈங்கில்லை). 442 says there is no Yama (நமன்இல்லை) for those who long for the shining nada at the crown. If நமன் இல்லை means escape from death itself, the two conflict; if it means freedom from death's fear or from rebirth, they do not.

Kural 269 says even leaping past Death (கூற்றம் குதித்தலும்) is possible for those who attain the power of austerity. 442 names a particular discipline that has that effect: taking joy in the nada at the crown (உச்சியில் ... நாதத்தை நச்சியே இன்பங்கொள் வார்க்கு நமன்இல்லை).

442 says those who take joy in the nada shining at the crown have no Yama. Thiruppugazh 162 asks to climb to the land without sun or moon and play among the nadas (நாதங்க ளொடுகு லாவி) in a flood of bliss. Both place the inner sound at the top of a yogic ascent and make delight in it the mark of arrival.
audit_text_issue: Both verses flagged uncertain; 162's middle splits are uncertain.

note: Both make the Lord a potter. 417 says he shapes the world and births as a potter shapes pot and jar (வனைவான் அவனே); 443 says that as the potter shapes from clay whatever is in his mind, the motionless world becomes this or that if Nandi wills (அசைவில் உலகம் அதுயிது வாமே). 443 adds that the world's shape follows his will alone.

445 says four times that he made the worlds, ages, elements, and life with flesh gladly (உகந்துநின்றே), under the chapter on grace. 2062 says why the made world belongs to grace: the insentient world is the playground of the Father's grace (அத்தன் அருளின் விளையாட் டிடம்சடம்), where he purifies the soul.

Both end on படைத்துடையான், the one who made and owns. 367 lists his possessions from Mal's gift to the enjoyments of the seven worlds; 446 extends making and owning to the gods and the many souls (பல சீவரை), and so to the one who stands as the Supreme.

447 says the First made the five great elements and stands bearing what he made (படைத்தவை தாங்கிநின் றானே). 966 says by what means: by the five letters he made the five elements and bears this wide world (அஞ்செழுத் தால்இவ் அகலிடம் தாங்கினன்).

Near-repeat: 3011 is 448 almost word for word (அகன்றான் அகலிடம் ஏழும்ஒன்றாகி ... சிவன்தான் பலபல சீவனு மாகி). The verse on Siva becoming the many souls stands in the chapter on grace and again in the closing hymn.

1622 shares 448's second line (இவன்றா னெனநின் றெளியனும் அல்லன்) but in the third changes Siva himself (சிவன்றான்) to Siva's feet (சிவன்றாள்) becoming many souls. Beside 448, 1622 reads the identity of Siva and souls as the feet's presence in them, the reading Siddhanta gives 448's ஆகி.
The same verse appears twice: 2926 reads ஆகிப் படைத்தன in line 2 where 457 reads மூழ்கின்ற முத்தனும், and 457's recorded variants are 2926's readings.
audit_text_issue: duplicate verse with divergent second line; one version is likely a corruption

note: Both list the body as bone, sinew and flesh. The Naladiyar asks which of these parts is the woman a man desires; Tirumular sees in the same parts a house built by the Lord and seeks its builder.

Both describe the body by its nine openings. The Naladiyar makes it a pot seeping filth and calls the man who admires it a fool; Tirumular makes the nine gates sluices set by the Lord, who dwells at its crown and is met there. The conflict is over the body's worth and depends on reading 470 as valuing the body, not only describing how it was made.
725 says Tirumular once thought the body a blemish, then found the Lord had made it his temple, and so cherishes it; 470 already finds the Lord set within the body he built.
Both use the seed or tuber and its sprout: 1932 says seed and sprout exist only together, 489 that the Lord is present as each stage of the growth.

Tirumanthiram 453 says that at the moment the two join (இன்புறு காலத்து) the Lord fixes 'பண்புறு காலமும் பார்மிசை வாழ்க்கையும்', the child's span and its life on earth. Kural 377 says no one, though he gathers crores, enjoys more than 'வகுத்தான் வகுத்த வகை', the share the ordainer allotted. The Kural names an allotting agent without saying when the allotment is made; the Tirumanthiram makes the Lord that agent and places the allotment at conception.

Both verses describe the soul passing from the kevala state into the sakala state as maya draws it out. 460 sets this in the womb: maya joins her brood to the soul in 'கேவலம்', and 'காமியம்' and 'மாயேயம்' take hold; 2229 says the soul in kevala moves through mahamaya and, as 'காமியம் மாமேயமும்' mingle, its bond becomes sakala. The same pair of technical words shows that the embryo chapter and the later doctrine of the states describe one passage.

Tirumanthiram 461 describes the body as a house the Lord built from bone (என்பு), nerve and red flesh, in which he set 'உயிர்நிலை', the seat of life, 'இன்பால்', sweetly. Kural 80 says 'அன்பின் வழியது உயிர்நிலை', the seat of life follows love, and that without it the body is 'என்புதோல் போர்த்த உடம்பு', bone wrapped in skin. Both set உயிர்நிலை against a frame of bone; the Kural makes love what keeps it alive, the Tirumanthiram makes the Lord who placed it there the one to seek.

Thiruppugazh 423, tracing the embryo's growth, notes 'உடல வெப்பம் உற்று', the body's heat rising in the swelling belly until birth. Tirumanthiram 462 says the Lord enters the whole body and 'அங்கியின் கோபம் தணிப்பான்', calms the rage of the fire within, so that the embryo is not harmed. The song records the heat as one more stage of a wretched making; the Tirumanthiram makes the same heat an occasion of the Lord's care.

Tirumanthiram 464, on conception, has something that enters 'எண்விரல்' and comes out 'நால்விரல்', eight finger-breadths in and four out. In the breath-control chapter, 576 says the breaths go out twelve finger-breadths, 'நீடுவர் எண்விரல் கண்டிப்பர் நால்விரல்', reach out eight and cut back four. The shared measure suggests that 464's obscure count is the breath reckoning of the yoga chapters applied to the forming body.

In 417 the Lord is the potter (வனைவான்) who shapes the world and births and makes 'சாலும் குடமும் சிறுதூதை', the jar, pot and small vessel. 468 works the figure out for one birth: the two set the clay in their pleasure, one alone forms 'துன்பக் கலசம்', the pot of sorrow, with nine water-jars, and 'வெந்தது சூளை', the kiln fires and it is done. The pair shows the potter of the protection chapter at work in the womb.

472 says the light that is born in the body spreads through it like 'நீரிடை நின்ற குமிழி நிழலதாய்', a bubble standing in water, a shadow. 2587 says the body passes into the Supreme like 'சாயா புருடன்', the shadow-man that vanishes, and like 'நீரிற் குமிழி', a bubble on flowing water. The same two figures, bubble and shadow, are used for the body's coming into being and for its going out.

475 says 'அருளல்லது இல்லை', there is nothing but grace, and that when the Lord gives a soul he also arranges 'இரு கைத்தாயர் தம்பால் வருகின்ற நண்பு', the love that comes to it from its two mothers. 270 says that love and Siva are not two, 'அன்பே சிவம்'. 475 applies that identity to the plainest human love, a mother's care for a newborn, which it traces to Hara's grace.

476 says the good Lady and the Light 'பல்லுயிர் எல்லாம் வகுத்து', set out all the many beings, and stand within them. 492 says 'சத்தி சிவன் விளையாட்டால் உயிராக்கி', Shakti and Siva in their play make souls, and enter their minds to make them full of Siva. Both give the making of souls jointly to Shakti and Siva and both have the makers stay inside what they make; 492 adds that the end is to make them Sivamayam.

Both verses on conception end with the child who will rule: 458 says a son matching his name 'பேரரசாளுமே', will rule a great kingdom, if the forces are rightly met, and 478 says 'தாண்மிகு மாகில் தரணி முழுதாளும்', if the strength is great he will rule the whole earth. The near-identical close shows that the chapter treats kingship, like sex and lifespan, as fixed by the balance at conception.

479 says that if after conception the breath runs five ('அஞ்சோடில்') the lifespan is a hundred, and if four, eighty. 773, in the chapter on testing the span of life, says that if left and right keep to their way 'தன்வழி அஞ்சில்', in five, it is 'நூறே', a hundred. The same reckoning of five and a hundred appears in both, so the embryo chapter's lifespan rule belongs to the breath-count of the ஆயுள் பரிட்சை chapter.

480 lists defects that come from the flowing breath (dwarf, lame, hunchback) and ends 'பாய்கின்ற வாயு மாதர்க்கு இல்லை', on one reading that the woman's breath does not decide these things. 481 then traces other defects (dullness, muteness, blindness) to 'மாதா உதரம்', the state of the mother's belly. Read that way, 481 limits 480: the mother's breath may not matter, but her body does.

486 says 'இட்டான் அறிந்திலன் ஏற்றவள் கண்டிலள்', the father who planted the seed did not know and the mother who received it did not see, and cries out at maya's lowness. 488 says the crow raises the cuckoo's egg 'அயிர்ப்பின்றி', without suspicion, and 'மயக்கத்தால்', out of delusion. Both make the parents ignorant of what they have made and raise, and name the cause as maya's bewilderment.

Both verses open with the same scene in nearly the same words: 453 'இன்புறு காலத்து இருவர்' and 'துன்புறு பாசத்து', 487 'இன்புற நாடி இருவரும்' and 'துன்புறு பாசத்தில்', birth from the parents' pleasure into painful bondage. 453 goes on to the Lord fixing the child's span at that moment; 487 says that one born so can still seek the Ancient (தொன்பு) and stand chanting. The near-repeat pairs what is fixed at conception with what remains open after birth.

Tirumanthiram 488 says that when a cuckoo's egg is put in a crow's nest the crow raises it 'மயக்கத்தால்', out of delusion, taking the stranger for its own. Naladiyar 30 says kin come unasked into the home and leave silently, like a bird 'சேக்கை மரன் ஒழியச் சேண் நீங்கு புள்', that leaves its nesting tree and flies far. Both figure the members of a household as birds that are not truly the nest's own; the Naladiyar dwells on their leaving, the Tirumanthiram on the parents' delusion in raising them.

490 says the Lord, though greater than all others, is mingled 'ஊனே சிறுமையுள்', within the smallness of flesh, and is known only 'தவத்தினின் உள்ளே', within tapas. 2008 calls the first Lord 'அணுவில் அணு', the atom within the atom, reached only by those able to divide it a thousandfold. Both set the greatest within the smallest and make reaching him a discipline; 2008 carries the smallness from flesh to the atom.
115 states that when Pati draws near, Pasu and Pasam do not remain; 497 describes those in whom this has happened: become Siva, free of பசுபாசம், the malas destroyed.
Both make embodiment serve release: in 474 the body is fashioned so that the bond may leave the soul, in 492 Shakti and Siva yoke souls to maya so as to make them full of Siva.

2240 sets out the three classes by their bonds: the kevalas with anava alone, the pralayakalas who hold maya, and the sakalas who have all three. 493 counts subdivisions within them, four vijnanars, three in pralayakala and three in sakala, 'பதின்மராம்', ten in all. The pairing shows the chapter on the three kinds of soul refining the scheme that the chapter on kevala, sakala and suddha states lays down.

495 says that within the second class are the bound with two malas, 'நூற்றெட்டு ருத்திரர்', the hundred and eight Rudras, while the sakalas have three. 2243 places the pralayakalas in maya and names 'நூற்றெட்டு உருத்திரர்' among them as well. The same group of 108 Rudras is set in the same middle class in both chapters.

496 says that those unable to wither the three malas 'சகலத்துளாரே', are in the sakala state. 2244 says those whom 'மும்மலம் கூடி முயங்கி மயங்குவோர்', the three malas join and bewilder, are the sakalas, from Brahma down to the worm, entering the womb. Both define the sakala by the three malas still in force; 2244 adds that this is the state of everyone who is born.
audit_text_issue: 496 line 1 and சத்தத் தமிழ்ந்து look corrupt.

note: 498 says the vijnanars dwell in anava's kevala, the next kind stay in maya with two malas, and the unknowing sakalas have the rest. 2241 gives the same scheme in plainer words: anava for the vijnanakalas, 'மாயை பிரளயாகலருக்கு', maya for the pralayakalas, and all three for the sakalas. Both tie the middle class to maya and give anava alone to the vijnanakalas, so the classification of chapter 48 matches that of chapter 165.
audit_text_issue: 498 line 2 repeats விஞ்ஞானர் where the pralayakalas are expected.

note: Both say a small gift in worthy hands grows beyond its size: the Naladiyar's banyan seed shades the sky, Tirumular's sesame of gold yields release and siddhi.
audit_text_issue: 501 line 3 runs தரும்நிலமத் together across the line division

note: Both say which gift truly counts. The Kural makes the recipient's need the test, calling all other giving a measured loan; Tirumular makes it the recipient's knowledge of Siva, and says gifts to fools bear no fruit however large. The conflict depends on taking மூடர் as the spiritually ignorant whatever their need.
audit_text_issue: 501 lines 3-4 look misdivided and garbled (தரும் at line start; பலமும்அற் றெபர)

note: 505 continues the point from the other side: a gift to those without conduct or vows is like milking a barren cow or a crop past its season.

Kural 269 says 'கூற்றம் குதித்தலும் கைகூடும்', even leaping over Death becomes possible for those who have the strength of tapas. Tirumanthiram 502 says some went and came to know the Lord who masters Death ('காலனை'), and 'தேவருமாமே', became even gods. The Kural gives the escape from Death to tapas; the Tirumanthiram gives it to knowing the Lord who is Death's master.

Tirumanthiram 504 says 'ஆவன ஆவ அழிவ அழிவன, போவன போவ புகுவ புகுவன', what is to become becomes and what is to go goes, as Nandi showed. Kural 376 says what is not one's own will not stay however one cherishes it, and what is one's own will not go however one throws it away. Both state that what is allotted comes and goes regardless of effort; the Tirumanthiram makes it the teaching of the guru, which the disciple then follows.

The converse case: the Naladiyar's small gift that reaches the hands of the worthy grows like a banyan seed until the sky looks small; Tirumular's gift to the undisciplined is a crop sown after its season. Both make the recipient's worth decide the gift's fruit.

250 tells the giver to give to everyone and not ask who they are; 506 calls giving to those without discipline and love a great fault. The two conflict if 506's ஈவது means giving in general; if it means imparting yoga teaching, they speak of different gifts.

The Kural defines true giving as giving to those who have nothing, all else being a loan expecting return; Tirumular judges the recipient by discipline and love, not by need. The conflict holds on the reading of 506 as about material giving.

507 says that even one guilty of the five great sins, if he gives to the Lord, the pure guru and those who have left desire, will not enter hell. 508 says that even wealth as large as a mountain, given to those who do not bow 'அண்ணல் இவன்' as to the Lord, sends 'ஈந்த இருவரும்', giver and receiver both, to the seventh hell. Read together, the recipient outweighs both the giver's sin and the size of the gift.

501 says gold the size of a sesame seed given to a knower of Siva bears fruit, while gold the size of the earth ('நிலமத்தனை பொன்') given to fools loses it. 508 says that even 'மண்மலை அத்தனை மாதனம்', great wealth as large as a mountain, given to those who do not bow to the Lord, sends both to hell. The chapter on the worthy recipient opens, and the chapter on the unworthy closes, on the same measure of earth-sized wealth; 508 adds that the giver himself is harmed.
The Kural's many who bathe with an air of distinction while their minds are stained, and Tirumular's deceitful who tramp from water to water: both deny that outer washing reaches the stain within.
116 says Nandi has made his home in the temple called this body; 513 draws the consequence for pilgrims, who search outside for one already inside.
510 says bathers alone cannot join the Lord; 512 lets the gods become meritorious by bathing in the Ganga. Bathing gains merit but not union, if the two are read together.

Kural 298 says 'புறந்தூய்மை நீரான் அமையும்', outer purity comes by water, and inner purity is seen by truthfulness. Tirumanthiram 509 says there are many holy waters 'உள்ளத்தின் உள்ளே', within the heart, and that those of deceitful mind who do not bathe there wander over hollow and height. Both deny that outer water cleans the inner person; the Tirumanthiram keeps the figure of bathing and moves the water inside.
audit_text_issue: Kural 298's first word appears as புறள்தூய்மை; standard text is புறந்தூய்மை.

note: Kural 294 says that one who does not lie 'உள்ளத்தால்', in his heart, dwells 'உள்ளத்துள் எல்லாம்', in the hearts of all the world. Tirumanthiram 511 says that the One felt 'உள்ளத்தின் உள்ளே', within the heart, is known by none of the 'கள்ளத்தினார்', the deceitful. Both make the heart the place of presence and make truth or deceit of heart the condition; the Kural speaks of a man's place among people, the Tirumanthiram of the Lord's place in a man.

The same link between rain and worship, run in opposite directions: in the Kural, if the sky dries up, festival and worship cease even for the gods; in Tirumular, if the pujas lapse, the earth has no rain.

Both list what declines when a guardian fails: in the Kural, if the king does not guard, cows give less and Brahmins forget their books; in Tirumular, if the temple pujas stop, kings come to harm and theft grows. The king is the cause in one and the casualty in the other.
241 says that when those whose ignorance remains take up the tuft and thread, the land withers and the king loses standing; 519 says the same of a Brahmin in name only who worships in the temple.

Kural 559 says that if the king bends justice ('முறைகோடி'), the sky withholds its rain. Tirumanthiram 517 says that if the pujas in the temples of the one who kicked Death lapse, the earth has no rain ('அவனி மழையின்றி') and kings lose their strength. The same pattern, a failure at the centre followed by drought, appears in two domains: the Kural places it in the king's justice, the Tirumanthiram in the temple's worship, and makes the king suffer it too.
524 makes the downward face the lower cosmos and the Lord of the aeon; 525 makes it the flower that opens a hundredfold and the endless Shakti.

Tirumanthiram 520 has the gods cry 'எம்பெருமான் இறைவா முறையோ', our Lord, is this just?, and the Supreme send the six-faced one to kill their enemy. Thiruppugazh 847 praises Murugan who threw the vel at old Sura 'முநிவோர் அமரோர் முறையோ எனவே', when the sages and gods cried 'is this just?'. The same cry of முறையோ starts the war in both; the Tirumanthiram tells it from Siva's command, the song from Murugan's vel.

339 says that when the gods begged ('வானவர் வேண்ட') because an asura was tormenting the world's lives, the Lord took the trident and killed him himself. 520 has the gods appeal in the same way about an asura's might, but the Supreme sends the six-faced one: 'தம்பகை கொல் என்ற'. The two follow the same pattern of the gods' plea and the asura's death; 520 gives the act to Murugan at Siva's command.

521 says no one knows the meaning of the darkened throat, and that 'உண்டது நஞ்சு என்று உரைப்பர் உணர்விலோர்', those without understanding say what he ate was poison. 2688 says that to take the poison from the salt sea 'ஆரமுதாக', as nectar, is the intent of the Lord with the shining throat. Both refuse the plain story of the poison: 2688 makes it nectar, and 521 makes the dark throat a sign of something else.

Kural 295 ranks one who speaks truth with the whole mind above those who do tapas and give gifts. Tirumanthiram 522 says the Lord knows the men who praise with lies, and that 'மெய்யே உரைக்கில்', if they spoke truth, he would make the gods worship them. Both set truthful speech above the acts usually praised; the Tirumanthiram makes truth the price of the highest honour and false praise of the Lord its failure.
229 says Brahmins who heard Vedanta and kept their craving have not truly heard it; 529 says Vedic Brahmins who dwell on pleasure forget the Lord. In both, Vedic standing is undone by desire.

526 says the Lord is easy (எளியன்) to those of clear knowledge and that the base who scorn him for it fall like a parrot to the cat; 392 calls him the Lord whose kindness is easy (நயன் எளிதாகிய நம்பன்) and the way to the fruit easy. Read together, the easiness 392 praises is the very thing 526 says the base mistake for smallness.

526 warns against scorning the Lord because he is easy (எளியன் என்று ஈசனை நீசர் இகழில்); 1578 shows the same error before the guru, where the utter fools say of Siva come as guru 'he is one of us' (நமர் என்பர) while the meritorious bow. Both locate the offence in despising the divine for having come near.

527 says gods and asuras perished (விளிந்தவர்) not knowing the knowledge that stands in truth; 528 opens with அப்பகையாலே, 'through that enmity', and names their war as the cause: they perished midway and did not reach the Lord. 528 supplies the reason 527 only implies.

529 says even Vedic Brahmins (வேதியராயும்) lost in pleasure and women's sulking abandon thought of the Lord; Kural 134 says a forgotten Veda can be learned again but a Brahmin's birth is ruined when conduct fails (பிறப்பொழுக்கம் குன்றக் கெடும்). Both deny that Vedic standing protects one whose conduct has gone.

Commentators read the Kural's வேந்தன் as Indra, who falls midway if those of exalted vows are angered; Tirumular names Indra's throne (வாசவன் பீடம்) and great kings' thrones as ruined when devotees are troubled.
Both start from not honouring the great (பேணாது, பேணார்); the Kural warns of ills that do not leave, Tirumular calls those who do it base.

Both use the good thing at hand left for a worse one: the ripe jackfruit for the wild date in 201, the gem for a stone and ghee and curd for bitter food in 536. One is about another man's wife, the other about leaving the guru's knowledge.

A near-repeat: 531 and 533 both threaten those who wound the teacher of the one syllable (ஓரெழுத்து) with birth as a dog (சுணங்கனாய்ப் பிறந்து) and death on earth (மாய்வர் மண்ணிலே). 533 makes the syllable a mantra (மந்திரம் ஓரெழுத்து) and adds a hundred outcaste births.

531 says those who speak to wound the teacher of the one syllable die as worms on the earth (மாய்வர் மண்ணிலே); Kural 898 says if the hill-like great are slighted, those who seemed to stand forever vanish from the earth with their line (மாய்வர் நிலத்து). The Tirumanthiram applies the Kural's warning about the great to the guru, with the same closing verb.

531 honours the teacher who made one syllable and its meaning understood (ஓரெழுத்து ஒருபொருள் உணரக் கூறிய); Thiruppugazh 176 calls Murugan the child guru (குழந்தைக் குருநாதா) who spoke the secret of the pranava into Siva's ear (செவியுட் பிரணவ ரகசியம்). The one-syllable teaching that makes a guru inviolable in 531 is, in the song, given by the son to the father.

532 says those who trouble the minds of a chaste wife, devotees and knowers lose wealth and life within a year (அத்தமும் ஆவியும் ஆண்டொன்றில் மாண்டிடும்); Kural 900 says even those with overwhelming support do not survive if those of great distinction are angered (உய்யார் ... சீரார் செறின்). Both make offence against the inviolable fatal whatever one's means; 532 widens the class to the chaste wife.

535 says falsehood before the true guru makes the good path decline and brings famine (பஞ்சமும் ஆமே); 519 says worship by a Brahmin who has only the name brings disease to kings and famine to the land (பஞ்சமும் ஆம்). In both a falsehood at the sacred centre is answered by famine on the land.

535 traces famine to falsehood in the presence of the true guru; Kural 559 traces failed rain to a king who bends justice (முறைகோடி மன்னவன் செய்யின் ... ஒல்லாது வானம் பெயல்). The same logic, a fault at the centre spoiling the land's harvest, runs in the guru's presence and in the king's rule.

536 likens the ritualist beside the knower to one who eats bitter things while ghee, milk and curd stand at hand (கைப்பட்ட நெய்பால் தயிர்நிற்க); Kural 100 likens harsh speech, when sweet words are there, to grabbing raw fruit while ripe fruit is at hand (கனியிருப்பக் காய்கவர்ந்தற்று). The same figure of choosing the worse food beside the better serves speech in the Kural and the path of knowledge in the Tirumanthiram.
534 threatens land, kings and Indra's throne when devotees are troubled; 537 sends those who speak ill of them to low hell. One names the public ruin, the other the personal one.

Kural 5 says the two kinds of deed (இருவினையும்) do not cling to those devoted to the Lord's praise; 538 says the jnani's good and cruel deeds (நல்வினையான கொடுவினை) are taken off by those who worship and those who revile him, and Siva's bliss enters once he is in the Lord's keeping. 538 gives a means by which both deeds leave, on the traditional reading of how they are divided.

The Kural asks for bearing wrongs done to one and then forgetting them; Tirumular places forbearance inward, as checking the creature of craving that grips the senses. Both call it forbearance, but the Kural's is toward others and Tirumular's toward oneself.

162 says that at death the body's dancing rhythm has ceased (ஆடும் இலையமும் அற்றது); 542 says the dancer who leaps from the field has a rhythm without limit (எல்லையிலாத இலயம்). The same word marks the body's rhythm that ends and the Lord's that does not.

The Naladiyar's drain water that joins a great river becomes holy water, and the lowborn who join the good stand like a hill; Tirumular says joining the great is supreme bliss. Both make the company one joins transform the joiner.
The Kural calls cherishing the great and making them one's own the rarest of rare things; Tirumular's verse begins with அருமை and ends with 'I have joined those strong in holiness'.
543 resolves to go along with those who run to the Lord and reach his feet with them; 547 tells it happening, going with the devotees' devotees and being called in at the gate.

543 says the poet will go with those able to run to the Lord and live in the light of those able to sing (பாடவல்லார்), and so reach his feet; Thiruppugazh 249 asks to end births by living among those who daily speak of Murugan through the Thiruppugazh (உரைத்திடுவார் தங்குழு மேவி) and so worship his feet. Both make the company of singing devotees the way to the feet.

545 says joining the great ones who stand in the path (பெரியார் உடன்கூடல்) is supreme bliss, and that only a few gain it; Kural 443 says cherishing the great and making them one's own (பெரியாரைப் பேணித் தமராக் கொளல்) is the rarest of rare things. The two chapters share a title, and 545 names as bliss what the Kural names as rare.

548 says the one great in skill swims the whirlpool of births (பிறவிச்சுழி நீந்தும்); Kural 10 says only those who reach the Lord's feet swim the great sea of births (பிறவிப் பெருங்கடல் நீந்துவர்). 548 keeps the swimming figure but sets it in the company of the holy, where the Kural sets it at the Lord's feet.

219 says that when the fire is worshipped and rises, the ills of deeds burn away like a wick; 551 calls sacrifice a mean path with no way through. The conflict depends on reading யாகத்திற் as the printed text has it, not the variant யாக்கத்திற்.
audit_text_issue: 551 has variant யாக்கத்திற்; 219's வீழிசெய்து is obscure

note: 552 names yama as the first limb; 554 lists what the man of yama is: one who does not kill, lie or steal, shares his food and is free of drink and lust.

550 promises to tell the armour, the placings and the gestures (கவச நியாசங்கள் முத்திரை) that lead with yama and niyama to samadhi; 1743 spells out the limbs placed in such a rite: heart, head, tuft, armour and eye (நெஞ்சு சிரம்சிகை நீள்கவசம் கண்). 1743 fills in the mantra rite 550 only names.
The Kural puts not killing first and not lying right behind it; Tirumular's list of yama opens in the same order, கொல்லான் then பொய் கூறான்.
Both name sharing one's food (பகுத்துண்டு, பகுந்துண்பான்) among the chief virtues; the Kural sets it beside protecting all life, Tirumular makes it part of the yogi's yama.
197 makes not killing the brightest flower in the worship of the guru; 554 puts it at the head of the yogi's restraints.

553 says the Lord granted grace to the four absorbed in him (அழுந்திய நால்வர்க்கு அருள்புரிந்தான்), teaching them the yamas; 67 opens the line of teachers with the four Nandis (நந்திகள் நால்வர்) who received Nandi's grace. The same four stand at the head of the teaching in both, and 553 says what they were taught.

557 counts sacrifice (மகம்) among the ten niyamas the yogi must keep; 551 calls the path of sacrifice a mean path with no way through. The conflict holds if 551's யாகத்திற் is read as printed; on the variant யாக்கத்திற் it vanishes.
554 lists not killing, not stealing and freedom from lust under yama; 556 repeats them under niyama with purity, compassion and forbearance. The division between the two limbs is not kept strictly.

556 lists purity and truthfulness (தூய்மை ... வாய்மை) among the ten rules of niyama; Kural 298 joins the two, saying outer purity comes by water but inner purity is seen through truth (அகந்தூய்மை வாய்மையால் காணப்படும்). The Kural shows how two items on 556's list depend on each other.
Both say a discipline can overcome Death (கூற்று): the Kural credits the power of tapas with leaping past Death, Tirumular the measure of the held breath with kicking him.

The Naladiyar's wise renounce in childhood because grey hair will surely come; Tirumular says purified breath turns the hair black. Read literally, they disagree about whether ageing can be undone; read symbolically, 575 is not about hair, and the tension dissolves.
Both turn on twelve: 576 says the breath goes out twelve finger-breadths, and 577 makes the twelve elephants that, once known, no longer keep day and night.

564 says the horse of the breath gives a hold to the true but leaps and throws the false (துள்ளி விழுத்திடும்); Kural 814 says better solitude than friends like an untrained horse that throws its rider in battle (அமரகத்து ஆற்றறுக்கும் கல்லாமா). The thrown rider figures false friendship in the Kural and unfit practice in the Tirumanthiram.

565 says the two horses of the breath come under control only with the guru's grace (குருவின் அருள்பெற்றால் ... வசப்படும்); 1679 says hold the reins of the running horse firmly (ஓடுங் குதிரைக்கு உசை திண்ணம் பற்றுமின்) and seek Nandi rather than put on a garb. Both make the restless horse the thing to master, and both send the learner to the Lord or guru rather than outward forms.

335 sets yogis who bind the breath and taste the nectar of knowledge-bliss against the deluded who drink liquor and lose their understanding; 566 says the horse of the breath gives intoxication without drinking toddy (கள்ளுண்ண வேண்டாந் தானே களிதரும்). 566 states as a promise the joy that 335 sets against drink.

566 says the controlled breath gives elation without toddy (கள்ளுண்ண வேண்டா ... களிதரும்); Kural 1090 says brewed liquor delights only those who drink it, unlike love, which delights by a look (உண்டார்கண் அல்லது அடுநறா).
