509 says there are many holy waters within the heart, and those who do not plunge into them wander over hollow and height; 1519 says those who bathed at the Kanni ford never thought of bathing in the Kanni ford, and if they did there would be no further birth. 1519 applies 509's inner tirtha to one named shrine, turning the famous outer bathing place into its inner counterpart.

Both name bathing at Kumari: 1519 (கன்னித் துறைபடிந் தாடிய) says the outer bathers lack the inner bathing that ends birth, and the Thiruppugazh song asks not to bathe at Kumari (குமரி கலித்துறை முழுகி) with a sorrowing mind and be mocked. In both the famous ford stands for an outward remedy the poet sets aside; Tirumular offers an inner ford, Arunagirinathar Murugan's feet.

1520 calls the Lord red, dark, white and green without giving a key; 1735 assigns colours to Sadasiva's five faces: crystal, saffron, collyrium (அஞ்சனம்), red and milk. Read together, 1735 supports taking 1520's colours as the colours of the Lord's faces, though the two lists do not match exactly (green is not among 1735's).

Both use the phrase சிறப்பொடு பூசனை: Kural 18 says festival and worship will cease, even for the gods, if the sky dries up; 1524 says the hill-girl, for those who stand doing worship with honour, cuts birth and sets them to worship (வழிபட வைக்கும்). Each makes worship depend on a giver outside the worshipper, rain in the Kural, grace in the Tirumanthiram.

725 says the speaker once held the body shameful, then saw the Highest had made it his temple and now cherishes it; 1529 says the Lord who lit up knowledge entered him, lit up his flesh (ஊனை விளக்கி) and stayed with him. 1529 carries 725's discovery further: the body is not only the Lord's dwelling but is itself made luminous by his entry.
725 says the Highest has made the body his temple; 1530 faults the six sects for not seeing the God who stands within the body. The doctrine of 725 becomes the charge against the sects.
1530 says the sects miss the God within the body; 1547 says that once one knows how to reach the light standing within, the quarrel among sects ends of itself.

The Kural calls understanding seeing the true thing in whatever thing, of whatever kind; Tirumular tells people to drop the claim that this or that sect is good and seek the God beyond the forms. Both look past the label to the thing.

Kural 340 asks whether the life that lodges in the body (உடம்பினுள் துச்சில்) has no home of its own; 1531 calls the body a hut full of holes (பொள்ளற் குரம்பை) which the Lord, a thief-chief, enters and leaves. Both see the body as a temporary shelter someone passes through; the Kural's lodger is the soul, Tirumular's is the hidden Lord, whom the sects fail to notice.

The Thiruppugazh song lists what rival sects call the ultimate (உருவென அருவென ... ஒளியென வெளியென) and asks to see the reality itself in silence; 1532 says the Lord is within and without for those who say so, and neither for those who say neither. 1532 gives a reason why each sect's formula seems confirmed, while the song turns from all the formulas to a silent seeing.

1534 says the six sects are nothing but waste (அவமல்லதில்லை அறுசமயங்கள்) and there is nothing but Siva; 1558 says the six sects are six roads to one city and those who call one good and another bad are dogs barking at a hill. On the plain reading of 1534 the sects are worthless, on 1558's they all lead to the goal; the tension eases only if 1534's 'Siva' is read as the one city all six reach.

1536 says Siva's path is the only path and all others are paths of becoming that hold a birth in bonds (பாசப் பிறவி); 1461 says letters, songs and the sixty-four arts do not remove birth bound in fetters (பாசப் பிறவியும் நீங்கா). Both use the same phrase to judge rival means: whatever else they achieve, they leave fettered birth in place.

Both call the deluded கலதிகள், the wretched: in 1538 they bray like donkeys and, not knowing the Lord who removes faults, are born and die every day; in 2562 the wretched, shown the way to see, cannot see and wander on the evil path. Together they make the fault not lack of guidance but failure to recognise what is in front of them.

Both call the Lord சேயன் அணியன், far and near: 3043 adds that he is unwavering (அலைவிலன்) and that no one knows his course; 1540 says he is pure to those who can look without wavering (துளக்கற). The pair puts the steadiness on both sides: the Lord does not waver, and only an unwavering gaze sees him.

1542 says to worship without making distinctions (பேதஞ்செய்யாதே) calling him Lord, and the First becomes that path; 2515 says there is no need to quarrel (பிணங்கவும் வேண்டாம்), for if the world agrees that 'our Lord is the Lord', all the hosts seek his feet. Both answer the quarrel of sects with undivided worship rather than the victory of one sect.

104 says Siva, Vishnu and Brahma are one in continuity and those who divide them (பேதித்து) quarrel; 1542 says to worship without making distinctions (பேதஞ்செய்யாதே). The same root names the fault in both: division among gods in 104, division among paths in 1542.

Both use the rare உரநெறி, the strong path, tied to the heart: in 1543 the Lord became the strong path and entered the heart (உளம்புகுந்தானை), in 1562 the lone flame stood on the strong path that crosses the sea of the heart. 1562 adds that the Lord stood there even while the speaker wandered seeking other paths, which 1543's demand that the mind become the path does not say.

1545 tells the reader to drop the delusion of men who say 'this sect or that is good' (அதுஇது நன்றெனும்); 2088 says the world, saying 'that god, this god' (அதுஇது தேவு), has come to loss. The same அதுஇது marks the fault in both, ranking sects in one and gods in the other, and 2088 names the loss that 1545 warns of.

Both use the phrase முதல்வன் அருளிலார், those without the First One's grace: in 1546 they keep to earlier paths and are bewildered, unable to go the red path; in 1992 they are without bliss and stand surrounded by darkness. The pair makes grace, not effort or sect, the line between those who reach and those who stay.

1549 says the great austerity that goes the right way cuts the clinging of strong deeds and brings one before the Lord; Naladiyar 51 says sin cannot stand before austerity as darkness before a lamp, but evil rushes back when good deeds are exhausted, as darkness when the oil runs out. The Naladiyar adds the condition 1549 leaves out: austerity's power over deeds lasts only while its store lasts.

Both name the Lord as the one without equal and make reaching him the cure for the mind: the Kural's தனக்குவமை இல்லாதான் removes the mind's anxiety, Tirumular's துணையிலி is reached by the mind that draws near.
329 calls those held by the mala of deluding sects great fools; 1556 says those who never leave their sect die before reaching freedom from birth. Both treat staying in a sect as the obstacle.

Kural 2 asks what learning has achieved if the learned do not bow at the feet of the one of pure knowledge; 1550 says those who recite the shastras claim to understand, but the First Lord stands among those who know கமை, forbearance. Both deny that learning reaches the Lord; 1550, on the reading of கமை as kshama, names forbearance rather than worship as what does.
audit_text_issue: Tirumanthiram 1550 lines 1 and 3 look corrupt (இமையங்கள், யமை).

note: Kural 7 says the mind's anxiety is hard to remove except for those who reach the feet of the incomparable one; 1551 says those who bear the Lord's feet are without equal, while those who never think of release stay in the world grieving and weeping (ஏங்கி ... அழுவாரே). Both make the feet the only cure for a grief the Kural calls மனக்கவலை and Tirumular shows as weeping.

187 says that even seeing all that grows on the branch die, people do not praise the Lord's feet; 1554 says that even seeing the sign of the boat spilling its load, people of cruel deeds do not think to cling to the red feet. Both turn on கண்டும், 'even seeing': the sight of perishing is in plain view and still does not turn anyone to the feet.

Naladiyar 25 says one who sees kin wailing as a corpse is carried to the burning ground (கண்டும்) still marries and thinks there is joy here; 1554 says those who see the boat break up (கண்டும்) still do not cling to the feet. Both are about the sight of death failing to teach; the Naladiyar's failure is to keep seeking pleasure, Tirumular's is not to seek the Lord.

1556 says those who never left their sect (நீங்காச் சமயம்) do not gain the experience free of ego and perish there; 2838 says those who stand in clarity without knowing even a trace of the sects in themselves (சமயச் சுவடும்) become lords over the gods. 2838 states the positive end of what 1556 shows failing: release lies in leaving no trace of sect, not in choosing the right one.
Both mock sectarian ranking with the image of one city: 1558's six roads and barking dog, 1568's Nandi laughing at those who name 'this penance, that penance' while all who understand enter the city.
1556 condemns those who stay inside their sect and perish; 1558 says all six sects lead to one city. The road is not the fault; refusing to go beyond it, or attacking the others, is.
Both make worship of the feet the fruit of knowing: the Kural asks what learning has achieved without it, Tirumular says his examining succeeded where the gods' failed because it ended in worship.

1557 says the First Lord moves among the six sects so that they seek his feet (தாளிணை நாட); 2753 counts the hundred and eight sects as means (சாதகமாகும் சமயங்கள்) among the things the Supreme's two feet dance through. Both make the sects instruments the Lord uses, set toward his feet, not rivals to him.

Both liken religious disputants to dogs: in 1558 those who say 'this is good, that is bad' are dogs barking at a hill, in the Thiruppugazh song the disputants who call good words evil and argue against true austerity are like dogs (நாயொப்பவர்). In Tirumular the fault is ranking any of the six roads, in Arunagirinathar it is attacking the true path; the same image serves a plea for tolerance and a plea for protection.
audit_text_issue: Thiruppugazh 1106: syntax of the first lines is uncertain.

note: A near-repeat inside the chapter: 1559 opens சைவப் பெருமைத் தனிநாயகன் and calls on all to reach Nandi and be saved (உய்யமினே); 1567 opens சைவ சமயத் தனிநாயகன் நந்தி and says he laid down one guru's path for salvation (உய்ய). 1567 names what 1559 only praises: the Siva path, the sanmarga, set out for those in the world.

Both name the letter ச recited (சகாரத்தை ஓதுமின், ஓதுஞ் சகாரம்) as part of a path: in 731 it joins bindu, ம and nada to make the yogi's path of dharma, in 1564 reciting it with the mind's twoness cast off brings the flame-light on Hara's path. The pair shows the same mantra-letter used in the yoga of the body and in the inner religion.

A near-repeat in the same chapter: both say Hara's path stands beyond what examination (ஆய்ந்துணர், ஆய்ந்தறி) can grasp, and both end with worshipping his red feet with folded hands (சேவடி கைதொழ). 1566 calls the result a bliss for those who plunge in, 1571 says examining that ends in worship saw this life and the next.

2073 sees virgins, the learned, ascetics and contemplatives each in their own enclosure (ஒருசிறை) and says they do not know the Lord's nature; 1568 says Nandi laughs at madmen who give two names, 'this penance' and 'that penance'. Both make the division of religious practice into rival compartments itself the sign of not knowing the Lord.

Both join the downward face (அதோமுகம்) to a garland of heads: 521 speaks of the downward face that bears the cosmos and of him who wears a garland of white skulls (வெண்டலை மாலை); 1569 gives the Lord a downward face beyond his five and a சிரமாலை. 521 supports reading 1569's சிரமாலை as the skull garland rather than a garland on the head.

104 says the First Lord, the jewel-coloured one and the lotus-born are one in continuity, and those who divide them quarrel; 1570 gives the First Lord Vishnu's own deed, measuring the seven worlds (உலகேழும் அளந்தவன்), and names Parasakti as standing undivided (பேதிப்பிலாமை). 1570 applies 104's claim by letting one god's epithet belong to the First Lord.

1540 says people deluded by the deceiver do not know the purpose the body serves (காயம் விளைக்குங் கருத்து); 1572 says the use of the body (உடம்பின் பயன்) cannot be known at all, being set in six unknowable sheaths holding a hidden cosmos. 1572 deepens 1540's charge: the body's purpose escapes not only the deluded but ordinary knowing.

Both use seed and sprout. 1932 makes them the inseparable cause and effect that reveal Hara's way; 1585 makes devotion and dispassion the seed and release-knowledge the sprout, which Shakti's grace makes grow.
1576 argues that the guru is pure Siva because the one beyond the worlds comes here and saves; 1581 states it flatly on Nandi's word and adds that people fail to grasp it.

The Kural asks what learning has achieved if it doesn't lead to the Lord's feet; Tirumular says even the knowledge of Vedanta cannot be known unless the Lord comes as guru. Learning is not enough in either, but for Tirumular the grace must come first.

1574 calls the guru who gathers and plucks out the bonds (பாசத்தைக் கூட்டியே கட்டிப் பறித்திட்டு) and joins one to release ஆசற்ற சற்குரு; 2052 gives the same title, ஆசற்ற சற்குரு, to those who remove the bond (பாசத்தை நீக்கி) and drive out impurity. Read together, the faultless true guru is defined in both places by one act, ending the bond, and 2052 adds the contrast with the guru moved by clamour.

1575 says the eight siddhis, yogic power and mantra knowledge are all learned by the Lord's grace (நாதன் அருளிற் பயிலுமே); Thiruppugazh 194 says what comes from knowing Murugan as the gem does not come by mercury and the like (இரதாதிகளால்), the alchemist's nine metals. Both deny that powers are won by technique and place them in grace, one against yoga and mantra, the other against alchemy.

115 lays down that pasu and pasam are beginningless like Pati and cannot reach Pati, but do not remain when Pati draws near (பதியணுகிற் பசு பாசம் நில்லாவே); 1577 names the guru as the one who removes the unaging bond of soul and fetter (மூவாப் பசுபாசம் மாற்றியே). The pairing shows the guru as the form in which Pati's drawing near happens.

1578 says fools look at Siva come as guru and see only one of themselves (நமர்), while the meritorious say 'this is the Father'; Kural 1071 says the base look exactly like human beings (மக்களே போல்வர் கயவர்). Both turn on human likeness misleading the eye, in opposite directions: in the Kural the man-shape hides less than a man, in Tirumular it hides Siva. The pairing depends on reading பொய்த்தகு கண்ணான் நமர் as mistaking the guru for an ordinary man.

1580 says Siva himself is the Siva-jnani (சிவனே சிவஞானி), so those who reach his feet gain release and the supreme world; 1909 describes the Siva-jnani in whose heart grace dwells, for whom Siva is everywhere and who, dying here, stands everywhere as the Lord. 1580 makes the knower Siva from Siva's side; 1909 shows the same identity from the knower's side.

A near-repeat: 1586 and 1629 have the same four lines (பின்னெய்த வைத்ததோர் இன்பப் பிறப்பினை ... மன்னெய்த வைத்த மனமது தானே), with only spelling differences. Placed in the chapter on the Siva-guru and again in the chapter on tapas, the verse about the Lord revealing himself in his time to the steadied mind is read once as the guru's work and once as the fruit of tapas.

1587 opens every line with சிவமான ஞானம் and makes Siva-knowledge itself siddhi, release and Siva's bliss; 1598 opens every line with திருவடி ஞானம் and makes knowledge of the feet itself Siva-hood, Sivaloka, freedom from mala and 'firm siddhi and release'. The two verses have the same form and the same claim, and set side by side they show that 'knowledge of Siva' and 'knowledge of the feet' are used as one thing.

1588: 'I have known and understood (அறிந்துணர்ந்தேன்) ... I was born and have ended this birth (பிறந்தொழிந்தேன்)'; Kural 356: those who have learned here and seen the true thing (கற்றீண்டு மெய்ப்பொருள் கண்டார்) reach the path of not coming back (மற்றீண்டு வாரா நெறி). The Kural states as a rule what Tirumular claims in the first person: knowing here ends the return to birth.

A near-repeat: 1589 and 1782 share all four lines (தரிக்கின்ற பல்லுயிர்க்கு எல்லாந் தலைவன் ... கருக்கொண்ட ஈசனைக் கண்டுகொண்டேனே) except that 1589 reads பிரிக்கின்ற இந்தப் பிணக்கு, 'this dividing quarrel', where 1782 reads பிரிக்கின்ற விந்து பிணக்கு, 'the strife of the dividing bindu'. The variant decides whether the obstacle to seeing the Lord who holds all as in a womb is a quarrel of views or the yogic bindu.
audit_text_issue: One of the two line-3 readings is probably a textual variant of the other.

note: Both are four-line anaphoras on திருவடி. 138 makes the feet Sivam, Sivaloka, the path and the refuge; 1598 makes knowledge of the feet the agent that makes one Siva, brings to Sivaloka, frees from mala and is release.

Both use the same words for the end state: beyond word (உரையற்று), without waves (திரையற்ற), shoreless (கரையற்ற). 134 describes those who understand the teacher's word; 1593 is the speaker's own passing beyond words.
Both narrate the guru placing his feet on the speaker's head: in 113 as a guard that melts him and removes the verdigris, in 1597 so that the path back to the womb is drained.
Both join the head to the Lord's feet: the Kural calls a head that does not bow to them useless, Tirumular says the old sages set the feet on their heads.
Both say the two deeds, good and bad, cease for one devoted to the Lord: the Kural through praising him, Tirumular through holding his feet in the mind.
Both make a death of the self the way to become Siva: 1907's living who have died to the three malas, 1595's speaker made Siva and made to die in the bliss beyond speech.

1591 narrates the moment: when the Lord gave his feet (தாடந்த போதே) he took the head, gave the sword-strength of knowledge and the rule of release; 2049 lists what the true guru does by giving his feet (தாள்தந்து, four times): protects, grants self-knowledge, takes the soul beyond the tattvas, quells the bonds. 2049 is the doctrine of which 1591 is the first-person event.

1592 says good Nandi first crowned him with his feet (தானடி முற்சூட்டி) and established him; 89, in Tirumular's account of his own history, says Nandi gave release and set his good feet on my head (அடியேன் சிரத்தினில் நற்பதமும் அளித்தான்). The feet set on the disciple's head as the sign of initiation is the same figure in both, and 89 places in the prefatory history the event 1592 describes in its technical terms.

1596 says Nandi set his feet in my heart, my eyes and my head (இதயத்தும் நாட்டத்தும் என்றன் சிரத்தும்) and how he did it cannot be told; 73 says Tirumular placed Nandi's feet on his head and set them within his mind (நான்தலை மேற்கொண்டு புந்தியின் உள்ளே புகப்பெய்து) before telling the Agama. The feet on the head and within the mind appear in both; in 73 the disciple takes them up, in 1596 the guru sets them.

372 tells how Brahma and Mal, each saying 'I am the Lord', faced the Supreme spread out as fire and searched for Hara's feet crying out; 1600 says 'I gained the shade of the anklet-bearing lotus feet' of the First Lord within the fire tall Mal could not know (நெடுமால் அறியா அழல்). The feet the gods could not reach by searching are, for the devotee, a shade he has entered.

1601 sets crowned kings (முடிமன்னர்) against kings of the feet (அடிமன்னர்) and says the crowned gods stand as subjects of the Lord; 2785 calls the Lord's flower feet the great jewel that sits on the crowns of the crowned gods (தாமுடி வானவர் தம்முடி மேலுறை மாமணி). Both place the feet on top of the gods' crowns, so head and foot reverse rank.

Kural 7 says that except for those who reach the feet of the incomparable one it is hard to remove the mind's anxiety (தாள்சேர்ந்தார்க் கல்லால் மனக்கவலை மாற்றல் அரிது); 1604 says the Lord's pair of feet is mantra, great medicine (மாமருந்து), tantra, gifts and the pure path. The Kural makes the feet the one remedy; Tirumular extends it so that every religious means is the feet.
Both make silence the mark of the finished state: 1611 says silence brings release and powers, 1634 that chant and sound are no longer needed once samadhi is in hand.

1605 says that even if the bonds spread, once ego goes (ஆங்காரம் நீங்கி) and one stays in that state, the unfailing state of nectar is reached; Kural 346 says one who cuts off the pride of 'I' and 'mine' (யான் எனது என்னும் செருக்கு) enters a world higher than the gods'. Both make loss of the ego the condition of the highest state, and 1605 adds that it holds even while bonds still arise.

1606 says the knower of the known finds release in the known (ஞேயத்தின் ஞாதுரு ஞேயத்தில் வீடாகும்); 2382 says the six ends subside in the known and the knower too subsides in it (ஞேயம் அடங்கிடும் ஞாதுரு), until even the mark of knowledge goes and silence becomes Siva's bliss. 2382 spells out the step 1606 compresses: the knower's 'release' is its subsiding into what it knows.

1607 says the reality appears as two, 'self' (தான்) and 'He' (அவன்), and once the self is offered as a flower at His feet, saying 'I' and 'He' is no good; 2820 says 'I searched calling it I and He' and the First of knowledge granted that 'I' and 'He' are not two (இரண்டில்லை). The same claim, that the duality of self and Lord falls away, reached in 1607 by offering and in 2820 by search and grace.

1608 says Nandi changed the thirty-six tattvas set in me (வாறாறு, ஆறாறு) and made me Siva; 2020 says to me who did not know the nature of the thirty-six (ஆறாறின் தன்மை) Nandi made it known, and then stood beyond the thirty-six. Both make Nandi the one who works on the thirty-six tattvas; 1608 says he remade them, 2020 that he made them known and went beyond them.

1609 says Nandi made me the Supreme so that I might know myself (தன்னை அறியப் பரனாக்கி) and stayed making me know myself; 2055 says that when the true guru's presence as the very self is revealed, the self must win itself (தானே தனைப்பெற வேண்டும்). 1609 tells the guru's part, 2055 the disciple's.
audit_text_issue: 1609 line 3 has a stray Latin character (தன்aன); misprint

note: 1610 lists what Nandi showed: an eye that does not see (காணாத கண்), a hearing that does not hear, a union that is no joining; 2074 speaks of the great Eye that is eye even to the unseeing, seen by those who see without seeing (காணாது கண்டார்). Both use the seeing that does not see for knowledge of the Lord beyond the senses.

1612 says those who through the three mudras turned back kala and breath and cut off bondage at the bright guru's feet are not born and do not die; 1892 says the mudra attained, fixed in the speech of silence and saved at the holy feet of supreme Nandi (நந்தி திருவடி), brings good release. Both end the practice of mudra at the guru's feet, not in the mudra itself.

Both set a light against darkness in the soul. The Naladiyar's lamp is a person's own tapas, which drives out sin until its oil runs out; Tirumular's light is Siva's grace that comes to the renounced soul at its ripe time.
Both put the full renouncer above the heavens: the Kural says he who cuts 'I' and 'mine' enters a world higher than the gods', Tirumular that only he who renounces the earth reaches the Lord's state.

1614 promises the abode of dharma to those who, never forgetting (மறப்பிலராய்), daily speak of the Lord who saw the tapas of renouncing beyond birth and death; 1626 says those who do great tapas without forgetting (மறப்பிலராகிய மாதவம்) win the ending of birth. In the chapters on renunciation and tapas the same word, மறப்பிலர், marks the practice that ends birth: unforgetting attention rather than hardship.

Kural 350 tells the renouncer to cling to the clinging of the one who has no clinging (பற்றற்றான்); 1616 names who that is: the righteous, unborn one with no one of his own (யாரும் இலாதான்), who lives in the burning ground and eats alms, himself a renouncer (துறவன்), and who cuts the births of those who renounce. Tirumular gives the Kural's 'one without attachment' Siva's face.

1616 calls Siva a renouncer who eats alms (உண்பது பிச்சை) and cuts the births of renouncers; 1888 asks why the creator of the seven worlds begs and answers that he begged so that devotees who live by begging might reach his feet (இரந்துண்டு தன்கழல் எட்டச்செய்தான்). 1888 explains the begging that 1616 only states: the Lord's alms-eating is the pattern for the renouncer's.

Kural 4 says those who reach the feet of the one without liking or aversion have no suffering anywhere (யாண்டும் இடும்பை இல); 1617 says the Lord made the path and the thorn, and the thorn pierces only those who slip from the path (நெறியில் வழுவின்). The Kural states that suffering is absent for those who hold to the Lord; 1617 gives the mechanism, that pain comes from straying, and leaves the maker, like the Kural's Lord, without will to hurt.

Kural 343 says the domain of the five must be crushed and all wants let go at once (அடல்வேண்டும் ஐந்தன் புலத்தை); in 1618 the five (ஐவர்) come like creditors demanding dues and the speaker says 'I owe them nothing' because his resolve is tapas to reach the feet. Both set the renouncer against the five; the Kural commands their defeat, 1618 shows it as refusal of a debt.

Kural 14: if the rains fail, ploughmen will not plough (ஏரின் உழாஅர் உழவர்); 1619: the sky gave rain (வானம் வழங்க) and a blue lily bloomed in the furrow, and yet the ploughman gave up ploughing (உழவொழிந்தான்). Tirumular's riddle inverts the Kural's farming fact: here the plough stops not because the rain failed but because it came and the field flowered, which supports reading the ploughman as a seeker whose effort ends at the vision.

1621 has a five-hooded serpent in the anthill of enjoyment that stops spreading its hoods and dancing (படம்விரித்து ஆட்டொழிந்து) and makes a single hood; 2037, in the chapter on restraining the five senses, has the five's dancing subside (அஞ்சு ஆடல் ஒடுக்க) and a serpent that has slain its bonds enter the opening and rest. Both picture the senses' restraint as a serpent's dance ceasing and gathering inward.

1623 opens with the nine gateways opening their channels (தூம்பு திறந்தன ஒன்பது வாய்தலும்); 470 says the Lord set the nine gates as sluices (மடைவைத்த ஒன்பது வாய்தல்) and the fire within the lotus at the head. Both treat the body's nine openings as the sluices of an irrigation channel, and 470's movement from the nine gates to the head supports the traditional reading of 1623's climb to the 'temple' as rising to the crown.
Both put the ascetic beyond death: the Kural says those who gain the power of tapas can leap past Death, Tirumular that for those who have withdrawn and let go, Yama is simply not there.
The Kural commends tapas because whatever one wants is gained as one wants it. Tirumular separates getting what one wants, which mere asking achieves, from tapas, whose greatness is ending birth.
Both define the ascetic by firmness under pressure: the Naladiyar's blessed push aside troubles that would break their vows, Tirumular's stay unblinking amid kings at war.

Both set inner work against learned talk: the Naladiyar calls those who prattle of grammar and astrology the greatest fools, Tirumular tells the reader to leave clever shastra-recitation for a moment's inward look.

Kural 25 makes Indra, lord of the wide heavens, witness to the strength of one who has quenched the five (ஐந்தவித்தான் ஆற்றல் ... இந்திரனே சாலுங் கரி); in 1627 Indra himself (இருந்திந்திரனே) comes to unsettle those who sit in tapas, and their minds stay set on Siva. In both Indra is the measure of the ascetic's power; 1627 places the ascetic's firmness in Siva rather than in his own strength.

1625 says none but those with the Lord's grace know what tapas is (திருவருள் பெற்றவர்க்கல்லாது); 1628 says the Lord cannot be approached except by those of rare tapas (அருந்தவர்க்கல்லால் அணுகலுமாகான்). Together they make a circle the chapter does not resolve: grace is needed to know tapas, and tapas is needed to approach the giver of grace.

1632 says tapas falls away once the samadhi of knowledge is reached; 1644 adds a second way past it, fellowship with those already in Siva's bliss, and names the end both serve: the mind becoming Siva.
Both tie want to the lack of tapas: the Kural says the poor are many because few practise austerity, Tirumular pictures those without tapas or learning whirling around for rice.
Both picture those who do no tapas as shut out and reduced to want: in the Naladiyar they cling to the outer door of others' houses, in Tirumular they run from crocodile to bear in search of rice.

The Kural asks for flawless learning followed by living by it; Tirumular says recitation (ஓதல்) is no longer needed once the Life of life is within. The two speak of different stages, so this limits learning rather than contradicting it.

1633 says that once samadhi is in hand dying is not needed (சாதலும் வேண்டாம் சமாதிகை கூடினால்). 2320 opens with the same condition, the samadhi where oneself becomes Him (சமாதிகை கூடினால்), and says malam is cut and the flawless body stays on the earth (ஈனமில் காயம் இருக்கும் இருநிலத்து). Read together, 2320 spells out what 1633's 'no need to die' means: the body itself remains, freed of defect.

A near-repeat: both verses run the same frame, X வேண்டாம் once a state is reached, and both name samadhi in hand (சமாதிகை கூடினால்) as the state that makes outward practice needless. 1633 sets aside recitation, desire and wandering; 1634 sets aside crying out, chant, purification and finally the mind itself (சித்தமும் வேண்டாம்), so the pair shows how far the list is pushed.

1635 says those who know the outcome (விளைவறிவார்) do the true tapas of old and surpass those of heaven and earth. Kural 266 says those who do tapas do their own work (தங்கருமம் செய்வார்) and the rest, caught in desire, do what is futile. Both treat tapas as the act of one who sees where deeds lead, the Kural naming the failure as அவம் and Tirumular the insight as விளைவு.

1636 says 'seeking, doing tapas, I saw the Siva-state' and 'joining, I saw the sounding anklets' (தேடித் ... கூடி ... குரைகழல்). 1654 runs the same verbs as a chain, தேடுவன் தேடி, கூடுவன் கூடிக் குரைகழற்கே, and ends in not letting go until release. The shared seeking-joining-anklets sequence, outside 1636's doubts about wasting the body, is the positive path both verses point to.

1637 says the worldly who listen to and serve the people of tapas (பணி கேட்கின்) may come face to face with Nandi. Kural 443 says the rarest of rare things is to cherish the great and make them one's own (பெரியாரைப் பேணித் தமராக் கொளல்). Tirumular carries the Kural's counsel on choosing great companions into the spiritual sphere, where service of the tapasvins becomes the way to the Lord.

1638 says to turn back the five so they do not stray into the field (புனத்திடை அஞ்சும் போகாமல் மறித்தால்), and then the light of the way becomes one's own. Kural 343 says the field of the five must be crushed (அடல்வேண்டும் ஐந்தன் புலத்தை) and all desires let go together. Both locate discipline in checking the five senses at their field; Tirumular adds the sword of understanding and the inner light that follows.

1639 says the sage gives release to devotees who bow and worship (பணிந்தடி யார்தொழ முத்தி கொடுக்கும்). 284 has the same words, பணிந்தடி யார்தொழ முத்தி கொடுத்தவர், and adds that even siddhas cannot discern him otherwise. The repeated formula shows Tirumular naming bowed worship, not knowledge or powers, as what the Lord answers with release.

1640 tells of gathering leaves and flowers 'for my father' yet not seeing the water that comes (வரும்புனல் காணேன்), and finding tapas only on reaching the summit. 1828 says for those who do good there are flowers and water (பூவுண்டு நீருண்டு) and the Lord sees and grants grace. 1640 limits 1828's plain assurance: flowers gathered in outer worship are a start, but the speaker found tapas only beyond them.

Kural 261 defines tapas as bearing the pain that comes and causing no pain to others (உற்றநோய் நோன்றல்). 1641 says that, truly seen, the tapas of those who take on hardship (இடரடை செய்தவர்) lies in a single mind holding the body (ஒருமனத் தாமே). Tirumular keeps the Kural's endurance but adds the condition that it counts as tapas only when the mind is one-pointed.

1643 says those who can tie the frisking calf in its stall (குழக்கன்று கொட்டிலிற் கட்டவல்லார்) will find the fruit ripening in the heart. 2024 says a beast will not keep to the road even when a learned mahout climbs on its neck and goads it (அம்மா வழிநடவாதே). Both picture the mind as an unruly animal; 2024 limits 1643's promise by stressing how rarely learning and force alone make it obey.

Kural 265 says tapas is striven for here because what is wanted is gained as it is wanted (வேண்டிய வேண்டியாங் கெய்தலால் செய்தவம்). 1644 agrees that the fruit of tapas (செய்தவப் பேறு) is the mind becoming Siva, but says tapas is not needed (செய்தவம் வேண்டா) for one who has kinship with those already in Siva's bliss. It adds a second route to the fruit the Kural ties to tapas alone.

Both make அருள் the wealth above wealth. The Kural's அருள் is compassion toward living beings, and its chapter is named அருளுடைமை; Tirumular takes the same chapter name for the Lord's grace, the source of wealth, knowledge and divinity.
1625 says that only those with the Lord's grace know what tapas is; 1645 widens the claim: knowledge of every kind, with wealth and greatness, comes from grace.

Both say that both kinds of deed, good as well as bad, must cease to cling, and both tie this to the Lord: the Kural to those who love his true praise, Tirumular to seeking his dwelling beyond the two.
The Kural says cling to the one without clinging in order to let clinging go; Tirumular vows not to let go of Nandi until release, a clinging that is the way out.

Kural 50 says one who lives on earth as life should be lived is placed among the gods (தெய்வத்துள் வைக்கப் படும்). 1649 says that by Siva's grace some become gods and some equal the deity (தெய்வத்தோடு ஒப்பர்). Both let a human be ranked with the divine; Tirumular puts the cause in grace, where the Kural puts it in the householder's right living.
audit_text_issue: Kural 50 text reads வான்உநற்யும் for வானுறையும்.

note: 1650 says that on nearing the Lord's paired feet knowledge grew like a lamp (விளக்கென ஞானம் விளைந்தது). 1442 says that when the truth beyond speech is attained the five subside and knowledge stands as a lamp's light (ஞானம் விளக்கொளியாய் நிற்கும்). The same lamp marks knowledge in both; 1650 makes it the fruit of grace at the feet, 1442 of the senses stilled.

1651 stacks chariots: body, maya and then the chariot of love (நேயத்தேரேறி) by which, with the stainless one's grace, He becomes this one. 226 says the true Brahmins ride the chariot of love (நேயத் தேரேறி) and, becoming love, are not drowned in maya (மாயத்துள் தோயா). The rare phrase sets love against maya in both, as the vehicle that carries one out of bewilderment.
Both condemn those who live by others while posing as renouncers: the Kural calls none more hard-eyed than they, Tirumular says the show of devotion they put on for food finds no feet of Siva.
241 says the land withers when the unawakened take up tuft and thread and that it is good to cut them off; 1656 repeats the harm, adding famine, and calls stripping the garb of the base a joy.
audit_text_issue: 1656 'பஞ்ச்மாம்' is a typo for பஞ்சமாம்; 'ஞானமில் லேர்' is odd.

note: Both put the world's welfare on the ruler's daily scrutiny (நாள்தோறும் நாடுக, நாடி நாடோறும): the Kural of those who do his work, Tirumular of all his people's conduct.
240 says the garb is true only for those who keep its way; 1660 restates the distinction of false and true garb and puts the test in knowledge.

1816 says that dancing, singing, weeping, wailing and seeking (ஆடியும் பாடியும் அழுதும் அரற்றியும் தேடியும்) the poet found Siva's great nature. 1655 uses the identical line to say that those who wear guises to eat in pomp will not see Siva's feet by these acts. The same acts are the way in 1816 and empty in 1655; 1655 adds the condition that they are not done for show and food.

1656 says that where men without knowledge wear the garb and live by begging, the land's honour decays and famine comes (வையகம் பஞ்சமாம்). Kural 559 says that if the king bends justice the sky withholds its rain (ஒல்லாது வானம் பெயல்). Both tie a public calamity of want to wrong at the head of the land, the Kural's to the ruler, Tirumular's to false ascetics the ruler should remove.

Kural 972 says birth is alike for all beings and distinction comes from the work one does (செய்தொழில் வேற்றுமை). 1658 sorts wearers of the garb by line, low (இழிகுலம்), right (வழிகுலம்), blamed and outcast (கழிகுலம்), and says the last are to be weeded out. The conflict holds only if 1658's குலம் words mean birth; if they name conduct, the verses agree.

1659 says those who practise false tapas go to hell (பொய்த்தவஞ் செய்வார் புகுவர் நரகத்து) and tapas holds only through true knowledge (சத்திய ஞானத்தால்). 1668 says those without knowledge belong to hell even in the garb (ஞானமிலார் வேடம் பூண்டும் நரகத்தர்). Across two chapters the same judgement is made, once of tapas and once of garb, with knowledge as the deciding thing.

Both say austerity's garb belongs only to those who already have austerity, and set தவம் against அவம்: for the Kural taking it up without it is futile, for Tirumular those great in futility cannot carry it.
audit_text_issue: kural:262 in the packet reads 'ஆகும் அதனை'; the standard text is 'ஆகும் அவமதனை', so the அவம் the note relies on is missing here.

note: Both make the false ascetic a hunter: in the Kural one hiding in a bush to snare birds, in Tirumular a வேடர் who wears the garb to kill, punning on the word for garb-wearer.

1662 lists ash, copper earrings and the rudraksha string as the emblems (சாதனம்) of the flawless Siva-yogi. 1670 asks what those emblems are worth and says they are not futile for Siva-gnanis and Siva-yogis (அவமான சாதனம் ஆகாது), though they are for others. 1670 takes 1662's inventory and adds the judgement that the emblems' worth depends on the wearer.

Nearly the same verse: 230 asks whether thread and tuft are Brahman and says the real thread is Vedanta and the real tuft knowledge; 1665 repeats this and adds Om as the means of seeing the supreme soul.

1666 says those who gladly wear the holy ash that is armour (கவசத் திருநீற்றை) will find deeds do not stay (தங்கா வினைகளும்). Thiruppugazh 651 calls the poet a man of two deeds who never wore the true holy ash (மெய்த்திரு நீறிடா இருவினையேனை) and asks Murugan to smear it on him. Both join wearing the ash to release from deeds, one as promise, one as confession.

Kural 133 says conduct is noble lineage (ஒழுக்கம் உடைமை குடிமை) and its lapse becomes low birth. 1667 says the ash of the sacred woods makes the form of those who have gained the stainless one's feet a high lineage (உயர்குலம் ஆமே). Both say high குலம் is made rather than born; the Kural makes it by conduct, Tirumular by ash and grace.
240 says the garb is the true garb for those who keep its way; 1668 goes further, that the knower is released even without it, so the garb is not needed at all where knowledge is.
The same move in another field: the Naladiyar says the beauty of hair and garment is not beauty and learning's is; Tirumular says garb does not save and knowledge does.

1669 says those of evil knowledge carrying the stain of sect (சமயத் துரிசு) have nothing to say, while those of good knowledge reach grace. Thiruppugazh 350 praises those who leave the loud sects (சமயத்துக் கத்துத் திரையாளர்) and their mass of learning and, by grace, reach the golden feet. Both set sectarian learning against grace as the way to the Lord.

1672 says devotees are only those who have gained Siva-knowledge (அடியார் சிவஞானமானது பெற்றோர்) and others are not devotees nor of that garb. 1862 says those who wear the ash crying 'Lord who rides the bull' are devotees (நீறிடுவார் அடியார்). The tension holds if 1862 offers ash and the cry as enough to mark a devotee; if it assumes the knowledge, the two agree.

1660 says a garb, even false, becomes a saving garb for those who have understood and known (உய்வேடமாகும் உணர்ந்தறிந்தோர்க்கே). 1673 says for the gnani even a handsome garb is fitting (சுந்தர வேடமும் நல்லவாம்), while for the one without knowledge nothing of it avails. Both make knowledge, not the cloth, decide whether a garb helps.

1674 says the Siva-gnani holds a lone temple set in its place (தானத்தில் வைத்த தனியாலயத்தன்). 1823 lays out that temple: the heart the great temple, the body the shrine, the soul the linga (உள்ளம் பெருங்கோயில் ஊனுடம்பு ஆலயம்). 1823 spells out the inner temple that 1674 names in a phrase, if தனியாலயம் is the gnani's own body.

1675 names the state of not being oneself and becoming Him (தானன்ற தன்மையும் தானவனாதலும்) as belonging to one released at Nandi's feet. 2320 names the samadhi where oneself becomes Him (தான்அவனாகும் சமாதி) and says malam and bound-soul nature go. The same தான் அவன் ஆதல் is in both; 2320 adds what is removed when it happens.

Both say the ascetic's outward marks are not needed: the Kural, neither shaving nor long hair if one gives up what the world condemns; Tirumular, no garb if one reins in the running horse and seeks Nandi.
Both make self-control the handling of animals: the Kural's goad of firmness guards the five senses as elephants, Tirumular's firm reins hold the running horse.
1660 says a garb saves only the knower; 1677 gives the reason: the garb is put on the body and falls away with it, so it cannot belong to the soul.

1676 says the true servants seek the golden Lord in their own body as the true thing (பொருளாம் தனதுடல் பொற்பதி நாடி). 725 says the poet once held the body shameful but saw within it the true substance (உறுபொருள் கண்டேன்) and now cherishes it as the Highest's temple. Both find the Lord as பொருள் within the body, 1676 making it the mark of the Siva garb.

Kural 338 says the bond of body and life is like a bird flying from its nest (குடம்பை தனித்தொழிய). 1677 draws a consequence for garb: a garb begun on the body falls away when the body does (உடல்கழன்றால் வேடம் உடனே கழலும்), so it cannot serve the soul. Tirumular applies the Kural's parting of body and life to the ascetic's outward marks.

1634 ends that even the mind is not needed for one who rests without action (செயலற்றிருக்கிலே). 1678 says those of the Siva garb, free of delusion with the great mind gone (மாமனம் அற்று), rest without action (செயலற்றிருப்பார்). The two chapters give the same end, mind gone and action stilled, once as the limit of tapas and once as the true Siva garb.

1679 asks what people will do by putting on a garb (வேடங்கொண்டு என்செய்வீர்) and tells them to rein the running horse and seek Nandi for bliss. Thiruppugazh 497 asks not to wander in ochre with matted hair, punishing the body (காவியுடுத்துந் தாழ்சடை வைத்தும் ... காயம் ஒறுத்தும்), but to be given the lamp of supreme knowledge. Both set aside the ascetic's outward guise for inner seeking of the Lord.
1680 shows the unripe choosing a teacher who cannot remove blindness and falling with him; 1693 gives the remedy: if you take a guru, take a good one, and give him body, life and goods.
Both condemn the split between word and deed: the Kural calls the bond with such people bitter even in a dream, Tirumular warns against saying one thing, thinking another and doing a third.
Both make the king's harsh punishment of the wicked a protection of the land: the Kural likens it to weeding the young crop, Tirumular says without it the earth falls to famine.
Both tie the land's famine to tolerating the wrong people: in 1656 the ignorant who wear the garb, in 1684 the sinners the king fails to drive out.

1681 says a magic mirror has arisen in the mind (மனத்தில் எழுந்ததோர் மாயக்கண்ணாடி) but the unripe do not polish it and go after outer things. 2109 says for those who stand within the mirror and know (ஆடியுளே நின்று அறிவு செய்வார்கட்கு) the Lord becomes like a cow in milk. The inner mirror is ignored in 1681 and used in 2109, showing what the unripe miss.

Kural 262 says tapas comes to those who have it, and for others taking it up is futile (அவம்). 1685 says all who stand in tapas without knowing that its karma rests in Siva gain only suffering in births (பவத்திடை நின்றதோர் பாடு). Both say tapas taken up without its inner ground is wasted; Tirumular names that ground as knowing Siva.

1687 says the unripe do not know the dawning (விடிவதறியார) and even when it dawns will not open their eyes. 2001 says the darkness of bond and ignorance vanished as dense darkness leaves at dawn (அருணோதயம் துன்றிருள் நீங்குதல் போல). Dawn is the coming of knowledge in both; 2001 tells it happening, 1687 tells of those who sleep through it.

1688 says that to a deluded disciple who wavers and does not think through the tattvas the teaching is not to be given (பித்தான சீடனுக்கு ஈயப் பெறாதான்). Kural 720 says speaking before those not of one's own kind is nectar spilled in a dirty yard (அங்கணத்துள் உக்க அமிழ்து). The same rule, that teaching is wasted on the unfit hearer, holds for the assembly and for initiation.

1689 calls the unworthy disciple one who does not fear birth and death (பிறப்பிறப் பஞ்சாதான்) and will not leave lust. 1696 calls the true disciple one who fears the binding round of births (ஆர்த்த பிறவியின் அஞ்சி) and keeps to dharma. The two chapters define the unripe and the ripe disciple by the same test, fear of birth, stated negatively and positively.
Both use the shadow that clings to the feet and never leaves: in the Kural it is the ruin that follows the evildoer, in Tirumular the true disciple's place at the guru's feet.

1823 calls the body the Lord's temple for those who have seen clearly; 1701 calls it a prison the teacher shows the disciple how to escape. The two can stand together if the body is a prison to the unreleased and a temple to the knower, but the images pull apart.

1690 says those who worship (தொழுதறிவாளர்) are the ones who know the flawless guru and the good way, while the rest know only ruin (அழிவறிவார்). Kural 2 asks what learning yields if the learned do not bow at the good feet of the pure knower (நற்றாள் தொழாஅர் எனின்). Both make worship the test of knowledge; Tirumular adds scripture as the eye (கருதி கண்ணாக) and the guru as the one to be known.

In 1691 the speaker vows to join no one else (இனி யாரொடுங் கூடேன்) and asks the Lord to kick him and gladly take him (உதைத்து உடையாய் உகந்து ஆண்டருளாயே). Song 447 asks Murugan, so that the poet bows to no one else and does not aim at worldly ties (செகத்தோர் பற்றைக் குறியாதே), to set his flower feet on him and rule him (மலர்த்தாள் வைத்து ... ஆள்வாய்). Both join turning from all others to a plea to be ruled through the Lord's foot.

1691 has the devotee stop his trembling (பதைதொழிந்தேன்) before he asks to be taken. 1692 answers that even while one trembles (பதைக்கின்ற போதே) the seed called the Supreme can be given to devoted singers, once the teacher sets their scattering mind straight (சிதைக்கின்ற சிந்தையைச் செவ்வே நிறுத்தி). Read together, the end of trembling is not a condition of receiving the seed but something the giver brings about.

Kural 34 makes a spotless mind (மனத்துக்கண் மாசிலன் ஆதல்) the whole of virtue. 1695 takes the pure mind further: polished like a great gem by work (தொழிலார மாமணித் தூய்தான சிந்தை), it is where the Lord takes his place, and then deeds fall away and his feet are seen. The Kural's end becomes Tirumular's precondition for grace.

1696's true disciple thinks on the supreme tattva (பர தத்துவம் உன்னி) and fears the binding round of births (ஆர்த்த பிறவியின் அஞ்சி). Kural 358 calls birth a folly (பிறப்பென்னும் பேதைமை) that departs when one sees the true thing (செம்பொருள் காண்பது). Both tie the escape from birth to fixing the mind on the highest reality; Tirumular adds that the seeker must also keep to dharma (அறநெறி சாத்தவல்லான்).

Kural 351 says inglorious birth comes from taking what is not real as real (பொருளல்லவற்றைப் பொருளென்று உணரும் மருள்). 1697 makes the first mark of the true disciple that he considers how the real and the unreal stand (சத்தும் அசத்தும் எவ்வாறென), and then joins that discernment to devotion and grace. The Kural names the error; Tirumular builds the cure into the disciple's training.

1697 starts the disciple with weighing the real and the unreal (சத்தும் அசத்தும்). 1431 describes those who have passed beyond the real and the unreal (சத்தும் அசுத்துந் தணந்தவர்) and sink into the Shakti of bliss. Together they give the beginning and end of the same road: discrimination first, then a state where the distinction no longer holds; 1697's 'Shakti of bliss' (ஆனந்தச் சத்தி) is the very place 1431 ends.

1698 describes the teacher placing his foot (அடிவைத்து) on the disciple's head, so that deceptive birth ends and he becomes a knower free of fault. In 2433 the Lord set his foot on the poet's head (கால்கொண்டு என் சென்னியில்) so that his bonds were cut again and again and his delusion cut. Both make the foot on the head the act that undoes bondage; 2433 speaks it as experience, 1698 as the rule of initiation.

1698 sets out the guru's initiation by placing his foot on the head (அடிவைத்த மாமுடி). In song 1219 Arunagiri asks Murugan to drive off his impurity with Siva's light and set the paired feet on his head (எனது முடிமேலே இணைதாள் அளித்து), then grant him the teacher's place. The same rite of the foot on the head passes from Tirumular's account of the guru to a devotee's plea to Murugan as guru.

1699 says that as the desire for knowledge grows and an unprecedented love turns to the supreme guru (வாராத காதல் குருபரன் பாலாக), the seeker becomes fit for the foot to be placed on him. In 1590, as love rose (இசைந்தெழும் அன்பில்), the guru came and placed his hand on the poet's head. Both make the disciple's rising love the sign that the guru's touch is due; 1699 states it as a qualification, 1590 as an event.

1700 tells the teacher to teach only those of ripe mind (மதிபக்குவர்க்கே உணர்த்தி). Kural 720 says that speaking before those not of one's own kind is nectar spilled in a dirty yard (அங்கணத்துள் உக்க அமிழ்தற்றால்). Both hold that teaching is wasted on the unfit; Tirumular makes ripeness the measure where the Kural speaks of the hearers' group.

1702 calls Vedanta the path of giving up desire and makes the true disciple one who bows to a Vedantin grounded in Siddhanta (சித்தாந்தத்து ... வேதாந்தி). 2393 states the doctrine behind this: becoming Siva is both Vedanta and Siddhanta, and apart from that each is in vain (அவம் அவம் ஆகும்). 1702 shows the joined teaching embodied in a single teacher.

The same verse appears twice. 1492's last line reads சாதா ரணங்கெட லாஞ்ச மார்க்கமே, which supports reading 1707's as 'this is the companion's path' (சகமார்க்கம்) rather than a statement about one person.
audit_text_issue: 1707 has காலந்தத்து for கலாந்தத்து, and 1492's last line சாதா ரணங்கெட லாஞ்ச மார்க்கமே looks garbled (likely கெடலாம் சகமார்க்கமே).

note: Nearly the same verse in a later tantra: the sixteen-petalled flower and pure knowledge becoming Siva's bliss. 2359 ends with the Lord united there, 1711 with knowledge ripening, so the second differs in who is the subject.

1704 counts the petals of the centres from the root upward (மூலம் கண்டு) and says that reaching their end one may see the feet of the one who has seen time (காலங்கண்டான் அடி). Song 188 asks that the breath, driven from the root up the pillar through the six centres (பாலங்கிளர் ஆறு), reach the Supreme's feet (பராபர பாதம்) in Jnana Sadasiva. Both chart the same ascent through the centres and end it at the Lord's feet.

1705 places the supreme Shakti above the sixteen kalas from medha to the end of nada (மேதாதி நாதாந்தம்). 709 joins Parai above (மீதான தற்பரை) as the sixteen kalas from medha rise (மேதாதி ஈரெண் கலை), and calls the light above the yoga of bliss. Both use the same series and set the same goal above it, Shakti or Parai, at its top.

1706 says that when one sees without the two, above and below, and without the natures of 'he' and 'I' (தான்என்றும் நான்என்றும்), the Supreme stands as a wishing tree. 1441 reports searching out 'I' and 'He' (நானென்றும் தானென்றும்) and reaching the state where there are not two. 1706 adds what follows the end of that division: the Lord gives like a rain cloud (கார்ஒன்று கற்பகம்).

1708 ends with practice purging the dross of the bodily elements so that the body itself is the fruit of the adharas (ஆதாரஞ் செய்போக மாவது காயமே). In 724 Tirumular learns the means of nurturing the body (உடம்பை வளர்க்கும் உபாயம்) because if the body perishes true knowledge cannot be won. On the reading that 1708 makes the perfected body the goal, it names one of the means 724 leaves unnamed.

1709 says the fifty letters are set in the adharas and above them, where it wells up, stands the one letter (ஓரெழுத்து). 965 says the fifty letters are all the Vedas and Agamas, and that once one knows what they become they go and become the five letters (அஞ்செழுத்து). Both reduce the fifty letters to fewer; 965 to the five syllables, 1709 further to one letter above them in the body.
1712 says the world has taken form as the linga; 1725 shows it in worship, with the earth as Shakti's base, the sky as the linga, the sea as its bath and the stars as its garland.

Both say the Lord took up the body as his temple (கோயில் கொண்டான்). In 725 that discovery turns Tirumular from scorning the body to caring for it; in 1722 it follows from the Lord being beyond all knowing.

2104 declares one kulam and one God; 1721 still gives each varna its own linga. The oneness of 2104 does not, in this chapter, remove ritual distinctions by birth, though 1721 claims no difference in worth.

1713 says what arises in the world arises as Shakti, in her form and qualities, and that this is Sadasiva himself (சதாசிவன் தானே). 401 says that Shakti, Tripura in the triangle born of bindu, settles as Sadasiva (சதாசிவமாகி அமைவாள்) and performs the five acts. Both make Sadasiva the form Shakti takes when the world comes forth.

1714 says Sadasiva gives enjoyment and release and that the six paths of the Agama (ஆகம அத்துவா ஆறும்) are Siva. 2184 counts those paths: thirty-six tattvas, seven crore mantras, fifty-one letters, two hundred and twenty-four worlds, eighty-one words and five kalas. Set beside 2184's inventory, 1714's claim is that the whole Agamic map of the cosmos is Siva himself.

In 1715 countless gods praise the Lord (ஏத்தினர் எண்ணிலி தேவர்) but do not grasp that he stands beyond the worlds and guards them. In verse 3 the undying gods hail him as the naked one (உலப்பிலி தேவர்கள் நக்கனென்று ஏத்திடும்), yet even those at his side do not know him (பக்கநின்றார் அறியாத பரமன்). Both separate the gods' praise from knowing; verse 3 adds the poet's answer, entering within to meditate (புக்குநின்று உன்னி).

1715: the gods hail the Lord loudly (ஆர்த்தினர்) but miss that he is beyond the worlds (அண்டங் கடந்து). 2942: no one has seen Nandi in the body, though all eight directions praise him as Lord (எண்டிசை யோரும் இறைவன் என்று ஏத்துவர்), and his servants drew bliss from beyond the worlds (அண்டங் கடந்த). Both set universal praise against the absence of knowing, and both place him beyond the அண்டம்.

1716 plays on சுடர் (flame) to say that fire, Brahma, Vishnu, the sun and Indra, the gods as the light of the eye, are all the Supreme as a cool light everywhere (தண்சுடராய் எங்கும் தற்பரம்). 2003 says he himself is the spreading light that stands as three lights in one (விரிசுடர் மூன்றும் ஒன்றாய்) and stands as Brahma and Vishnu. Both see the many gods and lights as the one Lord's light.

1717 says Siva gives grace from within the fixed, installed form (தாபரத்துள் நின்று), while those who worship the great Supreme find Shakti within the flower (பூவகத்து உள்நின்ற பொற்கொடி), likely the heart. 1445 lays out the same course: seek him in lands and temples (நற்றிருக்கோயில்), sing and bow, and then he takes the joined heart as his temple (நெஞ்சத்துக் கோயிலாய்க் கொள்வனே). Both treat the outer shrine as a real channel of grace that leads inward.

1718 reads the temple itself as Siva's form: the tower is the gross linga, Sadasiva the subtle one, the altar of offerings the bhadra linga. 2614 says he is not in the mansion, the hall or the temple (கோயிலுள் ளானலன்), but in the heart of those who have given up longing. If 2614 is read as denying the temple as his place, the two conflict; if as saying the temple without the heart is empty, 2614 only qualifies 1718.

1719 lists pearl, ruby and coral beside cooked and raw rice, flowers and sand (அன்னம் அரிசியாம் ... பூமணல்) as things that can be made the linga. 252 says anyone can give God a green leaf (யாவர்க்குமாம் இறைவற்கு ஒரு பச்சிலை). Placing the poor man's rice and sand beside gems, 1719 applies to the linga itself 252's point that worship is within everyone's reach.

1721 assigns the linga's material by birth: crystal for Brahmins, gold for kings, komalam for Vaishyas and the bana linga for Shudras (துறையடைச் சூத்திரர் தொல்வாண லிங்கமே). Kural 972 says birth is alike for all beings (பிறப்பொக்கும் எல்லா உயிர்க்கும்) and distinction comes only from the work they do. On the reading that 1721 fixes the form of worship by birth, the two conflict; 1721 does not say one worship is worth more, so the tension is over sorting by birth, not over rank.

1723 says that inside the flesh, a place made to fall away (உகலிடமாய் நின்ற ஊன்), the holy one stood as refuge (புகலிடமாய்). 725 tells how Tirumular once held the body shameful (இழுக்கென்று) until he saw that the Highest had made it his temple, and now cherishes it. 1723 keeps the body's perishability in view while finding the refuge in it; 725 draws the consequence for how the body is treated.

1724 makes the earth the Lord's flower-decked feet, the sky his crown and space his body. 2805 says he stands as the great earth and bears it with his feet (பெருநிலமாய் நின்று தாங்கிய தாளோன்), and as the cosmos and what lies beyond. Both read the earth as the Lord's feet; 2805 joins that cosmic image to the feet the devotee seeks.

On what the human body is: the Naladiyar breaks it into entrails, fat, blood, bone and sinew and asks which part is the beautiful woman; Tirumular says the body's very form is the Sivalinga, Chidambaram and Siva's dance. The conflict holds if the Naladiyar's verse is read as a verdict on the body and not only as a remedy for desire.
1823, in the chapter on Siva worship, makes the heart the temple, the body the shrine and the soul the linga; 1726 goes further and makes the body's own form the linga.

Both speak of the five senses as gates (வாயில்) to be mastered. The Kural praises the one who quenched the five sense-gates and the long life of those who follow him; Tirumular has Nandi enter the body by its gates and receive worship once the senses are put behind.

1728 has the body as the Lord's temple, with the five keeping its gates (வாயில்கொண்டு) and giving grace. 1823 builds the whole temple: heart the sanctum, body the shrine, mouth the tower gate (வாய்கோபுரவாசல்), and the five thieving senses its lamps (கள்ளப் புலன்ஐந்தும் காளா மணிவிளக்கே). Both turn the five from enemies into servants of the indwelling Lord; 1823 maps every part of the temple onto the body.
1726 says the human body's form is the Sivalinga, Sadasiva and the dance; 1750 says it of one's own body (தன்மேனி) and goes on to Siva-bliss and the Supreme itself.

Both start from the letter A. The Kural compares: as A comes first among letters, the Primal Lord comes first for the world; Tirumular makes the Lord himself the letter A, with Shakti as U, and the two become the earth and sound. The simile becomes an identity.
Both analyse Om into A, U and M with bindu and nada. 1926 places them in the ascent of the kalas; 1752 maps them onto the parts of the linga.

1730 gives Sadasiva's meditation form with five faces (முகம்ஐந்து), ten arms and fifteen eyes. 1569 says the Lord has five faces and also a sixth, turned downward (அதோமுகம்). Set together, 1569 adds to the five-faced form of 1730 a hidden sixth face that the meditation image leaves out.

1731 runs up the ladder Brahma, Vishnu, Rudra, Maheshvara, the five-faced one, bindu, nada and Shakti, and calls Sadasiva what is common to all (சாதாரணமாம்). 400 has Sadasiva and the others, Isa, Hara, Mal and Brahma, go out together within unfailing Shakti (போகாத சத்தியுட் போந்துடன்). Both treat the graded gods as one series held within Shakti and Sadasiva.

1733 places the six limbs, the four Vedas, chariyai and the religious systems (சமயம்) within the directions of Shakti. Song 575 defines Sivayoga as seeing the five elements, the six religions (ஆறு சமயமும்), mantras, Vedas, Puranas and letters abiding as one form (ஏக வடிவம்). Both gather the Vedas and the rival faiths into a single source rather than ranking them.

1735 gives the five faces as the zenith and the four quarters, each with a colour, and says they were granted to the poet (அடியேற்கு அருளிய முகம்). 1742 places the same five faces on the worshipper's body: Isana at the crown, Tatpurusha the face, Aghora the heart, Vamadeva the secret parts, Shakti the feet. Together they carry the five faces from the directions of space onto the body.

1736 counts Sadasiva's form, five faces, fifteen eyes, ten hands and ten weapons, and ends with him entering and filling the heart (நெஞ்சு புகுந்து நிறைந்துநின்றானே). Song 568 asks to hold in thought every day (நாளு நினைவது) Murugan's flower faces, twelve arms, two feet, consorts, vel and peacock. Both are meditation by counting the god's form limb by limb, one on Siva, one on Murugan, and both end the list in the devotee's mind.

1739 says that if one describes Sadasiva in other words he stands beyond them as surplus meaning (மிகைப்பொருளாய் நிற்கும்). Song 1175 names a reality that debaters cannot speak (வாதிகள் பாஷிக்கத் தகாது) and that no reason can state (ஏதுச்செப் பொணாதது). Both hold that speech falls short of the Lord; 1739 still keeps one sentence, that he is our Lord, while 1175 works only through negatives.

1742 places the five faces, which are also the five Brahma mantras, on the worshipper's body, from Isana at the crown to Shakti at the feet. Song 1165 lays the letters of நமசிவய on the Lord's form, na the feet, ma the belly, si the chest, va the mouth, ya the crown (நகரமிரு பாதமாகி ... வாய் வகரமாகி). Both map sacred sounds onto a body, head to foot; 1742 onto the worshipper's, 1165 onto the god's.

1744 matches the limbs of worship to the Lord's powers: the heart his power of knowledge (ஞான சத்தி), the tuft and armour his will (இச்சை), and action (கிரியை) in the eye. 2459 makes Shakti the body of the Supreme, taking on the distinctions of will, knowledge and the rest (இச்சையில் ஞானாதி பேதமாய்). 1744 applies 2459's doctrine to ritual, placing those powers on the limbs.

1747 ends: I stood and worshipped Siva's feet within my heart (நின்று தொழுதேன் என் நெஞ்சத்தின் உள்ளே). Verse 3 ends: entering in and meditating, I praise him every day (புக்குநின்று உன்னி யான் போற்றிசெய்வேனே). Both make the place of worship the inside of the worshipper; 1747 adds that the Lord already dwells and moves in the body (உடலின் உடன்கிடந்து).

1748: I brought him in and made my heart his temple (கோயில் என் நெஞ்சம்), I joined the Pure One and I bowed (பணிந்தேன்). 1445: sing, bow (பணிமின்), and when you have bowed he takes the joined heart as his temple (கூடிய நெஞ்சத்துக் கோயிலாய்க் கொள்வனே). 1445 gives as instruction what 1748 reports as done; in 1748 the poet brings the Lord in, in 1445 the Lord takes the heart.

1752 maps Om onto the linga: Om the pedestal, M the neck, U the inner circle, A the linga itself (இலிங்கம் அகாரம்), filled with bindu and nada. Song 1165 maps the five letters onto the Lord's body and adds அகர உகர and Om (அகரவுகர ... ஓம). Both treat the sacred syllables as the parts of the Lord's form.
audit_text_issue: Second half of Thiruppugazh 1165 is hard to construe.

note: Both open with A as first: the Kural uses it as a simile, as A is first of letters so the Lord is first of the world. Tirumular takes the letter literally: A and U, known rightly, are themselves the lingam.
1754 makes bindu the first pedestal and the union the lingam; 1757 names the parts plainly, bindu as pedestal and nada as lingam, and gives the pair the five acts.
Both end on the Lord dwelling in the speaker's mind; 1762 adds the contrast with the gods who seek him outwardly across the eight directions.

1752 lays the syllable Om over the lingam: ஓங்காரம் the pedestal, மகாரம் the neck, உகாரம் the inner circle, and இலிங்கம் அகாரம் the shaft itself. 1753 takes only the first two letters and says அகார உகாரம் இலிங்கம் தாமே, A as the Lord standing as all and U as the Lord within lives. Read together, 1753 explains what the A and U of 1752's diagram stand for.

1755 says the lingam that is Shakti and Siva is both தாபரம் (the installed one) and சங்கமம் (the moving one). 1857 draws the practical consequence of a moving shrine: a gift to the படமாடக் கோயில் (temple of images) does not reach the நடமாடக் கோயில் (walking temple), but a gift to the walking temple reaches the other. The pairing shows the சங்கமம் of 1755 is the living devotee to whom 1857 gives priority.

Both set the பொற்கொடி (golden creeper) inside the lingam. In 1717 the installed lingam becomes, for true worshippers, பூவகத்து உள்நின்ற பொற்கொடி; in 1756 the golden creeper rises with the light and the letters and ends as அகாரம். The shared image names Shakti as the living core of the lingam in both.

Both divide the installed lingam into the same three parts, பீடம், கண்டம் and இலிங்கம். 1752 maps them to the letters of Om; 1758 maps them to the soul, vidya and the Siva tattva, each as Shakti (சத்திநற் பீடம் தகுநல்ல ஆன்மா). The two verses give two readings of one diagram, sound and tattva.

1759 repeats மனம்புகுந்து: the Lord entered the mind, settled life and poured down இன்பம். 1804 repeats அகம்புகுந்தான்: by grace he entered the heart and made it ஆனந்தம். Both describe the Lord's entry into the inner self as the moment bliss begins, and 1804 adds that grace is the condition of that entry.

1760 calls the Lord the one whose temple is the minds of his devotees (தன்னடியார் மனக் கோயில்) and who settled in my mind. 1823 builds the whole temple inside the person: உள்ளம் பெருங்கோயில், the body the shrine, the mouth the gate, the soul the Sivalinga. 1760 states the claim in one phrase that 1823 works out part by part.

1761 speaks of the ஈசன் who made my mind his temple (என்மனம் கோயில்கொள்); 1748 says the speaker brought the bright One in and made கோயிலென் நெஞ்சம், my heart the temple. The two verses, in neighbouring lingam chapters, both move worship from the outer shrine to the heart.

2837 says the gods from Brahma and Mal on, wherever they stand, praise him as Lord (இறைவன் என்று ஏத்துவர்) while he abides. 1762 grants that the gods go round the eight directions praising him where he stood and lay, but sets against it its own constant praise and a Lord who is ஒன்றி என் உள்ளத்தின் உள்ளிருந்தான். It limits the gods' outward praise of 2837: the Lord they seek abroad is found within.

1764 counts four forms, four formless and one in the middle without naming them; 1776 names nine: Brahma, Vishnu, Rudra, Mahesa, the five-faced one, bindu, nada, Shakti and Siva, and calls them the lingam.
Both make Shakti with Siva the தாபரம்: 1755 of the installed lingam, 1772 of everything fixed, with no other.

1763 names the supreme Siva as உருவும் அருவும் உருவோடு அருவும், form, formless and form with formless. Thiruppugazh 736 opens on the same terms, காணொணாதது உருவோடு அருவது, and also names விந்துநாதம் among the Lord's forms. The two books share the Siddhanta scheme of the Lord's threefold manifestation, one applying it to Siva, the other to Murugan.

1763 ends with Sadasiva who gives தருவென, like the wishing tree; 1706 ends with the Supreme spread over the earth as கார்ஒன்று கற்பகம், the wishing tree with the generosity of the rain cloud. Both close a technical verse on the forms of the Lord with the image of the tree that grants every wish.

A near-repeat: 1764 says நாலான கீழது உருவம், the four above formless, and the one in the middle அருவுரு; 1810 says தலையான நான்கும் formless, Sadasiva அருவுரு, the lower four form, and the Lord all of them and yet one. Both give the nine forms by number, and 1810 adds that they are one Lord.

Both string the same titles: 1765 தேவர் பிரான், நால்வர் பிரான், நடுவுற்ற நந்தி; 1995 தேவர் பிரான், மூவர் பிரான், நால்வர் பிரான் நடுவாய் உரையாநிற்கும். The 'Lord of the four' in the middle is the teacher of the four sages in both, and 1995 makes explicit that he teaches (உரை) from the centre.

Both open with the world appearing in an inner object: 1769 கொழுந்தினைக் காணில் குவலயம் தோன்றும், 1794 குறிப்பினின் உள்ளே குவலயம் தோன்றும். In each the world is seen to arise from a point of focus within, and each goes on to the Lord standing in the mind (சிந்தையுளான், விகிர்தனும் நிற்கும்).

A near-repeat of the same verse: 492 reads சத்தி சிவன்விளை யாட்டால் உயிராக்கி ... சித்தம் புகுந்து சிவமயம் ஆக்குமே, 1771 சத்தி சிவன்விளை யாட்டாம் உயிராகி ... சித்தம் புகுந்து சிவம்அகம் ஆக்குமே. Both say the play of Shakti and Siva makes souls, yokes them in the two mayas, and ends by making the mind Siva; the variant endings (சிவமயம், சிவம்அகம்) give the same sense.
1773 says the Lord is too vast to be walked round; 1774 answers that water, flowers and his name, with knowing, are the way to circle him.

A near-repeat: 1773 and 2836 both list sea, water, wind and fire and end நீண்டகன்றானை வரைத்து (வரைந்து) வலம்செயு மாறுஅறி யேனே, I do not know how to bound him and walk round him. 2836 adds ஆகாசம் and நிலத்திடை வானிடை; the claim is the same, that a Lord who is the elements has no outside to circle.

1774 gives the one way to 'circle' the boundless Lord: bearing water and flowers and uttering his name (உரைத்து அவன் நாமம்). 1831 says worship, the gods and the sea are all his, and பேராயிரமும் பிரான்திரு நாமமும் are a way that never sates. Both put the name at the centre of worship of a Lord who cannot be bounded.

Kural 6 promises long life to those who keep the path of the one who quenched the five senses (பொறிவாயில் ஐந்தவித்தான்). In 1775 the devotee worships the feet and the First Lord gives grace so that வென்றுஐம் புலமும் மிகக்கிடந்து, the five senses lie conquered. The Kural credits the Lord with the quenching and asks the devotee to follow; Tirumular has the Lord's grace do the quenching in the devotee.

Both name the same nine: அயன், மால், உருத்திரன், மகேசன், ஐம்முகன், விந்து, நாதம், சத்தி, சிவன். 1731 says Sadasiva is what is common to them all (சாதாரணமாம் சதாசிவம்); 1776 says the lingam that takes these forms is பராநந்தி. Both make the nine one, naming the one differently.

1807 lists the nine forms from சிவமொடு சத்தி down to the lotus-born (பதுமத்தோன்) and says he dances as these nine (நவம்அவை யாகி நடிப்பவன்). 1776 lists the same nine from Brahma up and calls their lingam பராநந்தி. The order is reversed but the claim, one Lord in nine forms, is the same.

Both describe going through the red flame: 1777 செஞ்சுடர் ஊடுசென்று, 2719 செஞ்சுடர் மண்டலத்து ஊடுசென்று அப்புறம். 1777 ends in பரகதி through restraint of breath; 2719 ends in a state where the Lord never leaves the heart, reached through the five letters. The shared phrase marks one inner passage reached by breath in one verse and by mantra in the other.
Both describe the same rite: taking body, wealth and life, setting the feet and cutting the clinging; 1783 adds the power of grace and jnana and the guru becoming one with the disciple.
In 1594 the guru takes hold of the soul's three forms and takes the disciple to save him; 1784 makes the same taking of life, wealth and body, and adds that what he took was his own gift.
Both make the guru's hand on the disciple the moment of release: in 1590 the red guru places his hand on the head; in 1778 he places hand and feet and shows the way out of birth.
Both call a failure of understanding ghostly: the Kural's man who denies what the world holds to be is counted a demon, Tirumular's who don't know how body, breath and soul join are like ghosts.
Both make true knowing the end of suffering: the Kural's one who knows the support and lives so that clinging ends is not touched by the pains, Tirumular's who have awareness have no suffering.
Both describe the union by the image of flesh, or body, and the life within it, and both deny any 'I' and 'you' apart.

1778 describes Nandi's initiation: taking body, wealth and life, looking, placing his hand, setting his feet (அடிவைத்து) and cutting off birth. Thiruppugazh 1219 asks Murugan to drive off the twofold மலம் with சிவ வொளி, set இணைதாள் on his head, and grant him the place of a teacher (உபதேசிகப் பதம்). Arunagiri asks for the very initiation by the feet that Tirumular says Nandi gave.

1779 says the supreme guru took life, body and breath and saved me (உய்யக் கொண்டானே); 1594 says the guru took the soul's three forms (உயிர்முச் சொரூபமுங் கைக்கொண்டு) and saved me there (குய்யக்கொண் டானே). Both describe initiation as the guru taking possession of the disciple's whole being in order to save him.

1780 places what the teacher told him to think on உச்சிக்கும் கீழது உள்நாக்கு மேலது, below the crown and above the uvula, with the mouth closed. 599 says the ancient Being shows அண்ணாக்கின் உள்ளே அகண்ட ஒளி, an unbroken light within the palate. 599 names what is found at the place 1780 only locates.

1781 says the guru swept him clean and drew out all the dirt within (உள்ளமர் மாசெலாம் வாங்கி); 113 says the guru set his feet on his head, melted him and cut away the verdigris (களிம்பறுத்தான்). Both describe the guru's work as cleaning an impurity lodged inside, with different images, dirt and tarnish on metal.

1781 uses a merchant's image: the guru exchanged himself and me on level scales (தட்டொக்க மாறினன் தன்னையும் என்னையும்) and the trade went well. 1784 takes up the same exchange and says that since what he took (கொண்டான்) was his own gift, nothing can be said to have been taken. 1784 turns 1781's bargain into a gift that was never a trade.

2211 says the Lord fashioned the bonds, the five malas and the ஆறாறு தத்துவ பேதம் and set the instruments மலம்அறு மாறே, so that the malas may be cut. 1787 describes souls wandering through the body, the states and ஆறாறு, and thanks Nandi who gave them pure grace. 2211 gives the purpose of the thirty-six; 1787 is the soul that has passed through them and received the grace.

1788 says that on nearing him there is no difference such as நானென நீயென, I and you; 1706 says that when one sees without தான்என்றும் நான்என்றும் the Supreme stands everywhere. Both make the vanishing of the 'I' against 'he' or 'you' the mark of reaching the Lord.

1011 says that when the self becomes He and He the self, அறிவன் சிவமாக, the knower becomes Siva. 1789 pushes further: அவனை அறியில் அறிவானும் இல்லை, if one knows him there is no knower left, and he and he become this one. 1011 keeps a knower who becomes Siva; 1789 dissolves the knower itself.

1790 has the Lord standing 'I am this' (நானிது தானென) and pouring like the great cloud of the sky (வானிரு மாமுகில் போல்); 1706 has the Supreme beyond தான் and நான் standing as கார்ஒன்று கற்பகம், a wishing tree generous as a rain cloud. Both join the loss of the I-he distinction to the image of the Lord as a cloud that pours.
Both name the Lord அறவாழி அந்தணன். In the Kural only those who reach his feet cross the other seas; in Tirumular he himself gives the way of no birth and comes into the heart as kin.
Both give the Lord the five acts. 1927 says it of the Supreme as seed and root of cause and effect; 1809 says it with தானே in every line, adding that he also grants release.
1807 lists the nine forms he dances as; 1810 sorts them into four formless, Sadasiva as form-formless, and four with form, while keeping him one.
Both make bindu the source that becomes Mahamaya and all the worlds; 1813 adds the gods, mantras and Veda to what ripens from it.

1792 says அருளது ஆவது அறமும் தவமும், what grace is, is virtue and austerity. 258 says the two ways that end weariness are தவம் and அறம், which the Lord of unfailing renown makes fruitful (விளைக்கும்). Both place virtue and austerity inside the Lord's grace rather than as the soul's own achievement.

1793 says Nandi is hard to see (காண்டற்கு அரியன்) and far off to those who would touch or approach him (தீண்டற்கும் சார்தற்கும் சேயன்). Thiruppugazh 1050 opens with Murugan who cannot be touched or seen directly: தொட அடாது நேராக வடிவு காண வாராது. Both deny touch and sight as ways to the Lord; 1793 adds that the darkness ends when the heart lies longing within.

2581 says that unless the Knower dwelling there makes us know (அறிவான் இருந்தங்கு அறிவிக்கின் அல்லால்), we do not know what he knows. 1795 says ages went by in not discerning, and the Lord, who knows, comes near and knows (சார்ந்தறிவான்). Both deny that the soul knows on its own; 1795 adds the long time lost before he draws near.

1796 says that when ஊனே உருகி the flesh melts and one perceives awareness, the Lord is தேனே யனையன், like honey. 325 says in the samadhi where சித்தம் உருக்கி the mind melts and becomes Siva, one drinks the சுத்த மது, pure honey of Siva's bliss. Both join melting to honey as the taste of union.

1798 says people do not consider grace's subtlety in the five acts (அருள்ஐங் கருமத்து அதிசூக்கம்). 2062 says the insentient world is அத்தன் அருளின் விளையாட்டிடம் and that cleansing the soul of mala is the way of his ஐங்கருமம். Both make the five acts the work of grace rather than of bare power.

2016 asks what can be done with cows grazing in the field (கொல்லையின் மேயும் பசுக்கள்) unless they are led across the boundary and joined to the Lord's feet (இறைவன் அடிகூட்டி). 1799 says grace lets desire in through the senses (பொறிவழி யாசை), turns it into knowledge and gives அடியருள். 2016 states the need; 1799 describes how grace uses the senses themselves to lead the soul to the feet.

A near-repeat: lines 3 and 4 are almost the same, அருளான ஆனந்தத்து ஆரமுது ஊட்டி அருளால் என்நந்தி அகம் (அதும்) புகுந்தானே. 1800 sets birth, growth and decay inside grace; 1801 sets bathing in the sea of nectar and joining to the feet inside it. Each opens the same refrain with a different course of grace.

Kural 10 has a பிறவிப் பெருங்கடல், a great sea of births, which only those who reach the Lord's feet can swim. 1801 has the Lord bathe him in அமுதப் பெருங்கடல், a great sea of nectar, and join him to his feet (அடிபுணைந்து, which can also read as the feet becoming a raft, புணை). The same great sea and the same feet appear, but in Tirumular the sea is nectar to bathe in, not births to cross.

432 says the Lord who made birth for joy also shut it into the suffering of the bond (துன்பஞ்செய் பாசத் துயருள் அடைத்தனன்). 1802 calls that same act grace: பாசத்தில் இட்டது அருள், it was grace that put the soul into bonds, and grace that loosens love of them and gives release. 1802 gives the reason 432 leaves unsaid: binding too is the Lord's grace.

Both end in the same phrase, கூசற்ற முத்தி, release without shame. 1574 has the true guru gather the bonds, bind them and pluck them out (பாசத்தைக் கூட்டியே கட்டிப் பறித்திட்டு) and join one to that release; 1802 has grace put the soul into bonds and lead it to the same release. The pair shows the guru of 1574 doing what 1802 attributes to grace.
